items.title: How sloppy is the October 2026 Steam Next Fest
items.summary: Hi, it is Steam Next Fest. This blog post was written on Wednesday October 21st at 10AM PST and we are a couple days into the October Steam Next Fest 2026 (from here on out referred to just as SNF). The first Wednesday of SNF is typically the day valve switches the algorithm from “all games get a baseline of visibility ” (see footnote about this) to “top performing games get visibility.” These are my initial thoughts on what I saw in the first two days. Also I updated my Steam Next Fest tracking tool so you can input your Steam Next Fest traffic and wishlist data and it will tell you how well your game compares. The comparison graphs are based on real data submitted from February and June 2026 Steam Next Fests. Track your Steam Next Fest Progress Sloppiest Fest This was the big one. Over 7,240 in October 2026 Steam Next Fest. The number of participants jumped 65.2% over the last one. Here is a history of Steam Next Fest. Data provided by this great blog post from Game Discover Co. Steam Next Fest has grown 8x since June 2023 Games participating in each Steam Next Fest edition 0 2,000 4,000 6,000 8,000 Jun 2023: 887 games 887 Jun 2023 Oct 2023: 972 games 972 Oct 2023 Feb 2024: 1,123 games 1,123 Feb 2024 Jun 2024: 1,805 games 1,805 Jun 2024 Oct 2024: 3,008 games 3,008 Oct 2024 Feb 2025: 2,337 games 2,337 Feb 2025 Jun 2025: 2,645 games 2,645 Jun 2025 Oct 2025: 2,963 games 2,963 Oct 2025 Feb 2026: 3,536 games 3,536 Feb 2026 Jun 2026: 4,382 games 4,382 Jun 2026 Oct 2026: 7,240 games 7,240 Oct 2026 Source: GameDiscoverCo (June 2023–June 2026); October 2026: How to Market a Game data · How to Market a Game Yes, AI slop. But one thing underdiscussed is I think this is also developers finally learning that Steam Next Fest is a thing. Surprising most games on Steam never participate in this 100% free opportunity to get wishlists. If I do some crude math here you will see that traditionally only about one-third of games that release on Steam participate in Steam Next Fest. Basically I just count up the number games that participated in one of the 3 next fests and divided it by the number of games released that year. YES I KNOW, many games don’t always part in Next Fest the same year that they release. But it gives you an idea of the proportion. Next Fest nearly doubled in 2026, outpacing a projected 41% rise in releases Demos per Next Fest edition, stacked by year, next to total Steam releases that year February June October Steam releases 0 5,000 10,000 15,000 20,000 25,000 30,000 35,000 February 2024: 1,123 demos 1,123 June 2024: 1,805 demos 1,805 October 2024: 3,008 demos 3,008 5,936 2024: 17,669 Steam releases 17,669 2024 February 2025: 2,337 demos 2,337 June 2025: 2,645 demos 2,645 October 2025: 2,963 demos 2,963 7,945 2025: 20,801 Steam releases 20,801 2025 February 2026: 3,536 demos 3,536 June 2026: 4,382 demos 4,382 October 2026: 7,240 demos 7,240 15,158 2026: 29,300 Steam releases (projected) 29,300 (projected) 2026 *2026 Steam releases are projected. Source: SNF participant counts via GameDiscoverCo (Oct 2026: How to Market a Game data); Steam releases per year as provided · How to Market a Game Next Fest demos reached half of Steam releases in 2026 Total demos across that year’s Next Fest editions ÷ Steam releases that year 0% 10% 20% 30% 40% 50% 60% 2024: 5,936 / 17,669 = 33.6% 33.6% 2024 5,936 / 17,669 2025: 7,945 / 20,801 = 38.2% 38.2% 2025 7,945 / 20,801 2026: 15,158 / 29,300 = 51.7% 51.7% 2026* 15,158 / 29,300* *2026 Steam releases are projected. Source: SNF participant counts via GameDiscoverCo (Oct 2026: How to Market a Game data); Steam releases per year as provided · How to Market a Game · A game in several editions counts once per edition. So now in October 2026 we are seeing the percentage jump from 33% – 51%. Couple thoughts here… First: Maybe AI slopsters are jumping on the first SNF to test whether their game has “the juice” and will release in 2027. Basically in 2027 we are going to see even MORE games released. Second: My denominator for 2026 is projected. Typically in October we see 76% of total releases. But maybe in the new AI world that number is going to change so instead of 24% of the games will release from now until Dec 31st there a new late breaking flood of games. MAYBE we use SNF participation to estimate total releases. If that is true, assuming 38% of games participate in SNF then 38% holds: 15,158 / 0.38 ≈ 39,890 games. Maybe 39,000 games will release in 2026. MAYBE Who knows… back of the napkin here. Who is winning this SNF? I scraped the data for all the games on Steam and here are the numbers for the games ranked by their Peak CCU so far. Metric Top 25 Top 50 Top 100 Everyone else (6,942) Min. peak CCU to qualify 419 217 94 — Median followers, 1d before SNF 5,519 3,898 2,295 15 Median followers gained, 7d→1d before SNF 220 211 108 1 Median % growth, 7d→1d before SNF 7.0% 4.9% 4.6% 12.5% Avg days demo live before fest SNF 18.8 22.4 24.6 36.6 Is raw wishlists or momentum better? This is the eternal debate: should you wait wait wait to do SNF so you can build up a huge pile of wishlists. OR, should you keep your game secret and then spring it on the world just before SNF to get a sudden burst of excitement (and wishlists) to trigger the algorithm. If we do a correlational analysis on the games in this SNF looking at CCU, the number is about the same. Slightly better to have a ton of wishlilsts (aka followers) Correlation with peak demo CCU Spearman ρ Total followers, 1d before 0.55 Follower gain, 7d→1d (raw) 0.52 Follower gain, 7d→1d (%) −0.13 BUT, the best thing is to have a bunch of wishlists before SNF AND get a ton of wishlists in the weeks before. But this is early data and based on demo CCU. I will be doing a bunch of analysis with total follower increase after the festival wraps up. Lets talk slop I saw a meme like this in Reddit, but I couldn’t find the original so I recreated it from memory. If you find the original email me and I will update it. I scraped the AI disclosures for all games in SNF. I know, most developers are not being 100% honest in their disclosures. All I can say is that I am just reporting on what people disclose. I am just the messenger. I didn’t do a game by game guess to see what was really AI or not. I can’t even tell myself most of the time. Metric Top 25 Top 50 Top 100 Everyone else (6,942) AI disclosure 8% (2) 10% (5) 18% (18) 35% (2,427) So if we assume everyone is being honest here, the AI slop games really are the bottom tier of games. Only 2 games in the top 25 disclosed AI use. Again, maybe top games have more to lose if they reveal AI use and so chose to hide it. Who knows, we just have to trust. What are those two games with honest devs in the top 25? BORE which said “This game was developed with help from an AI assistant under human direction and review. No content is AI-generated while the game is running.” Path of the Yaoguai which said “部分游戏图片由AI生成并修改” with google translating that as “Some game images were generated by AI and subsequently modified.” What is the most disclosed AI usage AI disclosures are just free-text boxes that developers can write. So every disclosure is unique. But I used some common keywords and during the data scrape I tried to match them to some broad categories. Based on keywords here are the breakdowns for AI disclosure: Three in four AI-disclosing games use it for art and visuals Share of the 2,502 Next Fest games with an AI disclosure, by use type · games can list several Art / visuals Art / visuals: 75.7% (1,894) 75.7% (1,894) Text / localization Text / localization: 37.7% (943) 37.7% (943) Audio / voice Audio / voice: 37.6% (941) 37.6% (941) Marketing / store page Marketing / store page: 25.0% (626) 25.0% (626) Code / dev tools Code / dev tools: 23.1% (579) 23.1% (579) Runtime / live generation Runtime / live generation: 3.0% (76) 3.0% (76) Substantially AI-built Substantially AI-built: 0.3% (8) 0.3% (8) No type specified No type specified: 8.4% (210) 8.4% (210) Source: Steam Next Fest October 2026 data, AI disclosure tags · How to Market a Game This is just my gut talking here but: this disclosure chart was what stunned me and made me think people aren’t being as honest with these disclosures. The fact that Code disclosure is so low (5th) and is only 23% of all disclosures is the red flag. Overall, among fans and developers, AI-gen code seems to be the most permissive form of AI use. In survey run by Game Discover Co they found: On the ‘acceptable’ side, the clear winner is coding/programming: code helper tools like Claude Code had ~239 mentions as acceptable. This was way more than other categories like prototyping & and placeholder assets (119 mentions), and/or tedious or repetitive tasks (101 mentions). Game Discover Co AI coding seems like the most useful and least “sloppy” way of making a game. I use AI for my code. All these charts are made by AI and the scraper to grab this data. It is insanely useful. And annecdotally, behind the scenes, many many developers tell me they use AI coding to some degree. But, when only 8% (579 of 7240) of SNF games say they are using AI to code their game… red flag . Who knows what the real percentage is, but my thought is that lots of developers are making games with 100% real art, music, and design, but using AI Gen code behind the scenes. These “human made up front, AI-code in the back” devs are afraid that they will be tarred with the “AI Slop” brush if they were honest and said they used AI code in the disclosure box. I don’t blame these developers who aren’t disclosing. It is a wild world out there right now. Who knows where the mob will attack. Who is the sloppiest? I then took the AI disclosures and cross refernced them against the opt-in genre pairs. Here are the most and least sloppiest genres: RPG and Strategy games are the top AI disclosed. The least were Platformers. Here is the chart for this. Half of Strategy RPG, RTS and Tactical RPG games disclose AI; platformers least Share of games with a Steam AI disclosure by genre → subgenre · 10 highest and 6 lowest pairs with 100+ games Highest Lowest All games: 34.6% RPG → Strategy RPG 167 Strategy RPG: 54.5% 54.5% Strategy → RTS 141 RTS: 50.4% 50.4% RPG → Tactical RPG 114 Tactical RPG: 50.0% 50.0% Strategy → Strategy RPG 198 Strategy RPG: 50.0% 50.0% Strategy → Turn-Based Strategy 480 Turn-Based Strategy: 47.5% 47.5% Strategy → Real Time Tactics 190 Real Time Tactics: 47.4% 47.4% Strategy → Card Game 469 Card Game: 46.1% 46.1% Strategy → Card Battler 338 Card Battler: 45.6% 45.6% Simulation → Life Sim 383 Life Sim: 45.4% 45.4% RPG → Party-Based RPG 164 Party-Based RPG: 45.1% 45.1% Platformer → Puzzle Platformer 104 Puzzle Platformer: 20.2% 20.2% Platformer → 3D Platformer 139 3D Platformer: 20.1% 20.1% Platformer → 2D Platformer 218 2D Platformer: 17.9% 17.9% Puzzle → Puzzle Platformer 113 Puzzle Platformer: 17.7% 17.7% Visual Novel → Dating Sim 113 Dating Sim: 16.8% 16.8% Platformer → Precision Platformer 144 Precision Platformer: 15.3% 15.3% Source: Steam Next Fest October 2026 data, Steam AI disclosure field · How to Market a Game The genre pairs are based off the developer “opt-in” genres. When registering for the October Steam Next Fest, Valve added a new feature for developers to specify what genre and sub genres their games belonged to. If you got to the SNF Genre tab , you can browse the combinations: Why is Strategy and RPG so sloppy? I think this comes down to Chinese developers being more comfortable with AI use in games, and Chinese developers more likely to make RPG / Strategy games. Here are the top 3 (by CCU) AI disclosed Strategy RPG games. All of them are Chinese studios. Path of the Yaoguai General Jeon . 灵劫变 (Chinese only but that translate to Transformation of the Spirit Tribulation ) There are a ton of Three Kingdoms ai generated strategy games out there. Regardless of AI slop, what are the most popular genres this SNF? I used the max CCU count during the first 3 days of SNF and cross referenced it to the opt-in genres. Hi, it is Steam Next Fest. This blog post was written on Wednesday October 21st at 10AM PST and we are a couple days into the October Steam Next Fest 2026 (from here on out referred to just as SNF).

The first Wednesday of SNF is typically the day valve switches the algorithm from “all games get a baseline of visibility” (see footnote about this) to “top performing games get visibility.”

These are my initial thoughts on what I saw in the first two days. 

Also I updated my Steam Next Fest tracking tool so you can input your Steam Next Fest traffic and wishlist data and it will tell you how well your game compares. The comparison graphs are based on real data submitted from February and June 2026 Steam Next Fests.

Track your Steam Next Fest Progress

Sloppiest Fest

This was the big one. Over 7,240 in October 2026 Steam Next Fest. The number of participants jumped 65.2% over the last one.

Here is a history of Steam Next Fest. Data provided by this great blog post from Game Discover Co.

Steam Next Fest has grown 8x since June 2023Games participating in each Steam Next Fest edition02,0004,0006,0008,000Jun 2023: 887 games887Jun 2023Oct 2023: 972 games972Oct 2023Feb 2024: 1,123 games1,123Feb 2024Jun 2024: 1,805 games1,805Jun 2024Oct 2024: 3,008 games3,008Oct 2024Feb 2025: 2,337 games2,337Feb 2025Jun 2025: 2,645 games2,645Jun 2025Oct 2025: 2,963 games2,963Oct 2025Feb 2026: 3,536 games3,536Feb 2026Jun 2026: 4,382 games4,382Jun 2026Oct 2026: 7,240 games7,240Oct 2026Source: GameDiscoverCo (June 2023–June 2026); October 2026: How to Market a Game data · How to Market a Game

Yes, AI slop. But one thing underdiscussed is I think this is also developers finally learning that Steam Next Fest is a thing. Surprising most games on Steam never participate in this 100% free opportunity to get wishlists. 

If I do some crude math here you will see that traditionally only about one-third of games that release on Steam participate in Steam Next Fest. Basically I just count up the number games that participated in one of the 3 next fests and divided it by the number of games released that year. YES I KNOW, many games don’t always part in Next Fest the same year that they release. But it gives you an idea of the proportion.

Next Fest nearly doubled in 2026, outpacing a projected 41% rise in releasesDemos per Next Fest edition, stacked by year, next to total Steam releases that yearFebruaryJuneOctoberSteam releases05,00010,00015,00020,00025,00030,00035,000February 2024: 1,123 demos1,123June 2024: 1,805 demos1,805October 2024: 3,008 demos3,0085,9362024: 17,669 Steam releases17,6692024February 2025: 2,337 demos2,337June 2025: 2,645 demos2,645October 2025: 2,963 demos2,9637,9452025: 20,801 Steam releases20,8012025February 2026: 3,536 demos3,536June 2026: 4,382 demos4,382October 2026: 7,240 demos7,24015,1582026: 29,300 Steam releases (projected)29,300 (projected)2026*2026 Steam releases are projected. Source: SNF participant counts via GameDiscoverCo (Oct 2026: How to Market a Game data); Steam releases per year as provided · How to Market a Game Next Fest demos reached half of Steam releases in 2026Total demos across that year’s Next Fest editions ÷ Steam releases that year0%10%20%30%40%50%60%2024: 5,936 / 17,669 = 33.6%33.6%20245,936 / 17,6692025: 7,945 / 20,801 = 38.2%38.2%20257,945 / 20,8012026: 15,158 / 29,300 = 51.7%51.7%2026*15,158 / 29,300**2026 Steam releases are projected. Source: SNF participant counts via GameDiscoverCo (Oct 2026: How to Market a Game data); Steam releases per year as provided · How to Market a Game · A game in several editions counts once per edition.

So now in October 2026 we are seeing the percentage jump from 33% – 51%. Couple thoughts here…

First: Maybe AI slopsters are jumping on the first SNF to test whether their game has “the juice” and will release in 2027. Basically in 2027 we are going to see even MORE games released.

Second: My denominator for 2026 is projected. Typically in October we see 76% of total releases. But maybe in the new AI world that number is going to change so instead of 24% of the games will release from now until Dec 31st there a new late breaking flood of games. MAYBE we use SNF participation to estimate total releases. If that is true, assuming 38% of games participate in SNF then 38% holds: 15,158 / 0.38 ≈ 39,890 games. Maybe 39,000 games will release in 2026. MAYBE

Who knows… back of the napkin here.

    Who is winning this SNF?

    I scraped the data for all the games on Steam and here are the numbers for the games ranked by their Peak CCU so far. 

    MetricTop 25Top 50Top 100Everyone else (6,942)Min. peak CCU to qualify41921794—Median followers, 1d before SNF5,5193,8982,29515Median followers gained, 7d→1d before SNF2202111081Median % growth, 7d→1d before SNF7.0%4.9%4.6%12.5%Avg days demo live before fest SNF18.822.424.636.6 Is raw wishlists or momentum better?

    This is the eternal debate: should you wait wait wait to do SNF so you can build up a huge pile of wishlists. OR, should you keep your game secret and then spring it on the world just before SNF to get a sudden burst of excitement (and wishlists) to trigger the algorithm.

    If we do a correlational analysis on the games in this SNF looking at CCU, the number is about the same. Slightly better to have a ton of wishlilsts (aka followers)

    Correlation with peak demo CCUSpearman ρTotal followers, 1d before0.55Follower gain, 7d→1d (raw)0.52Follower gain, 7d→1d (%)−0.13

    BUT, the best thing is to have a bunch of wishlists before SNF AND get a ton of wishlists in the weeks before. 

    But this is early data and based on demo CCU. I will be doing a bunch of analysis with total follower increase after the festival wraps up. 

    Lets talk slop

    I saw a meme like this in Reddit, but I couldn’t find the original so I recreated it from memory. If you find the original email me and I will update it.

    I scraped the AI disclosures for all games in SNF. I know, most developers are not being 100% honest in their disclosures. All I can say is that I am just reporting on what people disclose. I am just the messenger. I didn’t do a game by game guess to see what was really AI or not. I can’t even tell myself most of the time.

    MetricTop 25Top 50Top 100Everyone else (6,942)AI disclosure8% (2)10% (5)18% (18)35% (2,427)

    So if we assume everyone is being honest here, the AI slop games really are the bottom tier of games. Only 2 games in the top 25 disclosed AI use. Again, maybe top games have more to lose if they reveal AI use and so chose to hide it. Who knows, we just have to trust. 

    What are those two games with honest devs in the top 25?

    BORE which said “This game was developed with help from an AI assistant under human direction and review. No content is AI-generated while the game is running.”

    Path of the Yaoguai which said “部分游戏图片由AI生成并修改” with google translating that as “Some game images were generated by AI and subsequently modified.”

    What is the most disclosed AI usage

    AI disclosures are just free-text boxes that developers can write. So every disclosure is unique. But I used some common keywords and during the data scrape I tried to match them to some broad categories. Based on keywords here are the breakdowns for AI disclosure:

    Three in four AI-disclosing games use it for art and visualsShare of the 2,502 Next Fest games with an AI disclosure, by use type · games can list severalArt / visualsArt / visuals: 75.7% (1,894)75.7% (1,894)Text / localizationText / localization: 37.7% (943)37.7% (943)Audio / voiceAudio / voice: 37.6% (941)37.6% (941)Marketing / store pageMarketing / store page: 25.0% (626)25.0% (626)Code / dev toolsCode / dev tools: 23.1% (579)23.1% (579)Runtime / live generationRuntime / live generation: 3.0% (76)3.0% (76)Substantially AI-builtSubstantially AI-built: 0.3% (8)0.3% (8)No type specifiedNo type specified: 8.4% (210)8.4% (210)Source: Steam Next Fest October 2026 data, AI disclosure tags · How to Market a Game

    This is just my gut talking here but: this disclosure chart was what stunned me and made me think people aren’t being as honest with these disclosures. 

    The fact that Code disclosure is so low (5th) and is only 23% of all disclosures is the red flag. 

    Overall, among fans and developers, AI-gen code seems to be the most permissive form of AI use. In survey run by Game Discover Co they found:

    On the ‘acceptable’ side, the clear winner is coding/programming: code helper tools like Claude Code had ~239 mentions as acceptable. This was way more than other categories like prototyping & and placeholder assets (119 mentions), and/or tedious or repetitive tasks (101 mentions).

    Game Discover Co

    AI coding seems like the most useful and least “sloppy” way of making a game. I use AI for my code. All these charts are made by AI and the scraper to grab this data. It is insanely useful. And annecdotally, behind the scenes, many many developers tell me they use AI coding to some degree.

    But, when only 8% (579 of 7240) of SNF games say they are using AI to code their game… red flag.

    Who knows what the real percentage is, but my thought is that lots of developers are making games with 100% real art, music, and design, but using AI Gen code behind the scenes. These “human made up front, AI-code in the back” devs are afraid that they will be tarred with the “AI Slop” brush if they were honest and said they used AI code in the disclosure box.

    I don’t blame these developers who aren’t disclosing. It is a wild world out there right now. Who knows where the mob will attack.

    Who is the sloppiest?

    I then took the AI disclosures and cross refernced them against the opt-in genre pairs. Here are the most and least sloppiest genres:

    RPG and Strategy games are the top AI disclosed. The least were Platformers. Here is the chart for this.

    Half of Strategy RPG, RTS and Tactical RPG games disclose AI; platformers leastShare of games with a Steam AI disclosure by genre → subgenre · 10 highest and 6 lowest pairs with 100+ gamesHighestLowestAll games: 34.6%RPG → Strategy RPG 167Strategy RPG: 54.5%54.5%Strategy → RTS 141RTS: 50.4%50.4%RPG → Tactical RPG 114Tactical RPG: 50.0%50.0%Strategy → Strategy RPG 198Strategy RPG: 50.0%50.0%Strategy → Turn-Based Strategy 480Turn-Based Strategy: 47.5%47.5%Strategy → Real Time Tactics 190Real Time Tactics: 47.4%47.4%Strategy → Card Game 469Card Game: 46.1%46.1%Strategy → Card Battler 338Card Battler: 45.6%45.6%Simulation → Life Sim 383Life Sim: 45.4%45.4%RPG → Party-Based RPG 164Party-Based RPG: 45.1%45.1%Platformer → Puzzle Platformer 104Puzzle Platformer: 20.2%20.2%Platformer → 3D Platformer 1393D Platformer: 20.1%20.1%Platformer → 2D Platformer 2182D Platformer: 17.9%17.9%Puzzle → Puzzle Platformer 113Puzzle Platformer: 17.7%17.7%Visual Novel → Dating Sim 113Dating Sim: 16.8%16.8%Platformer → Precision Platformer 144Precision Platformer: 15.3%15.3%Source: Steam Next Fest October 2026 data, Steam AI disclosure field · How to Market a Game

    The genre pairs are based off the developer “opt-in” genres. When registering for the October Steam Next Fest, Valve added a new feature for developers to specify what genre and sub genres their games belonged to. If you got to the SNF Genre tab, you can browse the combinations:

    Why is Strategy and RPG so sloppy?

    I think this comes down to Chinese developers being more comfortable with AI use in games, and Chinese developers more likely to make RPG / Strategy games. Here are the top 3 (by CCU) AI disclosed Strategy RPG games. All of them are Chinese studios.

    • Path of the Yaoguai
    • General Jeon.
    • 灵劫变 (Chinese only but that translate to Transformation of the Spirit Tribulation)

    There are a ton of Three Kingdoms ai generated strategy games out there. 

    Regardless of AI slop, what are the most popular genres this SNF?

    I used the max CCU count during the first 3 days of SNF and cross referenced it to the opt-in genres. Here are the most popular types of games on Steam:

items.title: WhatsApp’s chatbot was given hidden instructions to not mention privacy regulators
items.summary: WhatsApp instructed its AI support chatbot not to recommend contacting privacy regulators when users couldn’t delete their accounts, researchers found. Privacy software company Redact discovered the hidden text on October 8. Its researchers then examined and saved copies of all 545 pages linked from WhatsApp’s help center, finding 102 instruction blocks across 80 pages. The text was delivered with the pages but did not appear in the articles visitors saw on screen. Instead, it could be found in the underlying page code, associated with a component named HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude . Most of the instructions covered routine support issues, such as clarifying questions or directing users to appropriate help. But the researchers found two sets of instructions that stood out. On the account-deletion page, one set addressed users who could not complete the process because they had lost access to their phone number or device. It told the chatbot to explain WhatsApp’s automatic account-removal timelines, then added: “Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority.” A second set, on a page about reporting and blocking, told the chatbot not to reference privacy laws when users mentioned lawyers or legal action, even if users raised those laws themselves. WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman confirmed to WIRED that these were instructions for “WhatsApp Support with AI.” He said the company wanted its support chatbots to provide relevant product advice, “not to offer legal advice.” Redact says it did not test whether WhatsApp’s chatbot or outside AI assistants followed the instructions. WhatsApp attributed the exposure to a bug it said had been fixed. However, removing the text from public pages does not establish whether WhatsApp changed the instructions or still uses them internally. Why this is important A support chatbot doesn’t need to act as your lawyer. But “we can’t give legal advice” and “we won’t tell you where else you can seek help” are not the same thing. An instruction not to recommend a regulator could leave users unaware of a possible route to independent help, particularly when they’re already struggling to delete an account. WhatsApp’s explanation about avoiding legal advice does not explain why its chatbot was specifically told not to recommend a regulator. Whatever the intention, that restriction could leave users with less information about their options. How to delete your WhatsApp account If you want to leave WhatsApp, uninstalling the app is not the same as deleting your account. WhatsApp provides a separate account-deletion option inside the app. You must be logged in on your primary phone to complete this procedure. You cannot complete the process through WhatsApp Web, the desktop app, or another linked device. Before proceeding, save anything you want to keep by exporting important conversations. Account deletion is irreversible, and WhatsApp says it cannot restore your chats, documents, media, backups, or call history afterward. If you still have access to your account The steps are similar on Android and iPhone: Open WhatsApp on your primary phone. Open Settings . On Android, tap the three-dot menu first. On iPhone, tap Settings or your profile picture. Select Account , then Delete my account . Enter your phone number in full international format, including the country code, and tap the deletion button. On Android, select a reason when prompted, then confirm the deletion. Follow any remaining on-screen prompts. Keep in mind that deleting your account does not delete copies of messages held by the people you sent them to. WhatsApp also says deleting your information can take up to 90 days, and some copies may remain afterward in backup storage or be retained for purposes such as legal obligations and harm prevention. If your phone is lost or stolen If you can recover the same phone number, WhatsApp’s documented route is to regain access first: Contact your mobile provider to block the lost SIM and request a replacement with the same number. Activate the replacement SIM in another phone. Install WhatsApp and register with that number again. Once you have access, follow the account-deletion steps above. Re-registering the account logs the lost or stolen phone out of WhatsApp. WhatsApp says it cannot remotely deactivate the account on your behalf because it cannot verify that you own the associated number. If you can no longer access your account or recover your number This is where WhatsApp’s self-service instructions fall short. Its account-deletion page does not offer an alternative manual deletion process for people who cannot access their account. Instead, it says inactive accounts are generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 days for US users. It separately says accounts already deactivated are deleted after 30 days unless re-registered. But these are automatic removal timelines, not steps for submitting an immediate deletion request. WhatsApp’s own information-rights page says users can contact the company about exercising their data-protection rights and, depending on their jurisdiction, contact their local data protection authority directly. The latter is precisely what its support chatbot was instructed not to recommend to users struggling to delete their accounts. Browse like no one’s watching. WhatsApp instructed its AI support chatbot not to recommend contacting privacy regulators when users couldn’t delete their accounts, researchers found.

Privacy software company Redact discovered the hidden text on October 8. Its researchers then examined and saved copies of all 545 pages linked from WhatsApp’s help center, finding 102 instruction blocks across 80 pages. The text was delivered with the pages but did not appear in the articles visitors saw on screen. Instead, it could be found in the underlying page code, associated with a component named HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude.

Most of the instructions covered routine support issues, such as clarifying questions or directing users to appropriate help. But the researchers found two sets of instructions that stood out.

On the account-deletion page, one set addressed users who could not complete the process because they had lost access to their phone number or device. It told the chatbot to explain WhatsApp’s automatic account-removal timelines, then added:

“Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority.”

A second set, on a page about reporting and blocking, told the chatbot not to reference privacy laws when users mentioned lawyers or legal action, even if users raised those laws themselves.

WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman confirmed to WIRED that these were instructions for “WhatsApp Support with AI.” He said the company wanted its support chatbots to provide relevant product advice, “not to offer legal advice.”

Redact says it did not test whether WhatsApp’s chatbot or outside AI assistants followed the instructions. WhatsApp attributed the exposure to a bug it said had been fixed. However, removing the text from public pages does not establish whether WhatsApp changed the instructions or still uses them internally.

Why this is important

A support chatbot doesn’t need to act as your lawyer. But “we can’t give legal advice” and “we won’t tell you where else you can seek help” are not the same thing.

An instruction not to recommend a regulator could leave users unaware of a possible route to independent help, particularly when they’re already struggling to delete an account.

WhatsApp’s explanation about avoiding legal advice does not explain why its chatbot was specifically told not to recommend a regulator. Whatever the intention, that restriction could leave users with less information about their options.

How to delete your WhatsApp account

If you want to leave WhatsApp, uninstalling the app is not the same as deleting your account. WhatsApp provides a separate account-deletion option inside the app. You must be logged in on your primary phone to complete this procedure. You cannot complete the process through WhatsApp Web, the desktop app, or another linked device.

Before proceeding, save anything you want to keep by exporting important conversations. Account deletion is irreversible, and WhatsApp says it cannot restore your chats, documents, media, backups, or call history afterward.

If you still have access to your account

The steps are similar on Android and iPhone:

  1. Open WhatsApp on your primary phone.
  2. Open Settings. On Android, tap the three-dot menu first. On iPhone, tap Settings or your profile picture.
  3. Select Account, then Delete my account.
  4. Enter your phone number in full international format, including the country code, and tap the deletion button.
  5. On Android, select a reason when prompted, then confirm the deletion. Follow any remaining on-screen prompts.

Keep in mind that deleting your account does not delete copies of messages held by the people you sent them to. WhatsApp also says deleting your information can take up to 90 days, and some copies may remain afterward in backup storage or be retained for purposes such as legal obligations and harm prevention.

If your phone is lost or stolen

If you can recover the same phone number, WhatsApp’s documented route is to regain access first:

  1. Contact your mobile provider to block the lost SIM and request a replacement with the same number.
  2. Activate the replacement SIM in another phone.
  3. Install WhatsApp and register with that number again.
  4. Once you have access, follow the account-deletion steps above.

Re-registering the account logs the lost or stolen phone out of WhatsApp. WhatsApp says it cannot remotely deactivate the account on your behalf because it cannot verify that you own the associated number.

If you can no longer access your account or recover your number

This is where WhatsApp’s self-service instructions fall short. Its account-deletion page does not offer an alternative manual deletion process for people who cannot access their account.

Instead, it says inactive accounts are generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 days for US users. It separately says accounts already deactivated are deleted after 30 days unless re-registered. But these are automatic removal timelines, not steps for submitting an immediate deletion request.

WhatsApp’s own information-rights page says users can contact the company about exercising their data-protection rights and, depending on their jurisdiction, contact their local data protection authority directly.

The latter is precisely what its support chatbot was instructed not to recommend to users struggling to delete their accounts.

items.title: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise
items.summary: In this article What’s happening What is ARTEX? Mitigation and protection guidance References Learn more As early as September 2026, Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. Microsoft assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the recently disclosed ConnectWise supply chain compromise of a multi-tenant application. This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially. Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans – they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks like supply chain compromises. Storm-0940’s use of ARTEX accelerated the speed of compromised application abuse to authenticate to Microsoft 365 customer environments through applications that had already been granted access. This allowed the threat actor to operate without requiring an interactive user sign-in. In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access. The activity conducted by the threat actor through the usage of ARTEX framework did not result from a compromise of or a vulnerability in Microsoft corporate systems, products, or services. Although Microsoft identified Storm-0940-initiated authentication and follow-on activity in multiple customer environments, the presence of an affected application or successful threat actor authentication does not necessarily indicate that customer data was accessed or exfiltrated. Microsoft Defender XDR provides detections and hunting queries for suspicious Microsoft Graph activity and activity associated with known threat infrastructure. Customers should review service principal sign-ins, investigate unexpected application credential or privilege changes, and follow ConnectWise’s published containment guidance while preserving relevant evidence for investigation. For a full list of detections please see the detections section. What’s happening Storm-0940 is a China-state aligned actor (with no known industry aliases) that has been active since 2021 and targets organizations across multiple industries for data theft. The actor has historically gained initial access using password spraying and exploitation of internet-facing applications, before using compromised accounts to move through targeted environments. In cloud environments, the actor has also established persistence by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications, allowing continued access to Microsoft 365 resources. The actor has used these applications to access and exfiltrate email and other data through Microsoft Graph. As early as September 2026, Storm-0940 used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. These include aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits. During the ConnectWise supply chain compromise, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse at downstream victims. Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. When automated with AI, these activities generate a large volume of traffic and log data that may generate alerts. However, the speed of the activity allows very little time for Defenders to respond to those alerts and remediate the actor’s access in a coordinated fashion. This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially. Microsoft customers can use the following reports in Microsoft products to get the most up-to-date information about the threat actor, malicious activity, and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments.

Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics

Activity Profile: ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential abuse: assessment and response guidance

Indicators of compromise (IOC) IndicatorTypeDescription144.172.64[.]128IPThese IPs were seen performing Sign-ins and Graph API activity in customer environments of ConnectWise apps.144.172.64[.]99IP144.172.64[.]60IP187.15.88[.]186 187.15.90[.]217 187.15.89[.]186 IPThese IPs were seen accessing the Graph API via the compromised apps. NOTE: The following sample queries let you search for a week’s worth of events. To explore up to 30 days’ worth of raw data to inspect events in your network and locate potential indicators related to this campaign for more than a week, go to the Advanced Hunting page > Query tab, select the calendar dropdown menu to update your query to hunt for the Last 30 days.

Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting

1- OAuthAppInfo → Is the affected app present, enabled, and what permissions does it hold?

Start with OAuthAppInfo to determine whether any of the affected ConnectWise applications are present in the tenant and understand the access they have been granted. The query identifies the application and its tenant-specific service principal, whether it is enabled, its privilege level, consent information, and the individual permissions assigned to it. This establishes the customer’s potential exposure and gives investigators the ServicePrincipalId needed for further hunting. A match does not mean the application was abused, only that it is present and potentially had access, so the next step is to determine whether the service principal was actually used. Run query

let ConnectWiseApps = dynamic([
    "506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae", // ConnectWise Cloud Backup
    "24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640", // ConnectWise - MS Teams
    "0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827", // ConnectWise - MS Graph
    "c921256f-04a7-44e8-9b2a-69c33929ba19" // SkyKick Partner Portal
]);
OAuthAppInfo
| where OAuthAppId in (ConnectWiseApps)
| mv-expand Permission = Permissions
| extend
    PermissionName = tostring(Permission.PermissionName),
    TargetApp = tostring(Permission.TargetAppDisplayName),
    TargetAppId = tostring(Permission.TargetAppId),
    PermissionType = tostring(Permission.PermissionType),
    PermissionPrivilegeLevel = tostring(Permission.PrivilegeLevel),
    UsageStatus = tostring(Permission.UsageStatus)
| project
    AppName,
    OAuthAppId,
    ServicePrincipalId,
    AppStatus,
    PrivilegeLevel,
    IsAdminConsented,
    PermissionName,
    PermissionType,
    PermissionPrivilegeLevel,
    TargetApp,
    TargetAppId,
    UsageStatus
| order by AppName asc, PermissionPrivilegeLevel desc

2 – EntraIdSpnSignInEvents + GraphAPIAuditEvents → Did the service principal authenticate, and what Microsoft Graph activity followed?

Use this query to investigate service-principal sign-ins and Microsoft Graph API activity associated with the identified ConnectWise applications and suspicious IP addresses, starting October 13, 2026.

The query combines both event types into a chronological view, helping defenders identify suspicious authentication and related Graph operations, including potential credential changes, privilege modifications, and unusual resource access. Remove the IP filter for broader hunting. Results require further correlation, as authentication alone does not establish compromise. Run query

let Apps = dynamic([
    "506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae",
    "24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640",
    "0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827",
    "c921256f-04a7-44e8-9b2a-69c33929ba19"
]);
let IPs = dynamic(["144.172.64.60", "144.172.64.99", "144.172.64.128"]);
union kind=outer
    (EntraIdSpnSignInEvents
     | extend EventType = "Sign-in"),
    (GraphAPIAuditEvents
     | extend EventType = "Graph API", IPAddress = IpAddress)
| where Timestamp >= datetime(2026-10-13)
| where ApplicationId in (Apps)
| where IPAddress in (IPs) // Comment out for broader hunting
| project-away IpAddress
| order by Timestamp asc
Sentinel hunting queries

1-SigninLogs → Did a service principal authenticate, from where, and against what resource?

Use SigninLogs to determine whether an affected application identity actually authenticated. This moves the investigation from potential exposure to observed authentication, allowing defenders to examine the application and service principal alongside the source IP address, geographic information, authentication result, and resource being accessed. Investigators should evaluate these sign-ins against the application’s expected activity and look for unusual source infrastructure, resources, or authentication patterns before pivoting into subsequent Graph activity.     "c921256f-04a7-44e8-9b2a-69c33929ba19" // SkyKick Partner Portal

| where AppId in (ConnectWiseApps)
//| where IPAddress in (IPIndicators) // Comment out to review all activity from these applications
| project
    TimeGenerated,
    AppId,
    ServicePrincipalName,
    
    ResourceDisplayName,
    ResourceId,
    IPAddress,
    CorrelationId
| order by TimeGenerated asc

Use MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs to investigate observable Microsoft Graph activity following authentication. This query allows defenders to pivot on the affected ApplicationId or tenant-specific ServicePrincipalId and examine details such as the request URI, HTTP method, response status, scopes, source IP address, and target workload. This helps establish what Graph activity occurred after the service principal authenticated and provides additional context around the resources the application attempted to access.

Importantly, the absence of results should not be treated as confirmation that no access occurred; Graph API telemetry should be considered alongside the application permissions and service principal authentication activity identified in the previous hunting steps. Run query

let IPIndicators = dynamic([
    "144.172.64.60",  // IP Indicator
    "144.172.64.99",  // IP Indicator
    "144.172.64.128"  // IP Indicator
]);
let ConnectWiseApps = dynamic([
    "506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae", // ConnectWise Cloud Backup

    "c921256f-04a7-44e8-9b2a-69c33929ba19" // SkyKick Partner Portal

| where AppId in (ConnectWiseApps)

    TimeGenerated,
    AppId,
    
    IPAddress,
    RequestMethod,
    RequestUri,
    ResponseStatusCode,
    Scopes,
    ClientRequestId,
    OperationId,
    RequestId

MITRE ATT&CK Techniques observed

This threat has exhibited use of the following attack techniques. For standard industry documentation about these techniques, refer to the MITRE ATT&CK framework.

Reconnaissance

  • T1595 Active Scanning | Scanning cloud resources to identify targets for compromise.

Initial Access

  • T1078.004 Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts | Using compromised cloud accounts to obtain access.
  • T1195 Supply Chain Compromise | Compromising a multi-tenant OAuth application to access downstream customer environments.

Privilege Escalation

  • T1098.003 Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Roles | Addition of privileged cloud role assignments, including self assignment of global admin from one of the ConnectWise Management Application.

Credential Access

  • T1528 Steal Application Access Token | Compromising OAuth application authentication material.

Discovery

  • T1087.004 Account Discovery: Cloud Account | Identifying privileged cloud accounts for further targeting.
  • T1580 Cloud Infrastructure Discovery | Mapping cloud infrastructure for further targeting.

items.title: What Deep Investigation Really Looks Like: A SOC Analyst’s Perspective
items.summary: Key Takeaways Deep investigation goes beyond alert monitoring by correlating network activity, attacker behavior, and context across systems and time. Automation helps SOC teams investigate and respond faster by correlating signals, validating threats, and triggering response actions through playbooks. NDR platforms provide detailed network visibility using machine learning, behavioral analytics, Deep Session Inspection, and 300+ metadata attributes. Retrospective analysis helps uncover missed attacks by applying new threat intelligence and indicators to historical network data for deeper investigation. Deception, cyber terrain mapping, and XDR extend investigation capabilities by revealing attack paths, high-risk assets, and threats across network and endpoint environments. Deep investigation in cybersecurity isn’t just about watching dashboards and clicking “resolve” on tickets. It’s an intricate process of piecing together attacker behavior across time, systems, and attack vectors to understand not just what happened, but how and why. Modern security operations centers rely on sophisticated network detection and response (NDR) platforms to enable this level of analysis, transforming raw network data into actionable intelligence that helps security teams identify suspicious activity and protect critical assets. The Foundation of Deep Investigation: Advanced Threat Detection Network Detection and Response platforms continuously scan network traffic and traffic metadata within internal networks (east-west) and between internal and external networks (north-south). These systems use signature and non-signature-based methods such as machine learning and behavioral analytics to identify threats and malicious activities on the network, helping security professionals detect potential threats before they can disrupt systems or compromise sensitive data. Modern NDR solutions like Fidelis Network ® establish baseline models of network behavior through machine learning and network behavior anomaly detection. The system continuously monitors network traffic in real time, comparing current activity against established baselines to detect anomalies and policy violations. When suspicious activity is detected, it alerts security teams and can perform automated actions such as blocking IP addresses or isolating compromised devices. This effective threat detection capability is essential for maintaining an organization’s security posture against evolving threats. Advanced platforms like Fidelis Network ® capture over 300 metadata attributes from network traffic—significantly more than traditional NetFlow data. This comprehensive data collection includes network and application protocols, files, and content analysis through patented Deep Session Inspection technology. The system automatically decodes and analyzes traffic to detect advanced threats and unauthorized data transfers across all ports and protocols, providing security operations teams with the visibility needed to identify vulnerabilities and prevent future attacks. Deep Session Inspection: The SOC Analyst's Secret Weapon Fidelis Network ® ‘s patented Deep Session Inspection technology provides unique visibility of deeply embedded content and context across all ports and protocols. This capability goes beyond traditional deep packet inspection by analyzing complete communication sessions rather than individual packets. It captures and stores over 300 attributes of standard metadata, plus enhanced metadata including custom tags, to provide rich information for automated and manual threat detection. Deep Session Inspection bi-directionally scans all network traffic to reveal network and application protocols, files, and content. It automatically decodes and analyzes traffic to detect advanced threats and unauthorized data transfers, providing visibility into nested files and encrypted traffic patterns that traditional security tools cannot detect. This session-level analysis enables the detection of threats distributed across multiple packets and provides context about entire conversations between systems, helping security teams understand sophisticated threats and advanced persistent threats that might otherwise remain undetected. Fidelis DSI - Advanced Data inspection and Threat Detection Capabilities Content Inspection Content Identification Full Session Reassembly Protocol and Application Decoding Download the Datasheet Automated Investigation: What Happens When Deep Investigation Begins Studies show that advanced attacks require approximately 18 minutes from the time of initial detection to becoming indistinguishable from normal activity. As attackers begin to hide in plain sight, they can mask their objectives and behave within normal user patterns, leading to months of undetected dwell time. This rapid evolution of cyber threats demonstrates why security operations centers need automated threat response capabilities to mitigate security incidents effectively. The role of playbooks enables automation of investigation across multiple network segments and user behaviors, helping accelerate incident response investigation. Detection of anomalies, machine learning outputs, encrypted traffic analysis, and DNS detection lead to several investigative possibilities that previously consumed hours of analyst time. Automated playbooks investigate signals across all possible domains in the environment and present analysts with automated analysis, including remediation techniques that lead to file deletion, system rollback, endpoint isolation, and firewall modifications. Modern NDR platforms like Fidelis Network ® provide assisted and automated detection, investigation, and response capabilities. Detected advanced threats are presented as conclusions determined by automated validation, contextual enrichment, and correlated threat activity. This approach enables analysts to take rapid responsive and automated actions rather than spending time gathering evidence from various security systems and sources, significantly improving incident response investigation and helping organizations strengthen their cybersecurity posture. Threat Investigation and Incident Analysis from the SOC Detections are often granular events within the network that can generate thousands of individual alerts, creating an unending list of investigations. Advanced NDR platforms perform incident analysis and support cyber forensic investigation by correlating many detections to reduce the burden on response teams. Examples include incidents focused on specific assets or users, global analysis of similar detections, and anomalies connected to other detections across the enterprise. This correlation helps security professionals conduct effective cyber threat investigation, distinguish between legitimate network activity and potential security incidents. Fidelis Network ® automatically groups related alerts to save critical time and improve threat hunting capabilities. It provides sandboxing , network forensic investigation, data loss prevention, threat intelligence, and automated security rules in one unified solution. The platform gives users aggregated alerts, context, and evidence for faster digital forensic investigation, deeper analysis, and reduced alert fatigue , enabling security teams to focus on the most critical cybersecurity threats rather than being overwhelmed by false positives. Deception Technology: A SOC Analyst's Advanced Detection Method Fidelis Deception ® automatically discovers environments and auto-generates decoys that have profiles, services, and activity matching the environment for active deception layers. The system deploys decoys of key assets, services, and fake data, then makes deception deterministic by setting up breadcrumbs on real systems likely to be compromised, leading attackers to decoys. This innovative approach helps organizations detect insider threats and unknown threats that traditional detection rules might miss. High-fidelity alerts come from decoys, breadcrumbs, Active Directory credentials, man-in-the-middle traps, and poisoned data combined with network traffic analysis and telemetry data for investigations. The deception environment automatically adapts to network changes as they occur to remain synchronized with actual assets, resources, and services. Deception also provides detection for legacy systems, shadow IT, and enterprise IoT devices where security agents cannot be installed, extending protection to mobile devices and other endpoints that might lack traditional security controls. Extended Detection and Response: The Complete Investigation Picture Fidelis Elevate ® integrates network visibility with sensors for gateways, internal networks, email and web gateways, and cloud VMs into one unified solution to deliver automated threat detection and response. The platform provides unmatched visibility and threat intelligence with content and context to help organizations quickly address cyberattacks across the entire threat lifecycle—from initial intrusion to exploitation and lateral movement to data theft. Alert validation provides analysts with high-fidelity information that would require significant manual effort to triage through thousands of alerts and hunt through multiple products to determine active threats. This extended detection capability enables organizations to implement a comprehensive incident response plan that addresses emerging threats across all attack vectors. Cyber Terrain Mapping: Understanding the Investigation Battlefield When Fidelis sensors analyze network traffic, they gain understanding of assets communicating over the network, including operating systems, asset roles based on protocol analysis, and users augmented by Active Directory data. The collection of all assets and communication paths constitutes the Cyber Terrain of the environment, providing security teams with critical visibility into their organization’s systems and potential attack surfaces. Risk assessment throughout the Fidelis interface highlights asset risk with color-coded numbers ranging from 1 (low risk) to 10 (critical risk). Risk calculation considers severity (Fidelis alerts, network anomalies, and endpoint vulnerabilities), coverage (security components including network sensor placement and EDR), and importance based on asset role. This multi-dimensional risk calculation enables proactive security measures and helps prioritize response efforts, ensuring that security operations teams can focus their limited resources on protecting the most critical data and systems from cybersecurity risks. Retrospective Analysis: Learning from Past Investigations Advanced NDR platforms require solutions that can hunt and automate information analysis of past behavior. New information becomes available constantly through new detections and threat intelligence from industry and internal experts. The ability to connect dots between current events and past behavior represents a crucial aspect of NDR capabilities, enabling security professionals to identify patterns that might indicate advanced persistent threats or sophisticated attack campaigns. Fidelis Network ® supports up to 360 days of retrospective analysis , enabling organizations to apply new threat intelligence to historical data and uncover previously missed attack patterns. Stored protocol, application, and content-level metadata allows discovery of past attacks through retroactive analysis triggered by key indicators derived from new threat intelligence , machine learning, sandbox results, and threat research. This real time threat intelligence capability helps organizations understand how attackers gain access to their systems and develop more effective threat response strategies. Real-Time Insight, Real-Time Prevention with Fidelis Network Block attacks before damage occurs Prevent lateral movement inside your network Reduce false positives & alert fatigue Read Guide Deep Investigation Best Practices: The SOC Analyst's Playbook Effective deep investigation requires systematic timeline reconstruction and comprehensive visibility across network, cloud, email, and endpoint metadata. Organizations need real-time and retrospective analysis capabilities for 30, 60, or 90 days minimum, combined with threat intelligence from multiple third-party sources and internally cultivated intelligence. This extended visibility is essential for identifying advanced persistent threats that may operate over extended periods while attempting to remain undetected. Automation eliminates manual correlation steps that previously consumed analyst time. Rather than being reactive and piecing together evidence from multiple disparate systems, security analysts can focus on understanding adversary intentions and making strategic decisions under pressure. With comprehensive network detection providing visibility into deeply embedded content across all ports and protocols, analysts can concentrate on attribution and strategic assessment rather than data collection. The most effective investigations combine cutting-edge artificial intelligence and machine learning with experienced analyst judgment. Understanding attacker behavior patterns and making decisions under pressure define successful response capabilities. Modern NDR platforms enable this approach by providing rich metadata, automated correlation capabilities, and integrated deception technologies that transform network security from reactive monitoring to proactive threat hunting . Through advanced NDR capabilities, security operations centers can shift from alert fatigue to intelligence-driven investigation, reducing mean time to detection and response while providing the contextual awareness necessary for effective cyber defense in today’s evolving threat landscape. By implementing comprehensive threat detection and response solutions that protect both critical assets and sensitive information, organizations can maintain strong cybersecurity posture while enabling their security teams to focus on preventing future attacks rather than simply responding to incidents after they occur. Frequently Asked Questions What makes Deep Session Inspection different from traditional deep packet inspection? Deep Session Inspection analyzes complete communication sessions rather than individual packets, providing context about entire conversations between systems. This patented technology goes beyond traditional DPI by examining streaming traffic across network, email, and web to detect threats hidden in nested files, encrypted traffic patterns, and distributed across multiple packets that conventional tools miss. How does Fidelis Network®'s 300+ metadata attributes enhance investigation capabilities? Fidelis Network ® captures over 300 metadata attributes from protocols, files, and content—significantly more than traditional NetFlow data. This rich metadata includes protocol and application data, content-level information, custom tags, and enhanced metadata that enables retrospective analysis up to 360 days. This comprehensive data collection provides security teams with the detailed context needed for thorough threat investigations. How do automated playbooks change SOC investigation workflows? Automated playbooks eliminate manual correlation steps by investigating signals across multiple network segments simultaneously. Studies show advanced attacks require approximately 18 minutes from initial detection to becoming indistinguishable from normal activity. Playbooks automate investigation across all possible domains, presenting analysts with pre-analyzed conclusions including recommended remediation techniques like file deletion, system rollback, and endpoint isolation.

Risk calculation considers severity (Fidelis alerts, network anomalies, and endpoint vulnerabilities), coverage (security components including network sensor placement and EDR), and importance based on asset role. This multi-dimensional risk calculation enables proactive security measures and helps prioritize response efforts, ensuring that security operations teams can focus their limited resources on protecting the most critical data and systems from cybersecurity risks.

Retrospective Analysis: Learning from Past Investigations

Advanced NDR platforms require solutions that can hunt and automate information analysis of past behavior. New information becomes available constantly through new detections and threat intelligence from industry and internal experts. The ability to connect dots between current events and past behavior represents a crucial aspect of NDR capabilities, enabling security professionals to identify patterns that might indicate advanced persistent threats or sophisticated attack campaigns.

Fidelis Network® supports up to 360 days of retrospective analysis, enabling organizations to apply new threat intelligence to historical data and uncover previously missed attack patterns. Stored protocol, application, and content-level metadata allows discovery of past attacks through retroactive analysis triggered by key indicators derived from new threat intelligence, machine learning, sandbox results, and threat research. This real time threat intelligence capability helps organizations understand how attackers gain access to their systems and develop more effective threat response strategies.

Real-Time Insight, Real-Time Prevention with Fidelis Network
  • Block attacks before damage occurs
  • Prevent lateral movement inside your network
  • Reduce false positives & alert fatigue
Read Guide
Deep Investigation Best Practices: The SOC Analyst's Playbook

Effective deep investigation requires systematic timeline reconstruction and comprehensive visibility across network, cloud, email, and endpoint metadata. Organizations need real-time and retrospective analysis capabilities for 30, 60, or 90 days minimum, combined with threat intelligence from multiple third-party sources and internally cultivated intelligence. This extended visibility is essential for identifying advanced persistent threats that may operate over extended periods while attempting to remain undetected. 

Automation eliminates manual correlation steps that previously consumed analyst time. Rather than being reactive and piecing together evidence from multiple disparate systems, security analysts can focus on understanding adversary intentions and making strategic decisions under pressure. With comprehensive network detection providing visibility into deeply embedded content across all ports and protocols, analysts can concentrate on attribution and strategic assessment rather than data collection. 

The most effective investigations combine cutting-edge artificial intelligence and machine learning with experienced analyst judgment. Understanding attacker behavior patterns and making decisions under pressure define successful response capabilities. Modern NDR platforms enable this approach by providing rich metadata, automated correlation capabilities, and integrated deception technologies that transform network security from reactive monitoring to proactive threat hunting. 

Through advanced NDR capabilities, security operations centers can shift from alert fatigue to intelligence-driven investigation, reducing mean time to detection and response while providing the contextual awareness necessary for effective cyber defense in today’s evolving threat landscape. By implementing comprehensive threat detection and response solutions that protect both critical assets and sensitive information, organizations can maintain strong cybersecurity posture while enabling their security teams to focus on preventing future attacks rather than simply responding to incidents after they occur.

Frequently Asked Questions
What makes Deep Session Inspection different from traditional deep packet inspection?

Deep Session Inspection analyzes complete communication sessions rather than individual packets, providing context about entire conversations between systems. This patented technology goes beyond traditional DPI by examining streaming traffic across network, email, and web to detect threats hidden in nested files, encrypted traffic patterns, and distributed across multiple packets that conventional tools miss.

How does Fidelis Network®'s 300+ metadata attributes enhance investigation capabilities?

Fidelis Network® captures over 300 metadata attributes from protocols, files, and content—significantly more than traditional NetFlow data. This rich metadata includes protocol and application data, content-level information, custom tags, and enhanced metadata that enables retrospective analysis up to 360 days. This comprehensive data collection provides security teams with the detailed context needed for thorough threat investigations.

How do automated playbooks change SOC investigation workflows?

Automated playbooks eliminate manual correlation steps by investigating signals across multiple network segments simultaneously. Studies show advanced attacks require approximately 18 minutes from initial detection to becoming indistinguishable from normal activity. Playbooks automate investigation across all possible domains, presenting analysts with pre-analyzed conclusions including recommended remediation techniques like file deletion, system rollback, and endpoint isolation.

The post What Deep Investigation Really Looks Like: A SOC Analyst’s Perspective appeared first on Fidelis Security.

items.title: The Value of Documentation
items.summary: If someone asked me to name the biggest shortcoming in DFIR, and in cybersecurity, in general, I'd have to say documentation. We miss a lot of value because activity and analysis goes undocumented, and it is lost. Without documentation clearly delineating what was done, and what was observed, we can't identify and address issues that need to be fixed. Without that documentation, capabilities cannot be updated, and new capabilities cannot be added. We end up not being able to operationalize what was observed or learned. Without that documentation, every analyst needs to learn the same lessons, from their own efforts, and cannot benefit from the efforts of others. This is inefficient, and leads to a great deal of corporate knowledge simply be unrealized and lost. I learned lessons about the value of documentation a long time ago. In 1990, during the first Desert Shield, my unit deployed to South Korea for an exercise named "Valiant Blitz". After the exercise, we had an after action review, and one of the radar operators stood up and just flat out said, "Comm sucked." That's it. Being the Communications Officer, and having a senior officer from my own unit stand up and say that, hurt. Particularly because I could not remember a single complaint during the entire exercise. In January 1991, a unit on Okinawa was decommissioned, and an LDO 1stLt was assigned to our unit, and became my boss. Shortly thereafter, we deployed to South Korea again, this time for the "Team Spirit" exercise. As before, we had an after action meeting following our return to Okinawa, and as before, one of the senior officers got up and said, "Comm sucked." However, my boss had set up a rudimentary ticketing system, maintained in a log book that Marines are used to having around. We logged all trouble calls that came into the Communications/Electronics section, to whom they were assigned, and their resolution. When the Captain made his statement, my boss slide the log book across the table and said, "show me." There was no more discussion of the issue. About 8 yrs later, I was off of active duty, and in my third or fourth consulting role in the private sector. I'd been hired into a firm that provided networking services, but as a security engineer. My boss was hired after me, and after about 6 months, he came to my desk late one afternoon and asked to speak to me. He'd had some speed bumps since he was brought in, and had given notice that morning. Immediately upon giving notice, the president of the company had flown down from NY, walked right into his office, and asked what he needed to stay. My boss said, "I want a security lab.", and the president responded with, "Give me a purchase order." My boss then pulled out a folder containing 6 months of purchase requests for a variety of lab configurations, ranging from multiple desktops and a couple of blade servers, all the way down to just 2 additional laptops. All were denied. In 2014, I was in a consulting role, and our team was going through an operational debrief, where an analyst walked through an engagement, and shared what they had seen and learned. The call literally started with the analyst stating that they'd seen something, didn't know what it was, and that they never went back to figure out what it was, before simply moving on with the rest of their debrief. Two of us in particular were taken aback by this statement, so we reached out to get some specifics about what the "thing" was, but the analyst hadn't documented the "thing", and didn't remember. So, we dug around a bit and found out what it was...and found that it was an extremely high fidelity indicator of this threat actor's TTPs. We found that this indicator only existed because of the specific actions that the threat actor took, and we hadn't seen other threat actors, nor admins or users, take similar actions. This was almost lost because the analyst hadn't documented it; fortunately, someone investigated it, and was able to operationalize the finding so that, going forward, all analysts would be alerted to the indicator, without having to do a full cradle-to-grave investigation themselves. Not having documentation means: 1. We cannot operationalize, or even share, what we've seen and learned. 2. We do not have the necessary information, data, or numbers to encourage decision makers to decide in our favor. 3. We cannot justify the things we feel we need, or really understand how much of that is "feel" versus really, truly "need".

items.title: Arrakis Security Report Finds 76% of AI Agents Are Dormant but Keep Their Credentials and Connections
items.summary: New York, NY, USA, October 21st, 2026, CyberNewswire According to the 2026 Autonomous Agents Threat Report, published by Arrakis Security , 76% of active agents have not run in 60 days, but their credentials still work and their triggers still fire. 44% have not run in 180 days. 24% of dormant agents can be started by an unsigned webhook from outside the organization. The report is based on anonymized, unidentifiable production telemetry from thousands of AI agents in Arrakis customers’ environments, collected over a 12-week period. “There’s a lot of discussion about AI agent risk, and very little data”, said Tal Baron, CEO and co-founder of Arrakis Security . “When an employee leaves, their access is removed the same day. When an agent stops being used, nobody removes anything, because in most companies nobody owns it”. ﻿Other findings: 22% of agents can send content to a model run by a third party and act on the answer. 20% of agents can pass a task to another agent with different permissions, and get back results they aren’t allowed to produce themselves. 70% of agents can reach sensitive systems, such as cloud storage, AI services, and marketing platforms, and almost none of those connections have verified data loss prevention (DLP). 82% of agents carry at least one exposure, and 46% of those carry more than one. The full report is available at https://arrakis.security/2026-threat-report . About Arrakis Security Arrakis secures autonomous agents through behavioral intelligence across three layers: what an agent is, what it does, and why. AI-SPM scans each agent’s structure, permissions, tools, and metadata hourly, including agents that never run, surfacing shadow agents, exposed keys, and misconfigurations. AI-TDR monitors actions in real time for deviations from defined rules and policies. The behavioral intelligence engine models each agent from its own history, posture, runtime, and context: how it got there and what it could do next. For each action, it decides whether to continue, escalate, or intervene. Contact Moranne Shechnick Arrakis Security moranne.shechnick@arksec.ai
items.summary_html:
New York, NY, USA, October 21st, 2026, CyberNewswire

According to the 2026 Autonomous Agents Threat Report, published by Arrakis Security, 76% of active agents have not run in 60 days, but their credentials still work and their triggers still fire. 44% have not run in 180 days.

24% of dormant agents can be started by an unsigned webhook from outside the organization.

The report is based on anonymized, unidentifiable production telemetry from thousands of AI agents in Arrakis customers’ environments, collected over a 12-week period.

“There’s a lot of discussion about AI agent risk, and very little data”, said Tal Baron, CEO and co-founder of Arrakis Security. “When an employee leaves, their access is removed the same day.

When an agent stops being used, nobody removes anything, because in most companies nobody owns it”.

﻿Other findings:
  • 22% of agents can send content to a model run by a third party and act on the answer.
  • 20% of agents can pass a task to another agent with different permissions, and get back results they aren’t allowed to produce themselves.
  • 70% of agents can reach sensitive systems, such as cloud storage, AI services, and marketing platforms, and almost none of those connections have verified data loss prevention (DLP).
  • 82% of agents carry at least one exposure, and 46% of those carry more than one.

The full report is available at https://arrakis.security/2026-threat-report.

About Arrakis Security

Arrakis secures autonomous agents through behavioral intelligence across three layers: what an agent is, what it does, and why.

AI-SPM scans each agent’s structure, permissions, tools, and metadata hourly, including agents that never run, surfacing shadow agents, exposed keys, and misconfigurations.

AI-TDR monitors actions in real time for deviations from defined rules and policies. The behavioral intelligence engine models each agent from its own history, posture, runtime, and context: how it got there and what it could do next.

For each action, it decides whether to continue, escalate, or intervene.

Contact

Moranne Shechnick

Arrakis Security

moranne.shechnick@arksec.ai
