items.title: Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI
items.summary: Using temporary credentials is a security best practice to reduce the risk from credentials getting compromised. With AWS IAM Roles Anywhere , now your workloads outside of Amazon Web Services (AWS) will be able to access AWS resources by obtaining temporary security credentials in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) . IAM Roles Anywhere relies on public key infrastructure (PKI) to establish trust between your AWS account and certificate authorities that issues certificates to your workloads that run outside AWS. PKI involves the generation, distribution, and verification of digital certificates through public key encryption. In this post, we show you some best practices, considerations, and solutions for integrating your PKI with IAM Roles Anywhere. In this post, we assume that you have a foundational knowledge of IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere. For more information, see the IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere documentation. Note : As of July 2026, AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) supports exportable public certificates that can be used on workloads outside AWS (containers or on-premises). Additionally, ACM supports the ACME protocol for automated certificate issuance and renewal on external workloads. These capabilities complement IAM Roles Anywhere by providing both identity (using X.509 certificates for IAM Roles Anywhere) and encryption (using ACM public/private certificates) for hybrid environments. X.509 certificates for workload identity If you’re running multiple workloads in your infrastructure, you’re probably assigning unique workload identities and specific user permissions. In this environment, your workloads can use PKI tools like Active Directory Certificate Services to centrally manage and monitor the identities and permissions at scale. The same principles of segregating unrelated workloads apply to PKI and IAM Roles Anywhere. If you’re issuing certificates to your workloads today, they can probably be used with IAM Roles Anywhere without any changes. As shown in Figure 1, the access boundary and permissions of Workload A can be very different from that of Workload B when accessing AWS resources, depending on the organization’s needs . In such scenarios, it’s recommended to establish a unique machine identity for each workload. This can be achieved by issuing a separate X.509 certificate with distinct identity attributes signed by your certificate authority (CA) . To set up an effective PKI solution for machine identities, you must configure the appropriate certificate attributes and anchor the trust model around those attributes. Figure 1: Workloads outside of AWS accessing AWS services Temporary access credentials Workloads with distinct CA signed X.509 certificates exchange certificates with IAM, as shown in Figure 2, to get temporary security credentials for the session. The signature validation process used by IAM Roles Anywhere verifies the certificate issuer and the subject before providing the temporary credentials. To enable this verification process, an IAM Roles Anywhere trust model should be set up by either uploading your CA’s digital certificate as a trust anchor or by referencing an existing AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) certificate. In this post, we focus on using a trust anchor. To help define the appropriate scope for the temporary credentials, it’s recommended to configure distinct IAM roles for each workload to assume. Workloads must use X.509 certificates issued by your CA. These certificates are exchanged with IAM to get temporary security credentials for the session. Figure 2: Getting temporary credentials from IAM using CA issued X.509 certificate Setting up a trust model for IAM Roles Anywhere is a three-step process, see Extend AWS IAM Roles Anywhere to workloads outside of AWS for more information. Create a trust anchor. Set up IAM roles with the IAM Roles Anywhere trust policy that will be assumed by your non-AWS workload. Configure profiles with IAM roles and attach relevant session policies. This instructs IAM Roles Anywhere to use your selected session policies whenever you request credentials for any of the attached roles. Trust model The trust model is centered around setting up the right trust relationship between IAM Roles Anywhere and your CA by configuring a trust anchor . The model connects the role, the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal, and identities encoded in X509 certificates that are issued by a CA. Certificate attributes Certificates are a binary record with encoded key/value pairs as certificate attributes. Let’s look at one of the X.509 certificates to understand different attributes of certificate that are important for IAM Roles Anywhere PKI validation. The following is an example PEM encoded certificate file that can be decoded with tools like openssl . -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIKOzCCCSOgAwIBAgIQDlnyZvBeKjgHm1jJ++CbgDANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQsFADBE MQswC ........... -----END CERTIFICATE---- Certificate: Data: Version: 3 (0x2) Serial Number: e0:5d:b7:72:56:fa:75:e3 Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 Issuer: C=US, ST=CA, L=San Francisco, O=MyCompany Inc., OU=AC, CN=MyCompany CA Validity Not Before: Sep 15 00:09:17 2023 GMT Not After : Sep 18 00:09:17 2023 GMT Subject: C=US, O=MyCompany, OU=eCommerce, CN=WorkloadA Subject Public Key Info: Public Key Algorithm: id-ecPublicKey Public-Key: (384 bit) pub: 04:3b:74:e1:68:06:fa:b0:3d:fe:f7:5f:74:80:05: X509v3 extensions: X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:ecommerce.mycompany.com, DNS:*ecommerce.mycompany.com, URI:spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical CA:FALSE X509v3 Key Usage: critical Digital Signature Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 30:64:02:30:19:a7:a0:33:49:ce:e1:cb:76:6e:c0:f3:c5:66: IAM Roles Anywhere extracts values from the subject Common Name (CN), issuer, and Subject Alternative Name (SAN) fields of the authenticating certificate and makes them available for policy evaluation through the sts:sourceIdentity and principal tags. When configuring your PKI, set short validity periods on the certificates issued to workloads. Short-lived certificates limit the window of exposure if a certificate is compromised and reduce the need for active revocation. "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/DNS": "ecommerce.mycompany.com" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/URI": "spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA" Note : An empty Subject CN in a certificate isn’t supported by IAM Roles Anywhere. Trust policy and effective permissions of credentials IAM Roles Anywhere clients fetch temporary credentials for IAM Roles using the API method CreateSession . To successfully authorize this API call, the IAM role trust policy should trust the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal as shown in the following example. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession", "sts:SetSourceIdentity" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA" }, "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": [ "arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID" ] } } } ] } As a security best practice, consider using additional condition statements to evaluate the session PrincipalTag attributes extracted from the certificate to further restrict authorization of temporary credentials. If the workloads have ephemeral certificates with a dynamic subject CN, then the issuer or SAN principal tags can be used to define condition statements in the trust policy. The trust anchor shown in the preceding trust policy helps establish the trust between IAM Roles Anywhere and the CA in your PKI. Plan for trust anchor placement Depending on the CA platform, you can configure one or more intermediate certificates in your PKI certificate hierarchy, as shown in Figure 3. The certificate level the trust anchor is placed at affects which end-entity certificates IAM Roles Anywhere accepts, and therefore which workloads are authorized to assume a role. To create a trust anchor, export the certificate bundle for the issuing CA certificate from your external CA platform in PEM-encoded format and upload it to the trust anchor console . Figure 3: Certificate hierarchy in an external PKI See the Solution deployment section to onboard a sample solution and verify your certificate bundle. Fine-grained access control is vital for security because it allows organizations to precisely define and restrict permissions, minimizing the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches. The effective permissions of the temporary security credentials are an intersection of resource-based, identity-based, and session policies as shown in Figure 4. By setting up the trust anchor and profile configuration in IAM Roles Anywhere with session policies, you can limit the permissions for each session. Figure 4: Effective permissions of session credentials Credential helper To obtain temporary security credentials from IAM Roles Anywhere, use the credential helper tool. This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs. The credential helper manages the process of obtaining temporary security credentials using IAM Roles Anywhere and returns them in JSON format. The private key of the workload and its CA signed certificate are the two critical parameters provided to the credential helper tool. To use this tool, you need both an end-entity certificate and a trust anchor created in IAM Roles Anywhere. As of December 2024, the credential helper (version 1.4.0 and later) supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0. The following is an example of how to obtain temporary security credentials: $ ./aws_signing_helper credential-process \ --certificate /path/to/certificate \ --private-key /path/to/private-key \ --trust-anchor-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID \ --profile-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:profile/PROFILE_ID \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::account:role/role-name-with-path When credential-process is used with AWS SDKs, the temporary credentials are stored in memory and refreshed automatically. However, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) invokes credential-process on every command. Each invocation creates a new IAM Roles Anywhere session, which adds latency to every CLI call. To avoid this delay when using the AWS CLI, we recommend using the update command, which writes refreshed credentials to a file that the CLI reads on each invocation without calling credential-process again. When you use update , credentials are written to a credential file on disk and any user or process who can read the credential file might be able to read and use those AWS credentials, so it’s recommended to use serve unless your business has a specific use case that needs to read AWS credentials from a file. The serve command can be used to vend temporary credentials through an endpoint running on the local host using the same URIs and request headers as Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2 ). When using serve , no AWS configuration files are needed because the AWS SDKs can discover the server endpoint. Just-in-time compared to short-lived certificates as workload identities To help mitigate the risk around the exposure of your business-critical resources to compromised certificate user sessions, it’s recommended to use certificates with just-in-time credentials or short-lived access credentials. Just-in-time certificates are issued by a CA for immediate use for authentication on a system or application. The CA uses the roles and policies defined in IAM to determine when, and under what conditions, a workload can establish a session. With just-in-time access, admins don’t have to worry about revoking access if the users’ access roles change. Because the access credentials are recreated for each access request, any role changes can be applied in real time. Just-in-time access requires support from your CA, so verify compatibility with your CA before implementing it. It’s recommended to tailor the validity periods for short-lived certificates to align with business requirements, workload lifecycle, and your organization’s risk tolerance. AWS Private CA offers a short-lived CA mode specifically designed for certificates with validity periods under 7 days. This mode is priced at $50 per month (compared to $400 per month for general-purpose CA mode), making it cost-effective for high-volume, ephemeral workload identities such as containers and serverless functions. For more information, see AWS Private Certificate Authority and How to use AWS Private CA short-lived certificate mode . See Zero trust on AWS for information about how short-lived credentials support a zero trust architecture. Best practices for private key storage Safeguarding private keys is of paramount importance in any environment. A private key is created by the certificate owner when requesting certificates with a Certificate Signing Request (CSR). The CA providing your certificate doesn’t create or have your private key. In fact, it’s recommended that no one outside your administrators should ever be given access to this material. Guardrails should be implemented to make sure the keys aren’t stored in an online repository. Using the credential helper with IAM Roles Anywhere, you can integrate with PKCS #11-compatible modules. For implementation details, see How to implement cryptographic modules to secure private keys used with IAM Roles Anywhere . With the credential helper (version 1.1.0 and later), IAM Roles Anywhere supports PKCS #11 integration, so you can use private keys stored in hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-based secure stores and avoid storing them to disk. Additionally, as of December 2024, the credential helper supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0, enabling private keys to be generated inside the TPM and marked as non-exportable. With TPM-backed keys, the private keys can’t be extracted even if the workload host is compromised. This is the strongest private key protection available for on-premises and hybrid workloads using IAM Roles Anywhere. If your organization doesn’t implement PKCS #11–compatible modules, IAM Roles Anywhere supports credential helper version 1.0.5 for X.509 certificates and private keys stored in macOS and Windows certificate stores. This delegates the signing operations to keys stored within those OS-specific certificate stores. In Windows, both CryptoAPI and Cryptography API: Next Generation (CNG) are supported; in macOS, Keychain is supported. In these environments, the private key will never be directly readable, and the signing operation would be delegated to the secure store instead, which will improve security posture of your environment. If you have multiple certificates, then use the --cert-selector flag of the credential helper tool to search for a specific certificate (and associated private key) through the certificate subject, issuer, and serial number. The corresponding keys are x509Subject , x509Issuer , and x509Serial , respectively. These keys can be specified either through a JSON file format or through the command line. The following is an example of both approaches: If you want to use a JSON file, it should be similar to this: [ { "Key": "x509Subject", "Value": "CN=Subject" }, { "Key": "x509Issuer", "Value": "CN=Issuer" }, { "Key": "x509Serial", "Value": "15D19632234BF759A32802C0DA88F9E8AFC8702D" } ] If the preceding example is placed in a file called selector.json , it can be specified with the --cert-selector flag through file://path/to/selector.json . The same certificate selector argument can be specified through the command line as shown in the following: --cert-selector Key=x509Subject, Value=CN=Subject Key=x509Issuer, Value=CN=Issuer Key=x509Serial, Value=15D19632 Monitoring trust anchor certificates Monitoring certificate expiry in PKI is crucial for maintaining secure communication, because expired certificates can lead to authentication failures, leaving systems vulnerable to unauthorized access. Compliance and regulatory requirements often mandate timely renewal of certificates, making monitoring certificate expiry essential to avoid legal penalties and maintain organizational integrity. Using IAM Roles Anywhere, you can receive notifications for CA certificate expiry and end-entity certificate expiry. IAM Roles Anywhere can send metrics, events, and notifications through multiple notification channels as shown in the following table: Event Channel Threshold Enabled CA certificate expiry CloudWatch, Amazon EventBridge , and AWS Health 45 days before expiry TRUE End-entity certificate expiry EventBridge and AWS Health 45 days before expiry TRUE The preceding notifications thresholds are default settings, which you can customize using the steps in Customize notification settings in IAM Roles Anywhere . Best practices for trust anchor certificate rotation Consider rotating your certificates using blue/green deployments to seamlessly roll out new certificates without affecting service availability. Use automation to integrate certificate rotation testing in your blue/green deployment pipeline. See the sample AWS CloudFormation template in the Solution deployment section to build your automation pipeline. As shown in Figure 5, two trust anchors have been created; one for each environment. Using this approach, you can test the certificate rotation process in a controlled staging environment before applying it to the production environment, thus reducing the risk of certificate-related outages. Figure 5: Trust anchor certificate rotation in blue/green deployment Solution deployment The sample solution template is available in the IAM Roles Anywhere — External PKI Integration repository on GitHub. It contains the following main steps: Creates a distinct IAM role with policies scoped to the resources that workload requires. Assigns a trust relationship to a IAM Roles Anywhere principal. Creates a trust anchor using a certificate bundle from an external CA. Creates a profile with the required IAM Roles. Parameters for this deployment are shown in the following table: Parameter Required Default Description TrustAnchorCertificateBody Yes — PEM-encoded X.509 certificate of your CA (includes BEGIN and END markers) WorkloadSubjectCN No WorkloadA Subject CN from the workload certificate, used in trust policy conditions WorkloadIssuerCN No MyCompany CA Issuer CN from the CA certificate, used in trust policy conditions WorkloadSANCN No WorkloadA SAN CN from the workload certificate, provides additional identity assertion SessionDurationSeconds No 3600 Maximum session duration in seconds (900–43200) NotificationEmail No (empty) Email address for certificate expiry notifications. When provided, creates an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic and an EventBridge rule Important : The SessionDurationSeconds value must not exceed the IAM role’s MaxSessionDuration setting, which defaults to 3600 seconds (1 hour). If you request a longer session than the role allows, the CreateSession API returns an error. The companion template keeps both values in sync by setting the role’s MaxSessionDuration to the same parameter value. If you configure the role separately, update its MaxSessionDuration to match your desired session length. For more information, see IAM Roles Anywhere CreateSession API . If the workload’s subject CN ( WorkloadSubjectCN ) doesn’t match the x509Subject CN of the authenticating certificate, the CreateSession call is denied. The same conditional verification applies to WorkloadIssuerCN and WorkloadSANCN . The template enforces three certificate attribute conditions in the IAM trust policy: issuer CN, subject CN, and SAN CN must all match the values configured as parameters. Additionally, the trust policy scopes role assumption to the specific trust anchor Amazon Resource Name (ARN), preventing other trust anchors in the same account from assuming that role. By understanding the trust model, using certificate attributes, and implementing fine-grained authorization, organizations can gain granular control over the effective permissions of these credentials. The choice between just-in-time and short-lived certificates as workload identities depends on your specific requirements. Adhering to best practices for private key storage is essential to maintain the integrity of your security infrastructure. Regularly rotating trust anchor certificates helps ensure the long-term trustworthiness of your system. As you embark on your journey to implement IAM Roles Anywhere and integrate it with your PKI, remember that a well-architected approach to certificate management is a cornerstone of robust and resilient cloud security. items.summary_html:
Using temporary credentials is a security best practice to reduce the risk from credentials getting compromised. With AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, now your workloads outside of Amazon Web Services (AWS) will be able to access AWS resources by obtaining temporary security credentials in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). IAM Roles Anywhere relies on public key infrastructure (PKI) to establish trust between your AWS account and certificate authorities that issues certificates to your workloads that run outside AWS. PKI involves the generation, distribution, and verification of digital certificates through public key encryption.

In this post, we show you some best practices, considerations, and solutions for integrating your PKI with IAM Roles Anywhere. In this post, we assume that you have a foundational knowledge of IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere. For more information, see the IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere documentation.

Note: As of July 2026, AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) supports exportable public certificates that can be used on workloads outside AWS (containers or on-premises). Additionally, ACM supports the ACME protocol for automated certificate issuance and renewal on external workloads. These capabilities complement IAM Roles Anywhere by providing both identity (using X.509 certificates for IAM Roles Anywhere) and encryption (using ACM public/private certificates) for hybrid environments.

X.509 certificates for workload identity

If you’re running multiple workloads in your infrastructure, you’re probably assigning unique workload identities and specific user permissions. In this environment, your workloads can use PKI tools like Active Directory Certificate Services to centrally manage and monitor the identities and permissions at scale. The same principles of segregating unrelated workloads apply to PKI and IAM Roles Anywhere. If you’re issuing certificates to your workloads today, they can probably be used with IAM Roles Anywhere without any changes.

As shown in Figure 1, the access boundary and permissions of Workload A can be very different from that of Workload B when accessing AWS resources, depending on the organization’s needs. In such scenarios, it’s recommended to establish a unique machine identity for each workload. This can be achieved by issuing a separate X.509 certificate with distinct identity attributes signed by your certificate authority (CA). To set up an effective PKI solution for machine identities, you must configure the appropriate certificate attributes and anchor the trust model around those attributes.

Figure 1: Workloads outside of AWS accessing AWS services

Temporary access credentials

Workloads with distinct CA signed X.509 certificates exchange certificates with IAM, as shown in Figure 2, to get temporary security credentials for the session. The signature validation process used by IAM Roles Anywhere verifies the certificate issuer and the subject before providing the temporary credentials. To enable this verification process, an IAM Roles Anywhere trust model should be set up by either uploading your CA’s digital certificate as a trust anchor or by referencing an existing AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) certificate. In this post, we focus on using a trust anchor.

To help define the appropriate scope for the temporary credentials, it’s recommended to configure distinct IAM roles for each workload to assume. Workloads must use X.509 certificates issued by your CA. These certificates are exchanged with IAM to get temporary security credentials for the session.

Figure 2: Getting temporary credentials from IAM using CA issued X.509 certificate

Setting up a trust model for IAM Roles Anywhere is a three-step process, see Extend AWS IAM Roles Anywhere to workloads outside of AWS for more information.

  1. Create a trust anchor.
  2. Set up IAM roles with the IAM Roles Anywhere trust policy that will be assumed by your non-AWS workload.
  3. Configure profiles with IAM roles and attach relevant session policies. This instructs IAM Roles Anywhere to use your selected session policies whenever you request credentials for any of the attached roles.
Trust model

The trust model is centered around setting up the right trust relationship between IAM Roles Anywhere and your CA by configuring a trust anchor. The model connects the role, the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal, and identities encoded in X509 certificates that are issued by a CA.

Certificate attributes

Certificates are a binary record with encoded key/value pairs as certificate attributes. Let’s look at one of the X.509 certificates to understand different attributes of certificate that are important for IAM Roles Anywhere PKI validation.

The following is an example PEM encoded certificate file that can be decoded with tools like openssl.

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIKOzCCCSOgAwIBAgIQDlnyZvBeKjgHm1jJ++CbgDANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQsFADBE
MQswC ...........
-----END CERTIFICATE----


Certificate:
    Data:
        Version: 3 (0x2)
        Serial Number:
            e0:5d:b7:72:56:fa:75:e3
    Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512
        Issuer: C=US, ST=CA, L=San Francisco, O=MyCompany Inc., OU=AC, CN=MyCompany CA
        Validity
            Not Before: Sep 15 00:09:17 2023 GMT
            Not After : Sep 18 00:09:17 2023 GMT
        Subject: C=US, O=MyCompany, OU=eCommerce, CN=WorkloadA
        Subject Public Key Info:
            Public Key Algorithm: id-ecPublicKey
                Public-Key: (384 bit)
                pub: 
                    04:3b:74:e1:68:06:fa:b0:3d:fe:f7:5f:74:80:05:
        X509v3 extensions:
            X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: 
                DNS:ecommerce.mycompany.com, DNS:*ecommerce.mycompany.com, URI:spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce
            X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical
                CA:FALSE
            X509v3 Key Usage: critical
                Digital Signature
    Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512
         30:64:02:30:19:a7:a0:33:49:ce:e1:cb:76:6e:c0:f3:c5:66:

IAM Roles Anywhere extracts values from the subject Common Name (CN), issuer, and Subject Alternative Name (SAN) fields of the authenticating certificate and makes them available for policy evaluation through the sts:sourceIdentity and principal tags. When configuring your PKI, set short validity periods on the certificates issued to workloads. Short-lived certificates limit the window of exposure if a certificate is compromised and reduce the need for active revocation.

"aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA" 
"aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA" 
"aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/DNS": "ecommerce.mycompany.com" 
"aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/URI": "spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA"

Note: An empty Subject CN in a certificate isn’t supported by IAM Roles Anywhere.

Trust policy and effective permissions of credentials

IAM Roles Anywhere clients fetch temporary credentials for IAM Roles using the API method CreateSession. To successfully authorize this API call, the IAM role trust policy should trust the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal as shown in the following example.

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": {
                "Service": "rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com"
            },
            "Action": [
                "sts:AssumeRole",
                "sts:TagSession",
                "sts:SetSourceIdentity"
            ],
            "Condition": {
                "StringEquals": {
                    "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA",
                    "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA",
                    "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA"
                },
                "ArnEquals": {
                    "aws:SourceArn": [
                        "arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID"
                    ]
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}

As a security best practice, consider using additional condition statements to evaluate the session PrincipalTag attributes extracted from the certificate to further restrict authorization of temporary credentials. If the workloads have ephemeral certificates with a dynamic subject CN, then the issuer or SAN principal tags can be used to define condition statements in the trust policy. The trust anchor shown in the preceding trust policy helps establish the trust between IAM Roles Anywhere and the CA in your PKI.

Plan for trust anchor placement

Depending on the CA platform, you can configure one or more intermediate certificates in your PKI certificate hierarchy, as shown in Figure 3. The certificate level the trust anchor is placed at affects which end-entity certificates IAM Roles Anywhere accepts, and therefore which workloads are authorized to assume a role. To create a trust anchor, export the certificate bundle for the issuing CA certificate from your external CA platform in PEM-encoded format and upload it to the trust anchor console.

Figure 3: Certificate hierarchy in an external PKI

See the Solution deployment section to onboard a sample solution and verify your certificate bundle.

Fine-grained access control is vital for security because it allows organizations to precisely define and restrict permissions, minimizing the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches. The effective permissions of the temporary security credentials are an intersection of resource-based, identity-based, and session policies as shown in Figure 4. By setting up the trust anchor and profile configuration in IAM Roles Anywhere with session policies, you can limit the permissions for each session.

Figure 4: Effective permissions of session credentials

Credential helper

To obtain temporary security credentials from IAM Roles Anywhere, use the credential helper tool. This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs. The credential helper manages the process of obtaining temporary security credentials using IAM Roles Anywhere and returns them in JSON format. The private key of the workload and its CA signed certificate are the two critical parameters provided to the credential helper tool. To use this tool, you need both an end-entity certificate and a trust anchor created in IAM Roles Anywhere. As of December 2024, the credential helper (version 1.4.0 and later) supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0.

The following is an example of how to obtain temporary security credentials:

$ ./aws_signing_helper credential-process \
--certificate /path/to/certificate \
--private-key /path/to/private-key \
--trust-anchor-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID \
--profile-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:profile/PROFILE_ID \
--role-arn arn:aws:iam::account:role/role-name-with-path

When credential-process is used with AWS SDKs, the temporary credentials are stored in memory and refreshed automatically. However, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) invokes credential-process on every command. Each invocation creates a new IAM Roles Anywhere session, which adds latency to every CLI call. To avoid this delay when using the AWS CLI, we recommend using the update command, which writes refreshed credentials to a file that the CLI reads on each invocation without calling credential-process again.

When you use update, credentials are written to a credential file on disk and any user or process who can read the credential file might be able to read and use those AWS credentials, so it’s recommended to use serve unless your business has a specific use case that needs to read AWS credentials from a file. The serve command can be used to vend temporary credentials through an endpoint running on the local host using the same URIs and request headers as Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2). When using serve, no AWS configuration files are needed because the AWS SDKs can discover the server endpoint.

Just-in-time compared to short-lived certificates as workload identities

To help mitigate the risk around the exposure of your business-critical resources to compromised certificate user sessions, it’s recommended to use certificates with just-in-time credentials or short-lived access credentials. Just-in-time certificates are issued by a CA for immediate use for authentication on a system or application. The CA uses the roles and policies defined in IAM to determine when, and under what conditions, a workload can establish a session. With just-in-time access, admins don’t have to worry about revoking access if the users’ access roles change. Because the access credentials are recreated for each access request, any role changes can be applied in real time. Just-in-time access requires support from your CA, so verify compatibility with your CA before implementing it.

It’s recommended to tailor the validity periods for short-lived certificates to align with business requirements, workload lifecycle, and your organization’s risk tolerance. AWS Private CA offers a short-lived CA mode specifically designed for certificates with validity periods under 7 days. This mode is priced at $50 per month (compared to $400 per month for general-purpose CA mode), making it cost-effective for high-volume, ephemeral workload identities such as containers and serverless functions. For more information, see AWS Private Certificate Authority and How to use AWS Private CA short-lived certificate mode. See Zero trust on AWS for information about how short-lived credentials support a zero trust architecture.

Best practices for private key storage

Safeguarding private keys is of paramount importance in any environment. A private key is created by the certificate owner when requesting certificates with a Certificate Signing Request (CSR). The CA providing your certificate doesn’t create or have your private key. In fact, it’s recommended that no one outside your administrators should ever be given access to this material. Guardrails should be implemented to make sure the keys aren’t stored in an online repository.

Using the credential helper with IAM Roles Anywhere, you can integrate with PKCS #11-compatible modules. For implementation details, see How to implement cryptographic modules to secure private keys used with IAM Roles Anywhere. With the credential helper (version 1.1.0 and later), IAM Roles Anywhere supports PKCS #11 integration, so you can use private keys stored in hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-based secure stores and avoid storing them to disk. Additionally, as of December 2024, the credential helper supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0, enabling private keys to be generated inside the TPM and marked as non-exportable. With TPM-backed keys, the private keys can’t be extracted even if the workload host is compromised. This is the strongest private key protection available for on-premises and hybrid workloads using IAM Roles Anywhere.

If your organization doesn’t implement PKCS #11–compatible modules, IAM Roles Anywhere supports credential helper version 1.0.5 for X.509 certificates and private keys stored in macOS and Windows certificate stores. This delegates the signing operations to keys stored within those OS-specific certificate stores. In Windows, both CryptoAPI and Cryptography API: Next Generation (CNG) are supported; in macOS, Keychain is supported. In these environments, the private key will never be directly readable, and the signing operation would be delegated to the secure store instead, which will improve security posture of your environment. If you have multiple certificates, then use the --cert-selector flag of the credential helper tool to search for a specific certificate (and associated private key) through the certificate subject, issuer, and serial number. The corresponding keys are x509Subject, x509Issuer, and x509Serial, respectively. These keys can be specified either through a JSON file format or through the command line. The following is an example of both approaches:

If you want to use a JSON file, it should be similar to this:

[
  {
    "Key": "x509Subject",
    "Value": "CN=Subject"
  },
  {
    "Key": "x509Issuer",
    "Value": "CN=Issuer"
  },
  {
    "Key": "x509Serial",
    "Value": "15D19632234BF759A32802C0DA88F9E8AFC8702D"
  }
]

If the preceding example is placed in a file called selector.json, it can be specified with the --cert-selector flag through file://path/to/selector.json.

The same certificate selector argument can be specified through the command line as shown in the following:

--cert-selector Key=x509Subject, Value=CN=Subject Key=x509Issuer, Value=CN=Issuer Key=x509Serial, Value=15D19632
Monitoring trust anchor certificates

Monitoring certificate expiry in PKI is crucial for maintaining secure communication, because expired certificates can lead to authentication failures, leaving systems vulnerable to unauthorized access. Compliance and regulatory requirements often mandate timely renewal of certificates, making monitoring certificate expiry essential to avoid legal penalties and maintain organizational integrity.

Using IAM Roles Anywhere, you can receive notifications for CA certificate expiry and end-entity certificate expiry. IAM Roles Anywhere can send metrics, events, and notifications through multiple notification channels as shown in the following table:

Event Channel Threshold Enabled CA certificate expiry CloudWatch, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Health 45 days before expiry TRUE End-entity certificate expiry EventBridge and AWS Health 45 days before expiry TRUE

The preceding notifications thresholds are default settings, which you can customize using the steps in Customize notification settings in IAM Roles Anywhere.

Best practices for trust anchor certificate rotation

Consider rotating your certificates using blue/green deployments to seamlessly roll out new certificates without affecting service availability. Use automation to integrate certificate rotation testing in your blue/green deployment pipeline. See the sample AWS CloudFormation template in the Solution deployment section to build your automation pipeline.

As shown in Figure 5, two trust anchors have been created; one for each environment. Using this approach, you can test the certificate rotation process in a controlled staging environment before applying it to the production environment, thus reducing the risk of certificate-related outages.

Figure 5: Trust anchor certificate rotation in blue/green deployment

Solution deployment

The sample solution template is available in the IAM Roles Anywhere — External PKI Integration repository on GitHub. It contains the following main steps:

  1. Creates a distinct IAM role with policies scoped to the resources that workload requires.
  2. Assigns a trust relationship to a IAM Roles Anywhere principal.
  3. Creates a trust anchor using a certificate bundle from an external CA.
  4. Creates a profile with the required IAM Roles.

Parameters for this deployment are shown in the following table:

Parameter Required Default Description TrustAnchorCertificateBody Yes — PEM-encoded X.509 certificate of your CA (includes BEGIN and END markers) WorkloadSubjectCN No WorkloadA Subject CN from the workload certificate, used in trust policy conditions WorkloadIssuerCN No MyCompany CA Issuer CN from the CA certificate, used in trust policy conditions WorkloadSANCN No WorkloadA SAN CN from the workload certificate, provides additional identity assertion SessionDurationSeconds No 3600 Maximum session duration in seconds (900–43200) NotificationEmail No (empty) Email address for certificate expiry notifications. When provided, creates an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic and an EventBridge rule

Important: The SessionDurationSeconds value must not exceed the IAM role’s MaxSessionDuration setting, which defaults to 3600 seconds (1 hour). If you request a longer session than the role allows, the CreateSession API returns an error. The companion template keeps both values in sync by setting the role’s MaxSessionDuration to the same parameter value. If you configure the role separately, update its MaxSessionDuration to match your desired session length. For more information, see IAM Roles Anywhere CreateSession API.

If the workload’s subject CN (WorkloadSubjectCN) doesn’t match the x509Subject CN of the authenticating certificate, the CreateSession call is denied. The same conditional verification applies to WorkloadIssuerCN and WorkloadSANCN.

The template enforces three certificate attribute conditions in the IAM trust policy: issuer CN, subject CN, and SAN CN must all match the values configured as parameters. Additionally, the trust policy scopes role assumption to the specific trust anchor Amazon Resource Name (ARN), preventing other trust anchors in the same account from assuming that role.

Conclusion

In this post, we discussed how AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, empowered by X.509 certificates, introduces a dynamic and secure way to manage workload identities and issue temporary access credentials. By understanding the trust model, using certificate attributes, and implementing fine-grained authorization, organizations can gain granular control over the effective permissions of these credentials.

The choice between just-in-time and short-lived certificates as workload identities depends on your specific requirements.

Adhering to best practices for private key storage is essential to maintain the integrity of your security infrastructure. Regularly rotating trust anchor certificates helps ensure the long-term trustworthiness of your system.

As you embark on your journey to implement IAM Roles Anywhere and integrate it with your PKI, remember that a well-architected approach to certificate management is a cornerstone of robust and resilient cloud security.

For additional deployment guidance, see Planning for your IAM Roles Anywhere deployment, which covers end-to-end deployment planning including network architecture, monitoring, and operational considerations.

If you have questions, you can start a new thread on AWS re:Post or reach out to AWS Support.

items.title: The AI Adoption Blind Spot: How Fake AI Tools Put Enterprises at Risk
items.summary: AI adoption is accelerating across enterprises, with employees increasingly relying on platforms like ChatGPT, Claude, and Microsoft Copilot for everyday work. Cybercriminals are exploiting this growing trust, distributing malicious applications disguised as legitimate AI tools to steal credentials, deliver malware, and gain access to corporate environments. Recent research by ANY.RUN reveals how attackers are impersonating popular AI brands to target corporate users, including developers and marketing teams. The findings highlight a growing challenge for security leaders: identifying threats hidden behind familiar applications before they lead to credential theft, compromised accounts, or wider business disruption. Who Is Most Exposed to Fake AI Attacks? Between April 15 and October 5, 2026, ANY.RUN researchers identified 1,258 public sandbox analyses linked to fake AI campaigns. The United States accounted for 16% of submissions with country information, ranking second after India (20%). US submissions also led in two major campaign groups involving fake Claude downloads and ChatGPT-themed attacks. The US is the second-largest source of submissions overall and ranks first in two major campaign groups The activity spans multiple industries. Technology appeared across all seven campaign queries examined by researchers, followed by telecommunications (six), education and consulting (five each), and manufacturing, healthcare, government, and finance (four each). Among US submissions, telecommunications and manufacturing appeared most frequently across the campaign queries. Attackers also tailor their methods to specific employee roles: Developers: Fake AI coding assistants and installation instructions can put source code, cloud credentials, and API keys at risk. In one sandbox session , researchers observed a counterfeit GitHub Copilot CLI page delivering malicious installation instructions. Marketing teams: Counterfeit AI advertising programs target employees with access to advertising budgets, billing systems, and business accounts. A fake Claude Ads campaign used a fraudulent Google sign-in window to capture credentials. Claude ads lure analyzed inside ANY.RUN sandbox Other corporate users: Fake desktop applications can expose employees to malware and browser-session theft. One trojanized Claude installer launched the legitimate application while secretly collecting browser data in the background. For business leaders, these findings show that fake AI threats are not limited to technology companies or IT departments . Exposure can arise wherever employees install AI applications or connect business accounts without adequate security oversight. Reduce the Impact of Fake AI Attacks. Detect malicious behavior earlier and contain threats faster. Strengthen Threat Response How Fake AI Attacks Unfold: From Trusted Brand to Corporate Compromise In every fake AI chain, the employee performs the key step ANY.RUN’s research highlights how attackers move from AI-branded lures to malicious execution and potential corporate compromise: Initial lure: Attackers impersonate ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini through counterfeit websites, advertisements, and shared AI conversations. Malicious delivery: Fake installers and setup instructions trick users into downloading malware or executing malicious commands disguised as legitimate installation steps. Payload execution: Once launched, malicious code can deploy information stealers or other malware on the employee’s device. Credential theft: Attackers attempt to collect passwords, session cookies, authentication tokens, and other sensitive data. Business impact: Stolen credentials and compromised sessions can enable unauthorized access to corporate systems, potentially leading to data exposure or further intrusion. Fake AI Threats Extend Beyond Windows Windows remains a major target for malware campaigns, but macOS devices are not immune. Fake AI installation pages can trick Mac users into copying malicious commands into Terminal, presenting dangerous actions as routine software setup instructions. For enterprises with mixed operating systems, this creates an additional investigation challenge. Limited visibility into macOS activity can leave security teams without the evidence needed to assess an incident , potentially delaying containment and leaving affected accounts or devices unidentified. AI attack asking the potential victim to download Claude on a macOS device Cross-platform behavioral analysis helps address this gap. For example, ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox supports Windows, Linux, Android, and macOS , allowing analysts to investigate suspicious files and URLs in isolated environments. Teams can observe malicious behavior, examine network connections, extract indicators of compromise (IOCs), and trace attack chains to determine what happened and what requires further investigation. Available operating systems inside ANY.RUN sandbox for cross-platform analysis With consistent investigation capabilities across operating systems, SOC teams can reduce blind spots, avoid fragmented investigations, and make more informed response decisions without relying on separate analysis workflows for every platform. Closing the AI Security Visibility Gap As AI adoption grows, enterprises need to ensure their security teams can investigate threats disguised as legitimate applications. This means looking beyond suspicious downloads to understand what executes on employee devices, which credentials may be exposed, and whether an attack has progressed further into the corporate environment. More than 16,000 organizations worldwide use ANY.RUN to investigate cyber threats and strengthen SOC operations. Teams using the solution report up to 36% higher detection rates, 21 minutes less MTTR per incident, and 30% fewer Tier 1-to-Tier 2 escalations . For enterprises, these improvements mean faster investigations, fewer unnecessary escalations, and more time for analysts to focus on critical threats. As attackers continue to exploit trusted AI brands, the priority for security leaders is clear: give SOC teams the cross-platform visibility and behavioral evidence they need to identify malicious activity early and contain threats before they cause wider business disruption. Help Your SOC Stop More Threats with the Same Team. Cut investigation time and reduce escalations. Scale SOC Performance

How Fake AI Attacks Unfold: From Trusted Brand to Corporate Compromise  In every fake AI chain, the employee performs the key step 

ANY.RUN’s research highlights how attackers move from AI-branded lures to malicious execution and potential corporate compromise: 

  1. Initial lure: Attackers impersonate ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini through counterfeit websites, advertisements, and shared AI conversations. 
  2. Malicious delivery: Fake installers and setup instructions trick users into downloading malware or executing malicious commands disguised as legitimate installation steps. 
  3. Payload execution: Once launched, malicious code can deploy information stealers or other malware on the employee’s device.

items.title: Node.js Releases Security Updates to Fix High-Severity TLS, DNS and Brotli Vulnerabilities
items.summary: Node.js has released security updates for its 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x branches to address ten vulnerabilities, including four high-severity flaws affecting DNS lookups, TLS certificate checks, and Brotli decompression. The supplied release details identify 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4 as the patched versions. The most serious potential outcome is remote code execution through the Brotli decoder. The October security update also covers HTTP connection handling, repeated random values, ZIP processing, and filesystem permission checks. Node.js scheduled the releases for October 21, 2026, and listed high severity as the highest risk across all three supported branches. CVE-2026-111497 affects the Brotli decoder in all three release lines. The supplied advisory describes an out-of-bounds write that permits remote code execution. This means the decoder can write outside its intended memory area. Applications that process untrusted Brotli-compressed content should receive particular attention during patch planning. However, the supplied notice does not explain the exact conditions needed for exploitation. Two high-severity vulnerabilities involve TLS certificate hostname checks. CVE-2026-105483 allows a hostname verification bypass when an IP address uses full-width digits, affecting Node.js 26.x and 24.x. Node.js Releases Security Updates CVE-2026-106069 involves hostnames that loosely resolve to an IP address and affects all three branches. Both concern whether a certificate correctly matches the intended destination. The fourth high-severity issue, CVE-2026-105482, causes dns.resolve to truncate names containing a NUL character. It affects all three release lines. The flaw raises concerns for applications that depend on consistent name handling before performing DNS lookups. These fixes follow earlier Node.js TLS authentication bypass patches , which also addressed differences in hostname handling and certificate verification. Three medium-severity issues broaden the update’s scope. CVE-2026-105481 allows a keep-alive socket to process a response written before its request was sent. CVE-2026-106072 concerns improper certificate validation for nonstandard IPv4 hostnames, allowing DNS certificate names to authenticate IP endpoints. CVE ID Severity Vulnerability Affected versions CVE-2026-105482 High DNS name truncation 26.x, 24.x, 22.x CVE-2026-105483 High TLS hostname verification bypass 26.x, 24.x CVE-2026-106069 High TLS hostname verification bypass 26.x, 24.x, 22.x CVE-2026-111497 High Brotli decoder RCE 26.x, 24.x, 22.x CVE-2026-105481 Medium HTTP request-response ordering flaw 26.x, 24.x, 22.x CVE-2026-106072 Medium Improper TLS certificate hostname validation 26.x, 24.x, 22.x CVE-2026-106074 Medium Repeated cryptographic random values 26.x, 24.x, 22.x CVE-2026-106070 Low ZIP validation failure exposes untrusted data 26.x CVE-2026-106071 Low Permission Model filesystem access bypass 26.x CVE-2026-106073 Low fs.realpathSync permission bypass 26.x, 24.x, 22.x CVE-2026-106074 affects cached random data stored in startup snapshots and single executable applications. Processes created from these artifacts can repeat values returned by crypto.randomUUID() and crypto.randomInt(). All three medium-severity flaws affect the 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x branches. The remaining issues carry low ratings. CVE-2026-106070 concerns attacker-controlled bytes returned after failed ZIP header checks. CVE-2026-106071 can grant excessive filesystem access through wildcard matching. Both affect 26.x. CVE-2026-106073 bypasses Permission Model checks through fs.realpathSync across all three branches. Previous Node.js Permission Model vulnerabilities also exposed gaps in filesystem restrictions. The release details also list updates to c-ares, CA certificates, Undici, OpenSSL, and SQLite, with branch coverage varying by component. Administrators should deploy the matching patched release, rebuild application images where needed, and restart affected services. Testing should cover outbound HTTPS connections, DNS handling, compressed content, and permission-restricted workloads. Teams should consult the official Node.js security announcement and avoid unsupported versions. The project warns that end-of-life branches remain affected even after security releases, so migrating to a supported branch is an important part of remediation. Editorial verification note: The live announcement retrieved during research still displayed the advance release notice, without the detailed CVEs or patched downloads. Those details above come from the release text you supplied and should be checked against the updated announcement before publication. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: PHP2Shell: Why websites are going offline for emergency security updates
items.summary: If you’ve encountered websites in maintenance mode today, it may be a security precaution. Reports of attacks targeting two critical PHP vulnerabilities have prompted warnings to install emergency updates and consider temporarily taking affected services offline until they can be patched. The vulnerabilities, known as PHP2Shell, are tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both carry a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10. Why this matters PHP is a programming language that works behind the scenes to power a large part of the web. It underpins WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, and many other applications, including software whose users may not realize PHP is involved. Successful exploitation could let an attacker run malicious code on an affected server without logging in. That code would run with the permissions available to the PHP process, potentially allowing attackers to steal application data, alter website content, or establish a backdoor . The PHP team says all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk. In some configurations, an attacker can trigger an exploit before the website’s own code even runs. Cloudflare’s chief technology officer, Dane Knecht, has reported “early attacks emerging,” while warning that firewall mitigations are only a stopgap. Emergency patches are now available The PHP team scheduled its emergency security updates for October 21 at 10:00 am ET (14:00 UTC). It has now released fixes in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 , and urges users to update immediately. Administrators should check with their hosting provider or operating system vendor for the appropriate updated packages. You may still encounter offline websites while administrators install the updates and check their systems. CERT-EU recommends identifying PHP-based applications and patching as soon as possible. Where an immediate fix is not feasible, it advises considering isolation of internet-facing applications from public networks. The risk may outlast today’s emergency The longer-term concern is forgotten infrastructure: abandoned websites, unsupported applications, and connected devices with PHP-based management interfaces. Vulnerable installations may remain exposed if nobody maintains them or a vendor no longer supplies updates. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive routine security updates from the PHP project. Administrators using those versions should check whether their vendor supplies a fix or arrange an upgrade to a supported version. Website owners should establish who updates their underlying PHP installation. Updating WordPress or its plugins is not the same as updating PHP. Hosting providers or server administrators may need to apply the fix. For visitors, temporary downtime alone doesn’t mean a website has been breached. It may reflect a protective decision while its administrators install updates. However, consumers need to be extra careful as a “trusted website” may no longer be trustworthy, and not just because of PHP2Shell, but also because of eight compromised TLS certificates . Shahak Shalev, Global Head of Scam and AI Research at Malwarebytes, said: “This is a goldmine for hackers. They can hijack real websites to take advantage of the site’s reputation to do things like phish people, serve malicious software from the trusted channel. The opportunities are endless.” What to do If you’re a website visitor: Some websites may temporarily go offline while they are patched. Watch for unexpected content, downloads, or redirects, and repeated login requests, even on familiar sites. If something looks wrong, leave the page. You don’t need to install PHP updates on your own device. If you’re a website owner: Ask your hosting or IT provider to confirm PHP fixes are installed , not just scheduled, across all your websites and applications. If they can’t patch immediately, ask whether affected services should temporarily be taken offline. If you manage your own servers, follow PHP’s update instructions . Using unsupported PHP? Check for a vendor fix or upgrade to a supported version. What Malwarebytes is doing Helping keep you safe from hacked websites: Malwarebytes web protection and Browser Guard block known harmful sites, scam pages, and dangerous downloads. Our researchers are watching for websites compromised through these flaws so we can quickly add them to our block lists. Updating our own websites: We use a managed hosting provider and are working with them to install the PHP fixes. We are closely monitoring our websites until the updates are in place. Stop threats before they can do any harm. Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks phishing pages and malicious sites automatically. Free, one click to install. Add it to your browser →

The vulnerabilities, known as PHP2Shell, are tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both carry a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10.

Why this matters

PHP is a programming language that works behind the scenes to power a large part of the web. It underpins WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, and many other applications, including software whose users may not realize PHP is involved.

Successful exploitation could let an attacker run malicious code on an affected server without logging in. That code would run with the permissions available to the PHP process, potentially allowing attackers to steal application data, alter website content, or establish a backdoor.

The PHP team says all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk. In some configurations, an attacker can trigger an exploit before the website’s own code even runs.

Cloudflare’s chief technology officer, Dane Knecht, has reported “early attacks emerging,” while warning that firewall mitigations are only a stopgap.

Emergency patches are now available

The PHP team scheduled its emergency security updates for October 21 at 10:00 am ET (14:00 UTC). It has now released fixes in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, and urges users to update immediately. Administrators should check with their hosting provider or operating system vendor for the appropriate updated packages.

You may still encounter offline websites while administrators install the updates and check their systems.

CERT-EU recommends identifying PHP-based applications and patching as soon as possible. Where an immediate fix is not feasible, it advises considering isolation of internet-facing applications from public networks.

The risk may outlast today’s emergency

The longer-term concern is forgotten infrastructure: abandoned websites, unsupported applications, and connected devices with PHP-based management interfaces. Vulnerable installations may remain exposed if nobody maintains them or a vendor no longer supplies updates.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive routine security updates from the PHP project. Administrators using those versions should check whether their vendor supplies a fix or arrange an upgrade to a supported version.

Website owners should establish who updates their underlying PHP installation. Updating WordPress or its plugins is not the same as updating PHP. Hosting providers or server administrators may need to apply the fix.

For visitors, temporary downtime alone doesn’t mean a website has been breached. It may reflect a protective decision while its administrators install updates.

However, consumers need to be extra careful as a “trusted website” may no longer be trustworthy, and not just because of PHP2Shell, but also because of eight compromised TLS certificates.

Shahak Shalev, Global Head of Scam and AI Research at Malwarebytes, said:

“This is a goldmine for hackers. They can hijack real websites to take advantage of the site’s reputation to do things like phish people, serve malicious software from the trusted channel. The opportunities are endless.”

If you’re a website visitor:

  • Some websites may temporarily go offline while they are patched.
  • Watch for unexpected content, downloads, or redirects, and repeated login requests, even on familiar sites.
  • If something looks wrong, leave the page.
  • You don’t need to install PHP updates on your own device.

If you’re a website owner:

  • Ask your hosting or IT provider to confirm PHP fixes are installed, not just scheduled, across all your websites and applications.
  • If they can’t patch immediately, ask whether affected services should temporarily be taken offline.
  • If you manage your own servers, follow PHP’s update instructions.
  • Using unsupported PHP? Check for a vendor fix or upgrade to a supported version.

items.title: Hackers Use AI-Powered Browsers to Hide Thousands of Fake Accounts and Bypass Security Detection
items.summary: Cybercriminals are using AI-enabled “antidetect” browsers to manage large networks of fake online accounts while making each profile appear to come from a different person, device, or location. Check Point Research reported that these tools can help a single operator or small group run thousands of accounts across social media and other platforms, making it harder for services to spot linked activity. The browsers have legitimate uses, but researchers documented their presence in criminal forums and marketplaces and described their use in fraud and account-takeover operations. Analysts at Check Point Research identified Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin as three tools with features that can support this activity. Their October 20, 2026 report says the platforms combine profile isolation and identity masking with automation, and in some cases AI integrations. The report does not claim that the browsers themselves are malware; it warns that criminals can misuse commercially available software to conceal coordinated operations. Hackers Use AI-Powered Browsers A website can collect details about a browser and device, including screen size, time zone, language, user agent, and graphics settings. Together, these details can help create a browser fingerprint. Platforms may compare fingerprints and activity patterns to identify accounts that appear to share a device or operator. Check Point says antidetect browsers can change or assign different values to profiles, making that comparison more difficult. A proxy seller on an underground forum listing Kameleo as part of a complete operational stack (Source – Check Point) The tools may also keep each profile’s cookies, local storage, and session information separate. Some can work with proxy services, which may make profiles appear to connect from different network locations. That can complicate checks based only on an account’s IP address or location. Cybersecurity News has also described how residential proxies can hide malicious traffic , although proxy use alone does not prove that activity is criminal. A more serious risk arises when criminals use stolen session cookies. A cookie can keep a user signed in after authentication; if it is stolen and reused, an attacker may access an active account without repeating the usual login process. Check Point says criminals can place stolen session data into a browser profile, potentially making the session appear familiar to a service. This is related to the risks in session-cookie theft and account takeover , where access to a logged-in session can undermine protections that focus on the initial sign-in. AI and automation increase the scale The report says AI features and automation can reduce the manual work needed to run many accounts. AdsPower, for example, advertises a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for connecting large language model workflows to browser profiles. The researchers describe a possible pipeline in which AI-generated text is paired with automated account activity and distribution. That does not mean every user of these products is conducting a campaign, but it can make coordinated misuse easier to scale. Some platforms also offer templates for repetitive actions and tools to build activity histories over time. This “warming” can make a new profile look less like a newly created account. Check Point warns that accounts may build credible histories or pass identity checks, which can delay detection until fraudulent activity begins. MultiLogin’s payment infrastructure (Source – Check Point) Potential misuse includes account takeover, payment fraud, fake loan applications, advertising fraud, phishing, malware distribution, and coordinated efforts to influence online discussion. The same concern applies to organizations whose staff accounts or customer accounts are targeted. A stolen session may be used to reach email, financial services, or other connected systems. The Cybersecurity News report on Microsoft 365 session theft after MFA offers a related example of why security teams need to monitor active sessions, not just passwords and login challenges. Check Point recommends looking beyond account behavior, because antidetect tools are designed to make individual profiles appear unrelated. Security teams should review network and infrastructure signals, including large-scale residential proxy activity, unusual browser fingerprint changes, and suspicious session-cookie patterns. Organizations should also check whether their session monitoring can identify unusual access to an already authenticated account. For platforms, account-level signals may still matter, but the report argues they should be combined with infrastructure analysis and investigation of suspicious patterns across profiles. For companies, security reviews should include scenarios in which a valid session is used from an unexpected device or network, even when no new password prompt appears. As with other session-hijacking methods, invalidating active sessions may be necessary when an account is confirmed compromised. The key point is that antidetect browsers are not a single malware family with one fixed signature. They are tools that can mask identity signals, while automation and AI can help criminals operate at greater scale. Defenders therefore need to link signals across accounts, devices, networks, and sessions instead of relying on one indicator alone. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- IoC type Indicator from the source Notes SHA-256 / file hash Not provided The report discusses commercial browser tools and their misuse, not a specific malware sample. Domain or IP address Not provided No campaign infrastructure is listed as an IoC. Detection signals Residential proxy activity at scale; unusual fingerprint changes; suspicious cookie-injection or pre-authenticated-session patterns Treat these as investigation leads, not proof of compromise. Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. items.title: Millions of PHP Instances Exposed - What Organizations Need To Do Right Now
items.summary: Two critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) have been published. Both vulnerabilities carry a severe CVSS score of 9.2 (more technical details are in the Unit 42 Threat Brief ). This is not just another high-severity vulnerability disclosure, it marks the opening chapter in a massive acceleration of cyberthreats that will define the foreseeable future. Because PHP is widely used globally (by some estimates, more than half of all websites), the sheer scale of this is massive. Navigating this new reality demands immediate imperatives, including continuous, proactive vulnerability discovery before adversaries weaponize code, and a modern defense strategy that pairs traditional patching with real-time virtual patching. At a footprint of 22 million exposed instances, relying on manual remediation cycles alone is not a viable defense. Don't wait for manual patches to expose your web footprint. items.title: Hackers Use Gentlemen Ransomware to Disable Windows Defender and Destroy Backups
items.summary: A ransomware operation known as The Gentlemen is using a mix of security tampering, service disruption and file encryption to make recovery harder for affected organizations. Its Windows malware can turn off Microsoft Defender’s real-time protection, add broad exclusions that reduce scanning, stop backup-related services and delete Volume Shadow Copies. These steps weaken defenses and remove common ways to restore files after encryption. The malware also targets more than files. It can clear event logs and other system records that investigators may need to understand what happened. The group uses a double-extortion model: attackers can steal data as well as encrypt it, raising the risk of public exposure even when a victim has backups. The sequence is a reminder that a successful ransomware response depends on protecting both systems and recovery data. Analysts from Acronis’ Threat Research Unit identified these behaviors in its technical analysis of The Gentlemen ransomware and associated tools. The report describes a Go-based ransomware-as-a-service operation that emerged in 2025 and targets Windows, Linux, network-attached storage and BSD systems. Acronis says the group has claimed more than 800 victims, though that figure reflects the group’s claims rather than independently confirmed infections. On Windows, the ransomware attempts to disable Defender’s real-time monitoring and add its process and the C: drive to the exclusion list. That may allow the malware to run with less interference while it prepares to encrypt files. It also stops selected processes and services linked to security tools, databases, virtual machines, email and backup products. Cyber Security News has previously covered how Gentlemen operators disable defenses and backup services during intrusions. The impact is not limited to security software. Stopping database or virtualization services can free files for encryption, while disrupting backup software may prevent routine recovery jobs from running. Hackers Use Gentlemen Ransomware Before encryption, the malware also attempts to remove available Volume Shadow Copies, which Windows can use to restore earlier versions of files. It can clear selected Windows logs, prefetch data and PowerShell command history, reducing the local evidence available to responders. Acronis found that the ransomware can establish persistence through scheduled tasks and Windows startup registry entries. It can also search for connected drives and, when the relevant option is used, network shares. With its spreading feature enabled, it can identify a domain and use PsExec to copy and run the ransomware on other workstations. This behavior connects one compromised machine to broader network risk, a pattern also detailed in Cyber Security News’ coverage of Gentlemen ransomware spreading across networks . The encryption process is designed to move quickly. The report says files under 1 MB are encrypted in full, while larger files may be encrypted in sections. Data leak site (Source – Acronis) The malware uses ChaCha20 for file encryption and elliptic-curve cryptography to protect the file keys. Encrypted files receive an extension that can vary between builds, and the malware leaves a ransom note in affected folders. Acronis also identified a separate tool used to terminate security processes. It drops vulnerable drivers, installs them as services and uses them to stop selected processes at the kernel level. One driver is linked to Safetica ProcessMonitorDriver, associated in the report with CVE-2025-70795; the other is Lenovo’s BootRepair.sys. The technique is known as “bring your own vulnerable driver”: attackers abuse a driver with a weakness to gain actions that ordinary user-level tools may not permit. For more context, see Cyber Security News’ report on vulnerable drivers used against EDR . For defenders, the warning signs include unexpected Defender setting changes, security or backup services stopping, unfamiliar driver installations, log clearing and rapid file changes across multiple systems. Organizations should investigate Organizations should investigate these events together rather than as isolated alerts. Acronis recommends keeping endpoint detection tools active, patching systems and drivers, limiting administrative access, monitoring PowerShell and remote administration tools, and segmenting networks to restrict spread. Backups should be regularly tested and protected with access controls that prevent ordinary compromised systems from deleting or changing them. Keeping critical copies offline or isolated from production can preserve a recovery path if attackers reach administrator accounts. Microsoft likewise advises restoring from verified offline or immutable backups after ransomware incidents. These measures cannot prevent every intrusion, but they can reduce the chance that one compromised device turns into a prolonged outage.
