items.title: How Fidelis Network Supports Zero Trust Network Security for the Department of Defense
items.summary: Key Takeaways Zero trust network security assumes that network location or previous authentication needs to prove its trustworthiness. Segmentation is only as good as the traffic evidence behind it, and protecting mission data means watching where that data goes. Deep Session Inspection and retrospective analysis give investigators more to work with than connection logs do. Zero Trust network security is best measured by what happens when trust is abused. Fidelis Network gives defense SOCs a way to detect suspicious communications and attacker behavior even when access looks authorized. The Department of Defense can verify every login, enforce strict access policy, and segment its networks, and still have no good answer to a simple question: What happens when an adversary starts operating through an account or connection the system already trusts? A September 2026 U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report [1] found that 6 of the 18 major DoD IT business programs it reviewed had not developed plans to implement Zero Trust architecture by the 2027 deadline. Much of that work falls under the following categories: Policy deployment Stronger authentication Tighter access rules Finer segmentation However, these controls decide who gets in and which paths are open in the network. They say nothing about whether the policies match how the network actually behaves, or what a trusted identity does after the door opens. A serious zero trust approach to network security has to answer three things. Do the policies hold up against real traffic? Is legitimate access being misused? Can suspicious behavior be investigated without disrupting critical operations? All three are network questions, and the network is where Fidelis Network ® earns an evaluation. It is built to examine activities even after access has been granted, which is the stage most Zero Trust programs do not cover. Trusting Your Zero Trust Architecture with Fidelis Security Enterprise-wide visibility Transactional monitoring Zero Trust in Action Read the Guide What Zero Trust Network Security Means for the Department of Defense Zero trust network security drops the assumption that network location or a previous authentication is trustworthy. Access is granted according to: Identity Device posture Policy Resource sensitivity It is calibrated again when the conditions change. Of the pillars in the DoD’s Zero Trust model, Network & Environment and Visibility & Analytics deserve the closest attention from network security leaders. Together they describe a requirement that goes beyond permission checks. Defenders need to see communications inside their environments, and they need enough evidence to recognize when behavior shifts. This is because the zero trust network security model is a decision framework, but a decision is only as reliable as the information behind it. Fidelis Network supplies the missing information through: Continuous traffic inspection Threat detection Investigation capabilities This helps security teams identify when apparently trusted activity deserves a closer look or a change in enforcement. How Does Fidelis Network Help with Zero Trust Network Security? Segmentation Starts with Knowing What Actually Communicates Implementing Zero Trust usually begins with a mapping problem. Before you can restrict communication between any two systems, you need to know the relationship between them. The systems that depend on each other should continue to communicate, but the ones that are not related their connection should not exist. In a large defense environment, those dependencies run across: Administrative systems Operational infrastructure Mission-support applications Remote installations Approved hybrid environments Segment too tightly and you break a service someone depends on. Segment too loosely and you leave adversaries room to move after a compromise. Most teams discover that the manually maintained inventory they planned around does not reflect what is really on the wire. The DoD Network & Environment pillar treats data flow mapping as a foundational capability, and Fidelis Network addresses it through: Passive asset discovery Asset profiling Risk assessment Cyber terrain mapping Rather than relying on inventories someone has to keep current by hand, it uses observed communications to identify assets, understand their relationships, and reveal the network paths between them. An architect can use that to ask practical questions: Which systems regularly talk to a given mission-support application? Is a management server reaching resources outside its expected operational area? Which unmanaged or legacy assets are showing up in traffic? Does the traffic between two segments reflect a real operational dependency? Consider a maintenance application that needs periodic contact with a system in another network zone. If the connection is blocked without understanding the dependency, the operations will get interrupted. And if it is left open permanently, it is a standing risk that nobody reviews. In such cases, observed traffic evidence enables the architect to separate an expected dependency from a connection that needs scrutiny, which means segmentation decisions rest on measured behavior instead of assumptions about how the environment works. Segmentation Does Not Stop an Attacker Who is Already Inside Micro-segmentation helps by limiting unnecessary communication between systems. But assuming segmentation will stop malicious activity is a mistake. Unfortunately, Zero Trust programs drift into it when enforcement becomes the main measure of progress. For instance, when an attacker who has compromised a trusted account spends most of the time moving between systems inside the policy-permitted zone, that movement may never produce a new perimeter event. In such cases if the security team is watching the boundaries will never be aware of the most consequential phase of the attack. This is the gap Fidelis Network ® Deep Session Inspection addresses, and it is where reliance on flow records or perimeter alerts falls short. Flow Data Deep Session Inspection (DSI) Flow data can establish: Two systems communicated When they communicated How much data moved DSI reassembles: observed sessions decodes supported application protocols extracts richer communication metadata and content where available. Fidelis Network combines deep session inspection with behavioral analytics and threat intelligence to flag suspicious activity across monitored traffic. The platform supports boundary-focused monitoring, and internal sensors are designed to analyze east-west traffic. For a defense SOC, the objective is to catch movement before the attacker reaches additional high-value resources, and in such cases, internal visibility is what makes that objective achievable. Inspecting Encrypted Traffic Without Assuming Everything Can Be Decrypted Encryption is essential to protecting military and defense communications, and security teams still have to investigate those communications. The practical question is how much can be learned without requiring access to every encrypted payload. Fidelis Network handles this with two complementary methods. The first is session metadata analysis . DSI examines available TLS and network metadata to identify suspicious patterns without decrypting the underlying content. The second is deeper content inspection where it is authorized. Fidelis supports decrypted traffic inspection through appropriate deployment integrations and policies, including supported proxy-based inspection workflows. Support for both is important in DoD environments, where encryption requirements, security boundaries, and mission sensitivity can restrict where decryption is permitted at all. Fidelis can examine encrypted traffic without treating all of it as readable content. In practice, that lets architects choose inspection methods to fit the technical and security constraints of each part of the network, instead of forcing one approach across all of them. Mission Data Needs Protection After Access is Granted Zero Trust is fundamentally not about controlling who enters the network, but protecting resources and information. For defense organizations, the exposure covers: Operational information Sensitive communications Personnel records Technical documents Other mission-related data Not every exposure involves a sophisticated intrusion. Key Takeaways
  • Zero trust network security assumes that network location or previous authentication needs to prove its trustworthiness.
  • Segmentation is only as good as the traffic evidence behind it, and protecting mission data means watching where that data goes.
  • Deep Session Inspection and retrospective analysis give investigators more to work with than connection logs do.
  • Zero Trust network security is best measured by what happens when trust is abused.
  • Fidelis Network gives defense SOCs a way to detect suspicious communications and attacker behavior even when access looks authorized.

The Department of Defense can verify every login, enforce strict access policy, and segment its networks, and still have no good answer to a simple question:

What happens when an adversary starts operating through an account or connection the system already trusts?

A September 2026 U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report[1] found that 6 of the 18 major DoD IT business programs it reviewed had not developed plans to implement Zero Trust architecture by the 2027 deadline.

Much of that work falls under the following categories:

  • Policy deployment
  • Stronger authentication
  • Tighter access rules
  • Finer segmentation

However, these controls decide who gets in and which paths are open in the network. They say nothing about whether the policies match how the network actually behaves, or what a trusted identity does after the door opens.

A serious zero trust approach to network security has to answer three things.

  • Do the policies hold up against real traffic?
  • Is legitimate access being misused?
  • Can suspicious behavior be investigated without disrupting critical operations?

All three are network questions, and the network is where Fidelis Network® earns an evaluation. It is built to examine activities even after access has been granted, which is the stage most Zero Trust programs do not cover.

What Zero Trust Network Security Means for the Department of Defense

Zero trust network security drops the assumption that network location or a previous authentication is trustworthy. Access is granted according to:

  • Identity
  • Device posture
  • Policy
  • Resource sensitivity

It is calibrated again when the conditions change.

Of the pillars in the DoD’s Zero Trust model, Network & Environment and Visibility & Analytics deserve the closest attention from network security leaders. Together they describe a requirement that goes beyond permission checks.

Defenders need to see communications inside their environments, and they need enough evidence to recognize when behavior shifts. This is because the zero trust network security model is a decision framework, but a decision is only as reliable as the information behind it.

Fidelis Network supplies the missing information through:

  • Continuous traffic inspection
  • Threat detection
  • Investigation capabilities

This helps security teams identify when apparently trusted activity deserves a closer look or a change in enforcement.

How Does Fidelis Network Help with Zero Trust Network Security?
Segmentation Starts with Knowing What Actually Communicates

Implementing Zero Trust usually begins with a mapping problem. Before you can restrict communication between any two systems, you need to know the relationship between them. The systems that depend on each other should continue to communicate, but the ones that are not related their connection should not exist.

In a large defense environment, those dependencies run across:

  • Administrative systems
  • Operational infrastructure
  • Mission-support applications
  • Remote installations
  • Approved hybrid environments

Segment too tightly and you break a service someone depends on. Segment too loosely and you leave adversaries room to move after a compromise. Most teams discover that the manually maintained inventory they planned around does not reflect what is really on the wire.

The DoD Network & Environment pillar treats data flow mapping as a foundational capability, and Fidelis Network addresses it through:

  • Passive asset discovery
  • Asset profiling
  • Risk assessment
  • Cyber terrain mapping

Rather than relying on inventories someone has to keep current by hand, it uses observed communications to identify assets, understand their relationships, and reveal the network paths between them.

An architect can use that to ask practical questions:

  • Which systems regularly talk to a given mission-support application?
  • Is a management server reaching resources outside its expected operational area?
  • Which unmanaged or legacy assets are showing up in traffic?
  • Does the traffic between two segments reflect a real operational dependency?

Consider a maintenance application that needs periodic contact with a system in another network zone. If the connection is blocked without understanding the dependency, the operations will get interrupted. And if it is left open permanently, it is a standing risk that nobody reviews.

In such cases, observed traffic evidence enables the architect to separate an expected dependency from a connection that needs scrutiny, which means segmentation decisions rest on measured behavior instead of assumptions about how the environment works.

Segmentation Does Not Stop an Attacker Who is Already Inside

Micro-segmentation helps by limiting unnecessary communication between systems. But assuming segmentation will stop malicious activity is a mistake. Unfortunately, Zero Trust programs drift into it when enforcement becomes the main measure of progress.

For instance, when an attacker who has compromised a trusted account spends most of the time moving between systems inside the policy-permitted zone, that movement may never produce a new perimeter event. In such cases if the security team is watching the boundaries will never be aware of the most consequential phase of the attack.

This is the gap Fidelis Network® Deep Session Inspection addresses, and it is where reliance on flow records or perimeter alerts falls short.

For a defense SOC, the objective is to catch movement before the attacker reaches additional high-value resources, and in such cases, internal visibility is what makes that objective achievable.

Encryption is essential to protecting military and defense communications, and security teams still have to investigate those communications. The practical question is how much can be learned without requiring access to every encrypted payload.

Support for both is important in DoD environments, where encryption requirements, security boundaries, and mission sensitivity can restrict where decryption is permitted at all.

Fidelis can examine encrypted traffic without treating all of it as readable content. In practice, that lets architects choose inspection methods to fit the technical and security constraints of each part of the network, instead of forcing one approach across all of them.

items.title: Google Upgrades Chrome With Gemini AI to Detect Fake Antivirus and Browser Update Scams
items.summary: Google has upgraded Chrome’s Enhanced Protection mode with a more powerful Gemini AI model to detect fake antivirus alerts , browser update scams, and other deceptive websites. Announced on October 20, 2026, the changes also introduce suspicious site warnings and protection against ClickFix attacks that trick users into running malicious commands. The update expands Google’s earlier work on AI scam detection. Chrome previously used an on-device Gemini model on supported devices to identify tech support scams. Google has now moved this analysis to a server-side model, extending the feature to all users who enable Enhanced Protection rather than limiting it to compatible hardware. Chrome Gemini AI Detects Fake Scams According to Google’s announcement , Gemini examines page content for signs of fraud. It identifies the brand a website claims to represent, assesses the page’s purpose, and produces a score showing how likely it is to be a scam. Safe Browsing combines these findings with domain reputation and other security signals before reaching a final verdict. This means Gemini does not decide whether to block a website by itself. Suspicious site warnings in Chrome (source: Google) Its analysis provides another layer of evidence, helping Chrome assess pages that use convincing security messages or browser branding to pressure visitors into taking unsafe actions. Google says Chrome sends page text for analysis only when a website shows strong scam indicators. The company says it processes this content temporarily and never logs, retains, or uses it to train its models. These safeguards apply to page content sent for this detection process. Chrome is also introducing two levels of site warnings for Enhanced Protection users. Suspicious site warnings flag deceptive patterns when Google has lower confidence about the threat. These warnings differ in appearance, wording, colors, and icons from warnings for confirmed dangerous websites. Dangerous site warnings in Chrome (source: Google) Known malicious sites will continue to trigger Chrome’s familiar full-page red warning. This approach lets Google warn about more potentially harmful pages while keeping possible risks separate from high-confidence threats. The update also addresses ClickFix, a technique that asks visitors to copy and run commands to repair a fake problem. Cybersecurity News has previously covered fake Chrome error pages that guide users into executing hidden PowerShell scripts. A ClickFix scam (source: Google) These attacks move malware downloads into tools such as PowerShell or cmd.exe, outside Chrome’s normal download checks. Related reporting on DriveSurge’s fake browser updates shows how attackers combine familiar update prompts with command-based infection methods. Chrome now detects suspicious commands copied during potential ClickFix attempts. It removes personally identifiable information from the copied content before sending it to Safe Browsing. A dangerous verdict triggers a warning, with checks designed to limit disruption to legitimate developer work. Users must enable Enhanced Protection to receive these features. Google provides instructions in its Chrome Safe Browsing guide. Google also stresses that Chrome will never ask users to repair the browser by copying and running commands from a webpage. items.title: LiteLLM Compromised – Hackers Injected an Infostealer and RAT in the Latest 1.107.0 PyPI Release
items.summary: LiteLLM version 1.107.0 was compromised on PyPI on October 21, 2026, spreading a credential stealer and a remote access trojan through all seven distributed wheel files. The malicious release also reached Docker images, putting developer systems, build runners, and AI services at risk. Aikido warned that anyone who installed the affected release should assume credentials were exposed. PyPI removed version 1.107.0, but taking down the package does not remove malware already installed or invalidate secrets attackers may have stolen. Socket’s investigation said its scanner flagged all seven wheels seven minutes after publication. Detection speed matters because automated dependency updates can pull a poisoned release into multiple environments before a human reviews the package change. How the LiteLLM Malware Runs The attack uses Python startup hooks rather than relying on an application to import LiteLLM. According to Wiz’s technical analysis , installation places three files, cook.pth , cook.py , and sitecustomize.py , directly inside Python’s site-packages directory. When Python starts, cook.pth imports cook.py , which decodes its hidden code and starts the credential theft routine. This means an unrelated Python command can trigger the payload after installation, even when the user never opens LiteLLM directly. The stealer searches for system information, browser data, developer secrets, cloud credentials, and authentication files used by AI tools. Reported targets include SSH private keys, AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials, browser passwords, and tokens for tools such as Claude and GitHub Copilot. Collected information is encrypted and sent through an HTTP POST request to www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck . Wiz identifies the destination as attacker controlled and designed to resemble LiteLLM infrastructure. The stealer also writes a marker at /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb , although that path can fail on Windows. A separate startup file, sitecustomize.py , provides the remote code loading path on Linux and macOS. It tries to retrieve domain.txt from the GitHub repository letters9813/pythonclient-test , then uses the returned address to download and execute another Python script from a /codepy endpoint. This gives attackers a route to run additional code when affected Python environments start again. However, capability should not be confused with confirmed activity. Wiz reported that domain.txt had not been populated during its analysis and that the repository was subsequently taken down. Container users also need to investigate. Wiz identified affected LiteLLM images on GitHub Container Registry and Docker Hub, including v1.107.0 , latest , main-latest , and main-stable . A familiar image tag therefore does not establish that a deployment is clean. The public incident discussion also points to build records naming Berri-AI/litellm , a lookalike repository that differs from the legitimate BerriAI/litellm project by one hyphen. That finding raises questions about release source validation, but does not establish the full intrusion path or attacker identity. Teams that installed LiteLLM 1.107.0 should isolate affected hosts and runners, preserve relevant logs, and treat accessible secrets as potentially stolen. Investigations should cover package installation records, container deployments, Python startup files, and outbound connections to the reported collection endpoint. Rotate and revoke exposed cloud keys, SSH keys, browser sessions, repository tokens, and AI service credentials from a clean system. Replacing only the LiteLLM package is not enough when stolen credentials can still provide access elsewhere. Wiz identified 1.106.2 as the most recent safe version in its report. Rebuild affected environments from trusted sources and pin container deployments to verified image digests rather than relying on moving tags. Review cloud and source control logs for unexpected access after installation. This is LiteLLM’s second reported supply chain compromise this year. Cyber Security News previously covered the LiteLLM supply chain attack involving versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 and the later investigation into exposed cloud keys and CI/CD secrets . Those earlier findings do not prove the same attackers caused this incident. They show why brief package exposure can create a much longer security problem. Removing a malicious release limits new downloads, while recovery still depends on finding affected systems, removing startup backdoors, and cutting off stolen access. items.title: China-Linked Hackers Turn Trusted Windows Applications Into Backdoors to Steal Credentials
items.summary: China-linked hackers are using trusted Windows applications to load hidden backdoors, collect system details, and steal Active Directory credential data. The group, tracked as BRONZE SANDCASTLE, places malicious files beside legitimate software, allowing familiar programs to run attacker-controlled code without changing the original application. The campaign shows how genuine software can become part of an attack chain. Similar China-linked DLL sideloading attacks have abused trusted applications to hide malicious activity, although shared techniques alone do not establish a connection between threat groups. Researchers from Sophos’ Counter Threat Unit and SophosLabs identified the malware while investigating incidents across Asia and Africa. Their technical report on the campaign, published October 20, describes attacks observed between August 2025 and August 2026 involving victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely South Korea. China-Linked Hackers Turn Trusted Windows Applications Sandboxie DLL sideloading is the group’s clearest technical marker. Attackers placed legitimate Sandboxie programs beside a malicious supporting library. When launched, the trusted application loaded that library and handed execution to the attackers. The report also documents abused components from Java, Krita, NVDA, LINE, and Microsoft Sysinternals. The malicious libraries typically read an encrypted payload from a local configuration file, decode it, and execute code in memory. This separates the visible application from the hidden backdoor and lets operators change payload behavior without replacing the loading library. Renamed executables further help the files blend into compromised systems. Sample DLL sideloading components (Source – Sophos) Other ShadowPad DLL sideloading campaigns have used a comparable three-part structure: a legitimate program, a malicious library, and an encrypted payload. That similarity provides useful context, but Sophos tracks BRONZE SANDCASTLE separately because its observed activity could not be reliably linked to BRONZE PRESIDENT or BRONZE ATLAS. Modified Meterpreter Payload Steals System Data The decoded backdoor uses a reflective loader, which places an embedded Windows program into memory. Although its structure resembles Metasploit shellcode, Sophos found custom function-resolution routines and a larger, more complex codebase than standard examples. Elements of COFFLoader also suggest custom features for use after a system is compromised. Researchers identified payload versions 1.1.5 and 1.1.7. The backdoor sends its control server a structured JSON message containing computer and user names, domain details, operating system version, internal and public IP addresses, process information, working directory, processor type, and startup time. Version 1.1.5 contacted dedicated control domains, while version 1.1.7 downloaded encrypted configuration files through GitHub. Connections to legitimate file-sharing and messaging services may also have supported operator instructions, although Sophos did not confirm that purpose. After gaining access, the operators used Windows network commands to inspect accounts and local networks. They also created Volume Shadow Copies before copying the Active Directory database. China-linked hackers are using trusted Windows applications to load hidden backdoors, collect system details, and steal Active Directory credential data.

The group, tracked as BRONZE SANDCASTLE, places malicious files beside legitimate software, allowing familiar programs to run attacker-controlled code without changing the original application.

The campaign shows how genuine software can become part of an attack chain. Similar China-linked DLL sideloading attacks have abused trusted applications to hide malicious activity, although shared techniques alone do not establish a connection between threat groups.

Researchers from Sophos’ Counter Threat Unit and SophosLabs identified the malware while investigating incidents across Asia and Africa.

Their technical report on the campaign, published October 20, describes attacks observed between August 2025 and August 2026 involving victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely South Korea.

China-Linked Hackers Turn Trusted Windows Applications

Sandboxie DLL sideloading is the group’s clearest technical marker. Attackers placed legitimate Sandboxie programs beside a malicious supporting library.

When launched, the trusted application loaded that library and handed execution to the attackers. The report also documents abused components from Java, Krita, NVDA, LINE, and Microsoft Sysinternals.

The malicious libraries typically read an encrypted payload from a local configuration file, decode it, and execute code in memory.

This separates the visible application from the hidden backdoor and lets operators change payload behavior without replacing the loading library. Renamed executables further help the files blend into compromised systems.

Sample DLL sideloading components (Source – Sophos)

Other ShadowPad DLL sideloading campaigns have used a comparable three-part structure: a legitimate program, a malicious library, and an encrypted payload.

That similarity provides useful context, but Sophos tracks BRONZE SANDCASTLE separately because its observed activity could not be reliably linked to BRONZE PRESIDENT or BRONZE ATLAS.

Modified Meterpreter Payload Steals System Data

The decoded backdoor uses a reflective loader, which places an embedded Windows program into memory. Although its structure resembles Metasploit shellcode, Sophos found custom function-resolution routines and a larger, more complex codebase than standard examples. Elements of COFFLoader also suggest custom features for use after a system is compromised.

Researchers identified payload versions 1.1.5 and 1.1.7. The backdoor sends its control server a structured JSON message containing computer and user names, domain details, operating system version, internal and public IP addresses, process information, working directory, processor type, and startup time.

Version 1.1.5 contacted dedicated control domains, while version 1.1.7 downloaded encrypted configuration files through GitHub.

Connections to legitimate file-sharing and messaging services may also have supported operator instructions, although Sophos did not confirm that purpose.

After gaining access, the operators used Windows network commands to inspect accounts and local networks. They also created Volume Shadow Copies before copying the Active Directory database.

This activity connects the backdoor’s remote access with attempts to obtain sensitive domain credential data. Previous Windows shadow copy abuse shows why this sequence matters: snapshots can expose protected database contents.

items.title: 5 takeaways from the State of Software Delivery Q3 Pulse report
Your AI agent fixed the bug, but what else did it change?
items.summary: Today we’re publishing patching-bugs and regression-hunt , two plugins that let engineers delegate patch development and regression checks to agents. Our patching-bugs plugin reproduces reported bugs, develops fixes, and tests them. The regression-hunt plugin checks whether any changes break previously working and supported behavior. Engineers can direct the work and review their results; maintainers can supply their own security assumptions and patching requirements, so the agents work within the project’s rules. We built patching-bugs and regression-hunt through Patch the Planet , our joint initiative with OpenAI, where we’ve co-authored hundreds of security patches for widely used open-source projects. Motivated by our major successes on projects like Scapy , our plugins draw on our analysis of merged patches and thousands of our engineers’ Codex sessions. The plugins provide maintainers with a structured workflow, evidence, independent checks, and best practices to improve their patching hygiene. In our preliminary evaluations, regression-hunt produces 25% fewer false-positive findings than a baseline Codex agent prompted to “review the PR for regressions.” Standardizing the patching process Our September post reported regressions introduced by some of our Patch the Planet patches. Since then, we’ve reviewed every patch that a Trail of Bits engineer authored and maintainers merged upstream. The review confirmed 21 regressions from over 130 PRs merged: 16 functional, one performance, and four build/test. None broke a security protection. (“Regression” refers to a new defect introduced by a change that breaks previously correct and supported behavior along a path a real user or attacker can reach.) For each patch, an agent looked for potential regressions, confirmed each one with a proof-of-concept (PoC) run before and after the change, and then passed the results to an engineer for review. The review was noisy: today’s bug disclosures arrive at an unprecedented speed and scale, and for patching to keep pace, the industry needs to increase its signal-to-noise ratio. The 21 confirmed regressions were identified among 58 candidates in a single run (~36% precision). But because agents take many different approaches and reach different results, each run generates more candidates to manually sort through. That led us to two conclusions: To introduce fewer regressions, we needed a standard way to write patches, with the same checks applied every time. To catch the regressions we still introduce, we needed a standard way to check for them, with written rules for what counts as a regression. Standardizing both steps also makes every run repeatable and comparable. No fixed checklist will catch every regression, so we collect agent trajectories from our engineers’ patching sessions, and use the tasks that an earlier version failed to benchmark for the next one (figure 1). Figure 1: Feedback loop for generating and evaluating patches. How we designed the plugins We used two primary sources to guide the design of our plugins: a review of every patch we merged upstream and the thousands of Codex sessions our engineers used to write those patches. This led to four principles that shaped our patching-bugs and regression-hunt plugins: Opinionated guidance in as few words as possible. We give the agent wide latitude and record only Trail of Bits’ judgment of what constitutes a good patch and a real regression. The goal is to direct the agent towards the desired result with the least possible guidance. Modular steps. You don’t have to run either plugin end-to-end, as both provide multiple skills that can be used in tandem or in isolation. Strict input and output schemas. Every step takes and returns a defined schema that includes the claim, the code revision, the required check, the raw evidence, and open questions. Fixed schemas reduce variability across runs and allow each step to verify the previous step’s work rather than trusting its summary. A live proof of concept for every claim. Every conclusion depends on a PoC run against a live deployment: a built, running instance of the project, reached through the interfaces a real user would use. When reproducing a bug, proving a fix, and confirming a regression, if a step can’t produce a live PoC, its result is inconclusive. regression-hunt reduces false positive rates The regression-hunt plugin (Figure 2): Enumerates candidate regressions by tracing the changed code (the diff) through its callers to its real interfaces. Reproduces each candidate regression on a live deployment of the system. Replays the PoC on the live deployment on a fresh-context agent. Judges the results of all the previous steps to validate that the proof meets the requirements of a regression. Figure 2: The regression-hunt workflow. In addition to the four principles above, there are two core aspects that are critical to the plugin: Defining a regression: The plugin has strong opinions about what a regression is and, more importantly, what a regression is NOT. The burden of proof is placed on the agent (specifically during the “adjudication agent” step) to prove that there is sufficient evidence to show that the suspected regression is not a false positive, an incomplete fix, a latent bug, a pre-existing bug, and so on. The plugin only reports a regression if all of these gates are passed. Incorporating a threat model: If a threat model is available, the orchestrator will intentionally pass this document as part of the global context for each individual agentic step. This is an attempt to require each step/agent to refer back to the threat model before reaching its conclusion. Our review of merged PRs yielded a set of 21 confirmed regressions that we could use to evaluate regression-hunt. We used the whole set to compare the plugin with a baseline Codex agent prompted to “review the PR for regressions.” Across those runs, regression-hunt produced 25% fewer false-positive findings than the baseline, with a 95% confidence interval of 14% to 38%. Its strict evidence requirements also left some known regressions classified as borderline: the plugin identified a possible regression but did not gather enough evidence to confirm it. Fewer false positives therefore came with a tradeoff in how many known regressions it could confidently report. Next, we’ll investigate why these cases remained borderline and improve the plugin’s strategies for gathering evidence. Our goal is to confirm more real regressions while giving maintainers clearer information when the evidence remains inconclusive. patching-bugs streamlines best practices from thousands of agent sessions The patching-bugs plugin is a distillation of all the best practices we’ve identified by analyzing thousands of Codex sessions by Trail of Bits engineers (Figure 3). In addition to the more traditional capabilities (such as reproduction on live deployments and independent adversarial review), the plugin emphasizes: The three-arm proof : The proof runs the same reproduction against three specifications: the original code must fail, the patched code must pass, and a complete revert must fail again. Bringing the bug back by removing the patch provides stronger evidence that the patch—rather than an unrelated environment or test change—actually fixed the bug. Invariant-guided repair: The patch attempts to fix the underlying, violated security invariant rather than fix the specific bug. This helps generalize the patch for possible variants of the same bug class. Incorporates regression analysis: The plugin mandates that regression-hunt is run to ensure that any patch goes through the same standard pipeline to check for mistakes. Figure 3: The patching-bugs workflow. What’s next for the plugins Both patching-bugs and regression-hunt will continue to evolve. Our engineers are using them in their Patch the Planet work now, and we’re collecting data on how they’re being used, what works, and what doesn’t. That data, along with better evaluations, will shape the next version’s capabilities: Evaluate patching-bugs. We’re building an evaluation that measures whether the plugin’s patches fix the reported bug and its variants without introducing regressions. Learn from agent traces. We’re analyzing the first batch of trace-level data from our engineers’ sessions. It will show whether Codex follows the rules and definitions required at each step, which steps it skips, and where its evidence is weakest. Make the plugins more configurable. patching-bugs already reads a project’s own patching guidelines (more on that in a bit). Next, we want maintainers to be able to choose whether to minimize patch sets—or, when broader coverage is worth more false positives, to loosen regression-hunt’s rules to surface more candidates. These plugins encode best practices we’ve found for an agent to patch a bug properly, and they improve when you tell them how your project works. The plugins work best when you input two kinds of project knowledge: A THREAT_MODEL.md , which tells agents what counts as a vulnerability or a regression. The regression-hunt plugin passes it to every step, so each agent has to check its conclusions against the file. It should define the following: assets whose compromise matters, trust boundaries, access controls, supported configurations, specifications on what is or isn’t a vulnerability, and evidence required for a valid bug report ( example ). A PATCHING_GUIDELINES.md (or AGENTS.md ) , which tells agents and patching-bugs how your project wants fixes written. It should outline how to build and test the project, how big a fix should be, where a fix should go, how to present proposed changes, and what a regression test must show ( example ). For our Patch the Planet work with GPAC, our engineers wrote a threat model and a project-specific patching skill that captures how GPAC’s maintainers want bugs reproduced, what evidence a fix needs, and what a patch must preserve. Liboqs and validator.js have also published threat models in accordance with our guidance. The more comprehensive and specific these files are to your project, code conventions, and operating style, the better the output you’ll receive. The industry needs to focus on patching As AI accelerates bug discovery, we need to turn those findings into reliable fixes just as quickly. Solutions need to balance speed and quality: an agent needs to understand a report, decide what needs to change, and check that a patch fixes the issue without introducing regressions. Our patching-bugs and regression-hunt plugins bring what we’ve learned from Patch the Planet into that workflow, helping maintainers move from a bug report to a patch they can confidently review and ship. Install patching-bugs and regression-hunt , add a THREAT_MODEL.md and a PATCHING_GUIDELINES.md to your repository, and put them to work on your next bug report. Give the tools your project’s context so they can help you focus on the right fix and validate it faster. Then share your feedback , including comments about where our defaults don’t fit your project. Those real-world cases will help us build the next version.

items.title: Salt Security wins three InfoSec Innovator awards
items.summary: Salt Security has won three categories at Cyber Defense Magazine’s 2026 Top InfoSec Innovators awards, recognising its work in agentic AI and API security. The company received the Most Promising Agentic AI Security Solution, Trailblazing AI-based Cybersecurity Innovation and Transformational API Security Solution awards. The awards were announced at CyberDefenseCon 2026 in Orlando as part of the programme’s 14th annual edition. The recognition comes as organisations face challenges in overseeing AI agents and securing the APIs through which they access data and carry out tasks. Salt Security’s State of Agentic AI and API Security 2H 2026 report, released this month, surveyed more than 380 security and technology professionals. It found that nearly half of enterprises had confirmed or suspected that an AI agent took an unauthorised action in the past year. Fewer than one in five could automatically stop a misbehaving agent. “Our research shows that the governance gap is not theoretical: agents are already acting in ways organizations did not intend, and most organizations cannot stop them in time. We are honored to be recognized as leaders in addressing that problem,” said Roey Eliyahu, CEO of Salt Security. The company’s Agentic Security Platform discovers AI agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and APIs within an organisation’s environment. It also governs their connections and permissions, monitors agent behaviour during operation and identifies vulnerabilities before deployment. Gary S. Miliefsky, publisher of Cyber Defense Magazine, said the judging criteria included an understanding of emerging threats, cost-effective solutions and innovation that could help reduce cyber risk. The full list of winners is available on the Cyber Defense Awards website .

items.title: PHP Releases Emergency Patches for PHP2Shell Flaws Threatening Millions of Web Servers
items.summary: PHP has released emergency security updates for two critical vulnerabilities that could let unauthenticated attackers run code on vulnerable web servers. Tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and collectively called PHP2Shell , the flaws affect PHP’s handling of memory during web requests. The PHP project rates both vulnerabilities 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. Administrators should update PHP as soon as possible. The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The vulnerabilities affect earlier versions in those branches. PHP 8.1 and older are no longer supported by the project, though some Linux distributions and long-term support providers may offer backported fixes. Administrators using older releases should check with their vendor or plan a move to a supported version. PHP branch Affected versions Patched version PHP 8.2 Earlier than 8.2.35 8.2.35 PHP 8.3 Earlier than 8.3.36 8.3.36 PHP 8.4 Earlier than 8.4.27 8.4.27 PHP 8.5 Earlier than 8.5.12 8.5.12 PHP2Shell Flaws According to the PHP2Shell research website , researchers from Wiz Research, OpenAI Codex Security, and Calif uncovered two critical vulnerability classes in PHP’s core engine. CVE-2026-109618 stems from how PHP responds to an out-of-memory condition. PHP previously used a mechanism called longjmp() to exit the current operation when memory ran out. In some situations, that sudden exit could leave request data partly initialized. PHP’s later shutdown process could then read or act on the invalid data, opening a path to remote code execution. The PHP advisory explains that multipart form data can help trigger the memory problem. For example, a request may contain many headers within a part, or many empty file fields that still make PHP create metadata. Nested field names can add to the memory needed to process the request. The advisory also describes a case where a multipart request without a usable content length can pass an early size check while PHP continues parsing data. These conditions can exhaust memory even when a request appears to stay within some configured limits. The impact is especially clear for Apache’s mod_php. The PHP security advisory says researchers validated unauthenticated code execution over HTTP against this setup, using default PHP input and memory limits. The request can reach the vulnerable state before the application’s own code starts. The risk differs across server setups. For PHP-FPM, the advisory says source analysis indicates susceptibility, but the same complete exploit was not demonstrated for that server setup. CVE-2026-109619 involves stale global state in long-running PHP workers. A worker may retain a reference to memory from a request after PHP has freed that memory. If an error or other event interrupts cleanup, and a later request reaches that leftover state before PHP resets it, the worker may use invalid memory. The advisory describes confirmed paths involving fatal errors, error-reporting data, and session upload-progress handling. Whether a specific server is exposed depends on its PHP setup, configuration, application, and extensions. The second flaw matters because web workers handle requests one after another. A state left behind by one request can affect a later request handled by the same worker. The PHP advisory’s confirmed cases include a mod_php scenario. It also describes a PHP-FPM path that depends on an application operation and a later request reaching the same worker. These details make the setup important, but they do not reduce the urgency of patching. The fix for CVE-2026-109618 changes PHP’s handling of out-of-memory errors. Instead of abruptly leaving an operation in a way that can expose incomplete request state, PHP delays a graceful memory error until a safe point. A separate hard limit handles more severe memory pressure. The related fix for CVE-2026-109619 resets a wider range of request-related global state so that a worker is less likely to carry invalid references between requests. Researchers identified flaws that impact PHP web deployments across various server configurations, including Apache with mod_php and PHP-FPM. Estimates of exposure highlight the seriousness of the issue: BleepingComputer reported that VirusTotal estimated there are over 5.1 million PHP hosts visible online. This figure represents an estimate of potentially exposed hosts, rather than a count of confirmed vulnerable or compromised servers. After upgrading, administrators should restart PHP workers and check that all web-facing pools and services are using the patched version. Updating the command-line PHP package alone may not update a separate PHP-FPM service or an Apache module. If an update cannot happen immediately, temporary measures can reduce some risk but do not replace patching. It also recommends limiting request sizes and multipart inputs at the frontend. Administrators should avoid RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA , which can cause allocation failures on the vulnerable path. For the stale-state flaw, the advisory says there is no complete general configuration workaround. On PHP 8.5, disabling fatal_error_backtraces can remove the producer used in one confirmed case. Neither setting addresses every possible producer and consumer of stale state, so organizations should treat them only as temporary risk-reduction steps. Cybersecurity News has also reported on a public PHP2Shell testing tool and early exploitation attempts . These reports are a reason to prioritize upgrades, not a substitute for checking a system’s actual version and vendor guidance. The primary references are the PHP advisory for CVE-2026-109618 and the related advisory for CVE-2026-109619 . If organizations can’t patch immediately, reduce public exposure where possible, review PHP and web-server logs, and confirm which worker processes handle live traffic. Log checks can help identify errors, but clean logs don’t prove a system is safe. The strongest defense is to move every web-facing PHP installation to a fixed release and verify that the updated workers have restarted. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: APT28 Hackers Open Secret SSH Tunnel Into NATO Country’s Naval Shipbuilder Network
items.summary: Russian cyberespionage group APT28 used the Hookedge backdoor to reach a naval shipbuilder’s network in a NATO member state, steal login material and set up a hidden SSH tunnel. The intrusion lasted at least two months, according to a report by Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team. The report does not name the shipbuilder or the country. It also describes activity against organizations in a second NATO member state, including a law enforcement agency and a maker of military aircraft engines. APT28, also known as Fancy Bear and Forest Blizzard, is referred to as Swallowtail in Symantec’s report. Researchers from Symantec identified Hookedge activity at the three organizations. Their findings add detail to earlier public reporting on the malware, including this report on Hookedge targeting , which described the backdoor’s use of Word documents and web services. APT28 Hackers At the shipbuilder, the activity began on July 24, 2026, when a malicious Word document was opened from the Outlook attachment cache. Its hidden macro wrote several files to the user’s profile and started the infection chain. One of those files launched Hookedge, a backdoor that can fetch instructions, run commands and send back their output. The malware used a hidden Microsoft Edge window to contact webhook.site, a public web service. The use of a familiar browser and a legitimate service could make the traffic harder to spot among normal web activity. An earlier Hookedge campaign analysis also describes how the backdoor used Edge and webhook services to receive instructions and return results. The first commands gathered basic details about the infected computer and checked whether it could reach common online services. After a gap of about three days, the operators returned with a more active stage that used a dedicated server at 185.82.218[.]119 for tasking and data transfer. Symantec observed a burst of seven commands in about 30 seconds, suggesting an operator was working directly on the compromised system. Stolen key enabled a route back in The operators placed an SSH private key on the host and used it to open a connection to their server. The tunnel gave them a route from their own infrastructure back into the shipbuilder’s internal network. Unlike a short remote session, a tunnel can provide a continuing path through a compromised machine. Soon after it was opened, the operators checked internal hostnames, indicating that they were mapping the network. The SSH tunnel was one of two ways the attackers sought to obtain or use account credentials. They also ran a PowerShell script that caused the computer to send an NTLM authentication response to a local listener. NTLM is a Windows method for proving a user’s identity. Captured responses can create further risk if attackers can crack them or use them to try to access other systems. The operators checked account and group details, looked up more internal systems, and gathered information about running processes and installed updates. They stopped the SSH process the following day, but Hookedge continued to contact the operators’ server in later bursts. The report does not confirm why the tunnel was closed or what data, if any, was taken. This use of tunnels fits a wider pattern in which APT28 has relied on less obvious routes and services to support its operations. Cyber Security News has also reported on APT28 abuse of cloud services , a separate campaign that highlights why defenders should check how programs behave, not just whether a website is known or trusted. On July 31, the operators ran a program named ld.exe with an encrypted file called Events.dat. The loader decrypted its input in memory and called a function named ExecuteLoader. Symantec found that the file supplied to the loader was not recovered, so the final payload and its purpose remain unknown. The loader was still present on the host weeks later, and the Hookedge launcher was seen again on September 24. The report places the shipbuilder incident within a wider campaign against defense and government-related targets in two NATO countries. The combination of a backdoor, credential theft, internal network checks and a tunnel suggests a sustained effort to gain access and collect intelligence. The available evidence does not show whether the attackers reached other systems or obtained sensitive shipbuilding information. Organizations should investigate suspicious Word attachments, unexpected scripts in user folders, hidden Edge activity and unapproved SSH connections. They should review endpoint, email, DNS and proxy logs for the indicators below, check for signs of NTLM credential exposure, and rotate affected credentials if compromise is suspected. The report advises treating Hookedge activity as a possible ongoing intrusion rather than assuming that removing one file ends the threat. items.title: Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF
items.summary: Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester. These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper. Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error. With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability. And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans. Request inspection is not enough Cloudflare WAF protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin. For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show “false positives”, such as matching legitimate traffic — which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server. The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction. As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory: GET /download?file=../../config/database.ini Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence: 200 OK Content-Type: text/plain [database] username=app_service password=EXAMPLE_SECRET Full transaction detection provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone. A response rule can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker. Detection and mitigation are separate by design Full transaction detection extends the always-on detection framework we introduced earlier this year. Detections analyze traffic and attach metadata to the request and response, rules then decide what to do with those results. Separating those jobs gives customers visibility before they design a policy. Security teams can inspect detections in their own traffic, understand which endpoints and signatures are involved, and choose the response that fits their application. items.summary_html:
Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester.

These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper.

Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error.

With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability.

And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans.

Request inspection is not enough

Cloudflare WAF protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin.

For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show “false positives”, such as matching legitimate traffic — which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server.

The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction.

As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory:

GET /download?file=../../config/database.ini

Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence:

200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain
[database]
username=app_service
password=EXAMPLE_SECRET

Full transaction detection provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone. A response rule can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker.

Detection and mitigation are separate by design

Full transaction detection extends the always-on detection framework we introduced earlier this year. Detections analyze traffic and attach metadata to the request and response, rules then decide what to do with those results.

Separating those jobs gives customers visibility before they design a policy. Security teams can inspect detections in their own traffic, understand which endpoints and signatures are involved, and choose the response that fits their application. Similar to the approach for the request-based Attack Signature Detection, the outcome of the detections are stored in fields that can be accessed in the response custom rules or used in managed detections to block traffic.

Mirroring the request detection fields, the following new fields are added to our platform:

Field

Description

cf.waf.signature.response.confidence

Confidence values associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.categories

Categories associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.ref

Signature reference IDs, up to 10

The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability. It correlates suspicious input with response signals that indicate an exploit may have succeeded.

We will expand coverage over time by supporting other use cases, including detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals. This is important for the Internet beyond any one application: defenses can distinguish probing from evidence of impact, while detection of exposed data and services can reach customers that do not have a dedicated security team tuning every WAF rule.

Create rules on the response

Detecting evidence of exploitation is most useful if you can act on it in real time. Response custom rules turn full transaction detections into inline protection by blocking a matching origin response before it reaches the requester, although it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin.

Security teams can now combine request and response properties with detection results to decide which responses to block. When a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response.

Response phase controls are available in the Cloudflare dashboard at the bottom of the Security > Security Rules page, with both managed protections and custom rules.

We have released both managed and custom rules to all plans, including Free plans. Over time, we will follow the same approach we use for request detections, where managed detections for free plans focus on high-profile vulnerabilities, while paying customers get a richer catalog of detections.

Managed detections

All customers get the protection of the full array of transaction detections through the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default ruleset, which is designed for a simple one-click deploy and simplified configurability. When a signature matches, the managed detection will block the response and return a standard WAF block page.

You can edit the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default scope to run detections only on a portion of their applications, for example by excluding or restricting the detection to a specific path. Paying customers can use detection fields in custom response rules to create more tailored policies.

Custom rules

Custom response rules are designed to give customers full control of the rule logic. A useful rule can stop an administration interface from being exposed when an authentication gateway has not marked the request as internal. For example:

http.request.uri.path starts_with "/admin" and not http.request.headers["x-internal-user"][0] eq "true" and http.response.code eq 200 and http.response.headers["content-type"][0] contains "text/html"

This blocks only when an unauthenticated request targets `/admin` and the origin actually returns a successful HTML administration page. It does not block ordinary authentication failures, redirects, or non-administration traffic.

All customers can create up to three custom response rules supporting Log and Block actions. The fields and functions available in response to custom rules mirrors what your plan gives you access to in request custom rules already. Creating rules on the response body is not yet available.

Following the Attack Signature Detection approach, paying customers also have access to the outcome of attack detections through the cf.waf.signature.response.*  fields listed above. These fields can be combined with other parameters (such as a hostname, URL path, source IP, request header) to enable protection on a single path, or limit the policy to application-specific context. We are currently rolling out the response fields to all our accounts. If you don’t have access to them yet, please contact your account team.

Investigating matching requests

When a managed or custom response rule logs or blocks a transaction, the event is available in Security Events. This means responders can trace any detection back to the full context of the request and the specific rule that took action.

At the moment, both request-only rules and full-transaction rules are shown together in the same analytics page. In Security Events, the events generated by response rules are part of the Managed Rules or Custom Rules service. You can filter events belonging to a specific rule ID in the relative rule list section.

Get started today

Full transaction detection is generally available for all zones proxying traffic through Cloudflare. To verify that you’re protected, go to Security > Security Rules in the Cloudflare dashboard. If you want to customize your policy, start by reviewing full transaction detections in Security Analytics, then create the response phase policy that fits your application.

items.title: Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability
items.summary: Today, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed two vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as php2shell . The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic. Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with PHP foundation , OpenAI and Wiz among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure. Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customers using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell. Cloudflare successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customers while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers. We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic. Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The origin’s response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives. To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability. Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation. Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the changelog . The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users. What we know about the vulnerabilities PHP is used by almost 70% of websites . The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet. The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. If processing stops unexpectedly, for example because it runs out of memory, PHP fails to clean up the memory safely. These vulnerabilities arise when PHP handles an error and then tries to use data that was not fully set up or memory that has already been released. An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP requests to trigger these conditions. Large requests are one way to put memory under pressure, but the problem goes beyond consuming server resources. By manipulating the data PHP encounters in this invalid memory, an attacker may be able to crash a PHP process, expose sensitive information, or execute code provided by the attacker. The two vulnerabilities differ in when the unsafe memory access happens: Vulnerability What goes wrong CVE-2026-109618 PHP runs out of memory and interrupts its work before some internal data has been properly initialized. During cleanup of that request, PHP may use this unfinished data as though it were valid. CVE-2026-109619 A fatal error interrupts a request, leaving PHP holding references to memory that is released when the request ends. When the same PHP process handles a later request, it may follow those outdated references and access memory that is no longer valid and expose sensitive data. These flaws are in the PHP runtime, so updating website code or a plugin(s) alone does not fix these vulnerabilities. Administrators need to update the PHP software running their applications. If a hosting provider manages PHP, ask the provider to apply the security update. Administrators can follow the PHP advisory for affected versions and remediation instructions. Keep Cloudflare WAF protections enabled while patching. Restricting unnecessary uploads and limiting upload sizes can also reduce exposure, but these measures do not replace the PHP fix. New rules For Free customers, new rules have been released under the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset (Ruleset ID 77454fe2d30c4220b5701f6fdfb893ba). Free customers don’t have to take any actions to enable the protection. To override the ruleset behavior you can refer to our documentation .
