items.title: Advancing Agentic AI Security with Palo Alto Networks and NVIDIA
items.summary: AI is moving from answering questions to taking action. Agents can use tools, access enterprise data, and carry out work across systems on our behalf or autonomousl y . This creates opportunities for businesses to move faster, but it also changes what security must protect. An agent’s identity, the authority it carries, and the actions it takes all become security decisions. As enterprises put agents into production, they need controls that keep pace without hindering the work those agents are designed to do. Palo Alto Networks is working with NVIDIA to advance this goal across five connected areas in support of the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for safe AI agents: an AI gateway on NVIDIA Vera CPU systems; runtime protection on NVIDIA BlueField DPUs; agent identity governance on NVIDIA Sentry; AI factory visibility through an AI-driven, agentic security operations center (SOC); and partner services that help customers implement a secure architecture. Palo Alto Networks AI Runtime Security Extends Protection Across the AI Factory and Edge Until now, the AI factory conversation has centered primarily on compute capacity and token generation. But as autonomous agents execute higher-stakes workloads, runtime security has become just as essential. Agents can be steered past their guardrails, and a compromised host cannot be trusted to accurately report what occurred. To be effective, security teams require visibility and enforcement that operate independently of the host environment. Palo Alto Networks AI Runtime Security on NVIDIA BlueField DPUs isolates security processing in a dedicated infrastructure domain. Because BlueField sits in the path between agents and the models, data, and services they access, security policies are enforced in silicon — beyond the reach of a compromised host. This capability safeguards both GPU-accelerated AI workloads and CPU-based agent runtimes and is now generally available across AI factory and industrial edge deployments. Offloading security from the host node delivers two critical benefits: increased token throughput and stronger runtime protection across the entire AI factory. Deployment at scale must be manageable. Our work with Spectro Cloud manages the deployment and operation of AI Runtime Security on BlueField DPUs, enabling consistent management across the AI factory infrastructure — from the data center to distributed edge environments. Idira Governs the Identity Behind Every Agent Action Runtime protection answers what an agent is doing. Identity governance helps determine whether it is authorized to do it. An agent may act for a person, a team, or an autonomous business process, often requiring access to multiple tools and data sources across the organization. Granting an agent broad, persistent access creates risk, while making access too restrictive limits its usefulness. To achieve the optimal balance of control and agent access, Palo Alto Networks is advancing an integration between agentic identity security and NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField — bringing identity and delegated authority closer to where agent interactions are governed. The goal is to give each agent a verifiable identity, grant access appropriate to its task, and make its actions attributable. Once available, this solution will deliver zero-trust protection and tamper-resistant auditing for agents by moving the security controls — including identity — to the NVIDIA Bluefield DPU, separate from the host operating system. This addresses an immediate business need — enabling enterprises to scale agent deployments while retaining control over whose authority agents use and which resources they can reach. Bringing AI Factory Signals into Cortex Security teams need visibility into activity across the infrastructure that runs AI agents. Palo Alto Networks has announced an integration of Cortex XSIAM with NVIDIA DOCA Argus , which monitors host activity from BlueField’s independent trust domain. This provides security operations teams with runtime signals that do not rely on an agent installed on the host being monitored. By bringing those signals together with network, cloud, and identity data in an AI-driven SOC, security teams can investigate AI infrastructure in the context of the broader enterprise. items.title: Before you evaluate an AI SRE, give your existing agent context
items.summary: If you’re evaluating AI SRE products, you probably own most of one already. The coding agent your engineers use, whether that’s Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, can already investigate a Kubernetes cluster. What it usually lacks is context: what’s failing right now, and what changed before it broke. We measured how much that gap matters. The same agent and model worked through 50 broken clusters twice, once with a shell and raw kubectl, and once with read-only MCP tools that return that context: Claude Code, same model, same 50 faults Shell + kubectl Read-only cluster context Correct 45 46 Mean judge score (0 to 1) 0.905 0.936 Correct within 2 minutes 60% 86% Correct within 5 minutes 78% 90% Mean time to submit a diagnosis, right or wrong 191 s 64 s Median 87 s 44 s 90th percentile 632 s 94 s Mean tool calls per fault 16.3 9.8 With context the agent was slightly more accurate: 46 correct against 45, and a mean judge score of 0.936 against 0.905. Both arms were right on 44 of the same faults. The bigger difference was time, which is what counts during an active outage: nobody wants to wait fifteen minutes for an AI investigation while users are getting errors. With context, the agent had a correct diagnosis within two minutes on 86% of faults, against 60% with a shell. With a shell, one fault in ten took more than ten minutes. The gap was widest on the 14 faults where every pod reported Ready but the application was broken: 326 seconds on average with a shell, 79 with context. Fewer tool calls also means fewer model turns, which usually means lower token spend. So before you evaluate an AI SRE, give the agent you already have that context, and measure it. That gives you a baseline for what the product adds. How we ran it We ran 50 faults from SREGym , the open Kubernetes fault benchmark from Microsoft and UIUC, on a live 3-node Amazon EKS cluster. Both arms used Claude Code on Claude Sonnet 5 through Amazon Bedrock. One had a shell and raw kubectl. The other had read-only MCP tools from Radar, an open-source Kubernetes UI and MCP server that we maintain, with kubectl blocked so it couldn’t fall back to a shell. SREGym’s judge, Claude Opus 5 at temperature 0, graded the first diagnosis each run submitted. Context didn’t fix the model’s judgment. Both arms missed the same three faults. In one, a mutating webhook rewrote the pod’s memory limits at admission. In another, a PriorityClass mis-scoped as the global default changed the priority of newly created pods and set off preemption. Neither agent named the object responsible in either case. In the third, both found a real but unrelated misconfiguration and reported that instead of the DNS fault. Same model, same mistakes. The two arms also differed in permissions, since only the shell could write, so this run doesn’t say which kind of context did the work. Every tool call from both arms is published in a per-fault replay . What we mean by context Radar’s read-only MCP tools add four things on top of what kubectl returns: Current failures, already detected. A ranked list of what’s broken right now, so the first call starts from what’s failing instead of a full inventory. A change timeline. Spec changes and Helm release history, kept after Kubernetes events expire. Events last an hour by default (the API server’s –event-ttl flag), and many changes never produce one. Resources joined to their relationships. Owners, topology and related issues come back with the object, so the agent doesn’t fetch them one by one. Logs filtered to the errors. Diagnostic lines first, with secrets redacted. Since we maintain Radar, read the results with that in mind. None of the four depends on Radar specifically: any MCP server that returns the same context can be tested the same way. What the agent asked for One fault shows the difference. In the OpenTelemetry Astronomy Shop demo, the frontend Deployment had lost its CART_ADDR environment variable. Every pod reported Ready and nothing restarted. Both arms got the right answer: Shell + kubectl: 58 tool calls, 701.6 s (excerpt) 2.1s kubectl get pods -n astronomy-shop -o wide 2.2s kubectl get events -n astronomy-shop --sort-by=.lastTimestamp 10.3s kubectl logs -n astronomy-shop product-catalog-77497fdc44-f5nx9 --previous ... 423.6s kubectl run catsrc ...; kubectl cp astronomy-shop/email... 665.8s helm get values astronomy-shop -n astronomy-shop 674.6s kubectl get secret sh.helm.release.v1.astronomy-shop.v1 ... | base64 -d | base64 -d | gunzip 701.6s submitted: "The frontend Deployment in astronomy-shop is missing the CART_ADDR environment variable..." Read-only cluster context: 7 tool calls, 34.8 s 1.0s ToolSearch (loads the MCP tool definitions) 4.6s issues namespace=astronomy-shop 4.9s get_changes namespace=astronomy-shop 11.8s get_resource deployment/frontend 12.3s get_workload_logs frontend 19.8s get_workload_logs frontend 20.4s diagnose deployment/product-catalog 34.8s submitted: "The frontend Deployment in astronomy-shop is missing its CART_ADDR environment variable, which was removed from the container spec..." With a shell, the agent spent nearly twelve minutes on it, and ended by decoding Helm’s release Secret to diff the deployed manifest by hand. With the cluster’s recent changes one call away, it had the answer in 35 seconds. Across all 50 faults the transcripts show the same thing. Without context, the agent opened every fault with kubectl get pods and kubectl get events . On 24 of them it then went looking for history, in ReplicaSets, rollout history or Helm release values, because nothing it could read told it what had changed. With context, the agent asked for the same two things first, nearly every time. Current failures were its first call on all 50 faults, and the change timeline was its second on 35. Those are the two things the shell agent had to piece together from get pods, get events and rollout history. Much of the shell agent’s time went into rebuilding that context before it could start on the diagnosis. What you’re actually buying An AI SRE is several products sold as one: Part What it does What most teams already have Trigger Starts an investigation when an alert fires Alerting, but nothing that starts an agent Context What the agent can read: live state, recent changes, current failures kubectl and RBAC. Change history is the usual gap Reasoning loop The model, plus the harness that picks the next call Claude Code, Codex, Cursor Delivery Puts the answer in Slack, the ticket or the incident channel Partly Governance Whose identity it uses, what it may change, what gets recorded Kubernetes RBAC, and API audit logs if you’ve configured an audit policy If your team pays for a coding agent, it already has a reasoning loop, and the results above measure the context row on its own. When you evaluate a product’s context, check whether it: keeps change history after Kubernetes events expire starts from what’s already failing Context also isn’t tied to one agent. An MCP server can give the same read-only context to your coding agent or to an SRE agent: HolmesGPT , a CNCF Sandbox project, accepts remote MCP servers as toolsets. So you can test the context and the agent separately. If your coding agent with good context diagnoses as well as the AI SRE you’re trialling, judge the product on the other rows of that table, starting with the trigger. A coding agent investigates when someone asks it to. An AI SRE can start when the alert fires, while you’re asleep, and have an answer waiting by the time you open Slack. That’s a real advantage, and worth weighing on its own. What it runs as The shell transcripts also show why the governance row matters. The agent launched its own pods on 13 faults and ran exec, cp, port-forward or debug on 21. On 4 it pulled Secret data into its context, decoding it on 3. Read-only access doesn’t prevent that: the built-in view role excludes Secrets, but many “read-only” roles don’t. On one fault in the Social Network app it launched a pod that ran drop() on two of the application’s MongoDB collections to test a theory, then submitted a wrong diagnosis. SREGym’s prompt allowed all of this: it tells the agent a fix stage follows, says its kubectl can “inspect and modify resources”, and tells it not to ask for confirmation. An agent given write access and told to fix things will use that access while it’s still investigating. So check what an AI SRE runs as. It should: work with a read-only identity, with no exec and no access to Secrets record every call it made, so you can see what it read Test it yourself Give every contender the same model and the same read-only identity. Kubernetes’ built-in view role leaves out Secrets and grants no exec. This writes a kubeconfig that holds only a service account bound to it, so no contender can fall back to your admin credentials: kubectl create serviceaccount ai-eval -n default kubectl create clusterrolebinding ai-eval-view --clusterrole=view --serviceaccount=default:ai-eval TOKEN=$(kubectl create token ai-eval -n default --duration=8h) ADMIN_USER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.users[0].name}') kubectl config view --minify --flatten > ai-eval.kubeconfig export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/ai-eval.kubeconfig kubectl config set-credentials ai-eval --token="$TOKEN" kubectl config set-context --current --user=ai-eval kubectl config delete-user "$ADMIN_USER" kubectl auth can-i get secrets # should print "no" Run the same faults. SREGym has drivers for Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini CLI and OpenCode, and its Lite suite of 17 problems runs on kind with 8 vCPU and 16 GB of memory ( setup ): uv run main.py --suite sregym-lite --agent claudecode --model claude-sonnet-5 \ --judge-model --stages diagnosis --n-attempts 3 For an AI SRE product SREGym has no driver for, --use-external-harness --problem injects the fault and leaves the cluster broken for you to point the product at. Score at a fixed time limit, and repeat. Use a limit that matches your response target; we report two and five minutes. Run each fault more than once, because a gap of two or three faults in a single run can be noise. Record token spend per fault too. Then replay two or three of your own incidents on staging, with the same identity. Benchmarks inject faults into a freshly deployed app, and your incidents won’t look like that. What this doesn’t show We maintain Radar, and the context arm used Radar’s MCP server. The per-fault data is public so you can check our reading of it. Each arm ran each fault once. SREGym injects each fault minutes after deploying the app. That favours anything that tracks recent changes, Radar included. We measured diagnosis, not remediation. Start with context Give the agent you already have read-only access to the cluster’s current failures and recent changes, and measure it at a fixed time limit. Use that as the baseline for anything you trial: compare diagnosis first, then what the product adds around it. Before you replace the agent, measure what happens when you improve what the agent knows. Radar is an open-source (Apache-2.0) Kubernetes UI with a read-only MCP endpoint. The source and install instructions are at github.com/skyhook-io/radar .

items.title: Where to Find SSH (sshd) Logs on Linux and How to Export Them
items.summary: On Debian and Ubuntu, sshd writes to /var/log/auth.log. On RHEL, Rocky, Alma and CentOS Stream, it writes to /var/log/secure. If neither file exists, your system logs only to the systemd journal. Then the command you want is journalctl -u ssh on Debian-based systems, or journalctl -u sshd on the Red Hat family, Fedora and Arch. SSH is the front door of nearly every Linux server, which is why its logs show up in almost every Linux investigation. Prime Core has 11,632 sigma rules that run on Linux authentication logs like these, mapped to 643 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: brute force (T1110), logins with stolen credentials (T1078) and lateral movement over SSH (T1021.004). Below is how to find your sshd logs, export them, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Authentication logs are locked down on purpose, so a regular account usually gets nothing back. /var/log/auth.log on Debian and Ubuntu is readable by root and the adm group. /var/log/secure on the Red Hat family is root-only. The system journal is open to root and to members of systemd-journal, adm and wheel. Everyone else sees only their own user journal. If you run journalctl -u ssh as a normal user, you get an empty result and a hint that you’re not seeing messages from other users. That’s permissions, not a quiet server. The simple fix is sudo. If you’re setting up an account just for log collection, add it to adm or systemd-journal instead of handing out root. Our [Linux log permissions guide] covers the details. One more thing before you copy anything off a server: auth logs contain usernames, source IPs and hostnames. LogTotal sanitizes uploads, but check your data-handling policy first. Step 1: File, journal, or both? The table above shows the defaults, and defaults are exactly what cloud images and hardening scripts like to change. Spend ten seconds checking: ls -l /var/log/auth.log /var/log/secure 2>/dev/null systemctl is-active rsyslog If a file shows up and rsyslog is active, you have both: rsyslog copies messages out of the journal into a plain text file. Either source works, and the file is easier to copy around. If there’s no file, rsyslog simply isn’t installed. That’s the norm now: since Debian 12, rsyslog is no longer part of a default install, so a fresh Debian box has no auth.log at all. Fedora and Arch have worked this way for years. Go to Step 2b. While you’re here, check whether the journal survives a reboot: ls -d /var/log/journal If that directory doesn’t exist, journald keeps logs in memory under /run/log/journal, and a reboot wipes them. On a machine you’re investigating, that’s worth knowing before anyone decides to “just restart it.” One more point for incident work: if the box might be compromised, its local logs might be too. Wiping or editing auth.log is a classic cleanup step. If the server forwards logs to a SIEM, export from there as well and compare. Our [Splunk export guide] shows how. Step 2a: Export from auth.log or secure The current file only covers the last few days. Older entries sit in rotated files next to it. On Debian and Ubuntu they look like auth.log.1, auth.log.2.gz, and so on. On the Red Hat family they carry a date, like secure-20261012. If the incident started last week, you need those too. This pulls sshd lines from the current and rotated files, oldest first, into one file: # Debian / Ubuntu sudo zgrep -h ‘sshd’ $(ls -tr /var/log/auth.log*) > web-03_sshd.log # RHEL / Rocky / Alma sudo zgrep -h ‘sshd’ $(ls -tr /var/log/secure*) > web-03_sshd.log zgrep reads plain and gzipped files alike, so you don’t have to unpack anything. ls -tr sorts by modification time, so the oldest file goes first and the output stays roughly chronological. The sshd pattern also matches sshd-session, which matters on newer systems (see Step 2b). Why filter at all? Besides cutting noise, auth.log also records sudo, and sudo lines include full command lines. People do occasionally type passwords into those. Filtering to sshd keeps that out of the file. The exception is when you’re investigating what an attacker did after logging in. Then you want the sudo lines too: take the whole file and let LogTotal’s sanitize step do its job. Quick check before you upload: wc -l web-03_sshd.log head -3 web-03_sshd.log; tail -3 web-03_sshd.log Look at the timestamps. Depending on the rsyslog config, they’re either classic syslog (Oct 19 10:15:01, no year, no time zone) or full ISO 8601. If they’re classic, write down the server’s time zone (timedatectl). You’ll need it the moment you try to line these events up with anything else. Step 2b: Export from the systemd journal On journal-only systems, this is the whole job: sudo journalctl -u ssh -u sshd \ –since “2026-10-19 00:00” –until “2026-10-20 00:00” \ –no-pager -o short-iso > web-03_sshd.log A few choices in there are deliberate. Both unit names. The service is called ssh on Debian and Ubuntu and sshd almost everywhere else. journalctl combines repeated -u flags with OR, so the same command works on both families. Filter by unit, not by tag. A lot of older guides use journalctl -t sshd. Since OpenSSH 9.8, the server is split into two binaries, and per-connection messages, including logins, are tagged sshd-session instead of sshd. Filter by tag, and you lose exactly the lines you came for. This broke plenty of fail2ban and sshguard setups when 9.8 landed in 2024. RHEL 10 and other current releases ship OpenSSH 9.8 or newer. Filtering by unit catches every process that belongs to the service, whatever it’s called. -o short-iso . It gives you a syslog-style line with a full ISO 8601 timestamp, year and time zone included, so you don’t have to guess. [PROOF: confirm LogTotal parses short-iso; if not, use the default -o short]. If you’d rather keep every journal field (PID, boot ID, hostname, and so on), use -o json, which writes one JSON object per line. The file gets bigger, but nothing is lost. The time filters take relative values too: –since “2 hours ago” or –since yesterday. With a persistent journal, -b -1 limits output to the previous boot, which helps if the server was restarted after the incident. Don’t copy the binary .journal files from /var/log/journal and upload those. LogTotal reads text and JSON, and journal files are neither. What to look for once you have the file Most sshd lines fall into a handful of patterns: Line starts with What it means Failed password for from Wrong password for an account that exists Invalid user from The username doesn’t exist; typical of scanners cycling through admin, test, oracle Accepted password for / Accepted publickey for A successful login; the publickey line also carries the key’s SHA256 fingerprint Disconnecting authenticating user … Too many authentication failures The client hit MaxAuthTries Connection closed by … [preauth] Dropped before authentication, usually scanners and banner grabbers pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user The session actually started The sequence worth stopping for: a run of Failed or Invalid user lines from one IP, then an Accepted from the same IP. That’s a brute force that worked. Close behind: an Accepted for a service account, from an address nobody recognizes, at an hour nobody works. On OpenSSH 9.8 and later you may also see messages about penalties: sshd now temporarily refuses addresses that keep failing authentication. Treat them as a symptom. They tell you someone was hammering the port, not that anyone got in. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Reading a few hundred lines by eye is fine. Reading 40,000 isn’t. LogTotal is SOC Prime’s free service for running detection logic against a log file without setting anything up. It sanitizes what you upload and doesn’t keep your files. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in web-03_sshd.log. [PROOF: upload screen, size limit] Sanitize. [PROOF: what gets masked in an sshd log: usernames, source IPs, hostnames]. Look over the result before you go on. You know which of those names are sensitive in your environment. Review. [PROOF: what the results screen shows and how findings map to rules and ATT&CK techniques] What this looks like on real data. We generated sshd logs on a throwaway test VM: [PROOF: what was simulated, e.g. an SSH password-spraying run against a few common usernames, ending in one successful login]. The file came out to [PROOF: N lines, X KB]. LogTotal flagged [PROOF: actual findings, matched rules, ATT&CK techniques]. Want to try it before touching your own servers? [PROOF: link to the sample file] is the same file we used above. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix No such file or directory for auth.log rsyslog isn’t installed (default since Debian 12) Use journalctl, Step 2b Permission denied on the log file auth.log is adm-only, secure is root-only sudo, or add the account to adm journalctl -u ssh returns nothing, with a hint about other users You’re not in systemd-journal, adm or wheel sudo, or add the account to systemd-journal journalctl -u ssh returns nothing as root Wrong unit name for this distro Use -u ssh -u sshd Logouts are there, but no Accepted lines Filtering by tag (-t sshd) on OpenSSH 9.8+ Filter by unit instead Nothing older than the last reboot Volatile journal; no /var/log/journal The old logs are gone; check your SIEM or log forwarder The file only covers a few days Rotated files weren’t included Use the zgrep command with auth.log* or secure* Timestamps don’t line up with other sources Classic syslog timestamps carry no time zone Note the server’s time zone, or export with -o short-iso FAQ Where are SSH logs on Ubuntu? On a standard Ubuntu install, in /var/log/auth.log, plus the journal (journalctl -u ssh). Minimal cloud images sometimes leave out rsyslog. If the file isn’t there, use the journal. How do I see only failed SSH logins? sudo journalctl -u ssh -u sshd | grep -E ‘Failed|Invalid user’ on journal systems, or sudo zgrep -hE ‘Failed|Invalid user’ /var/log/auth.log* when you have the file. For anything beyond a quick look, upload the full sshd log instead. The failures only mean something next to the successes. What about last and lastb? They read the binary login records in /var/log/wtmp and /var/log/btmp. They’re handy for a quick look at who logged in, but they carry far less detail than sshd’s own log, and they’re just as easy for an intruder to tamper with. How do I collect sshd logs from several servers at once? For a one-off, a loop does it: for h in web-01 web-02 web-03; do ssh “$h” “sudo journalctl -u ssh -u sshd –since yesterday -o short-iso –no-pager” > “${h}_sshd.log” done That needs sudo to work without a password prompt on the remote side. Then the command you want is journalctl -u ssh on Debian-based systems, or journalctl -u sshd on the Red Hat family, Fedora and Arch.

SSH is the front door of nearly every Linux server, which is why its logs show up in almost every Linux investigation. Among them: brute force (T1110), logins with stolen credentials (T1078) and lateral movement over SSH (T1021.004). Below is how to find your sshd logs, export them, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

TL;DR

Distro familyLog fileJournal commandDebian, Ubuntu/var/log/auth.logjournalctl -u sshRHEL, Rocky, Alma, CentOS Stream/var/log/securejournalctl -u sshdFedora, Arch, minimal installs without rsyslognone by defaultjournalctl -u sshd Before you start: can you actually read them?

Authentication logs are locked down on purpose, so a regular account usually gets nothing back.

  • /var/log/auth.log on Debian and Ubuntu is readable by root and the adm group.
  • /var/log/secure on the Red Hat family is root-only.
  • The system journal is open to root and to members of systemd-journal, adm and wheel. Everyone else sees only their own user journal. If you run journalctl -u ssh as a normal user, you get an empty result and a hint that you’re not seeing messages from other users. That’s permissions, not a quiet server.

The simple fix is sudo. If you’re setting up an account just for log collection, add it to adm or systemd-journal instead of handing out root. Our [Linux log permissions guide] covers the details.

One more thing before you copy anything off a server: auth logs contain usernames, source IPs and hostnames. LogTotal sanitizes uploads, but check your data-handling policy first.

Step 1: File, journal, or both?

The table above shows the defaults, and defaults are exactly what cloud images and hardening scripts like to change. Spend ten seconds checking:

ls -l /var/log/auth.log /var/log/secure 2>/dev/null
systemctl is-active rsyslog

If a file shows up and rsyslog is active, you have both: rsyslog copies messages out of the journal into a plain text file. Either source works, and the file is easier to copy around.

If there’s no file, rsyslog simply isn’t installed. That’s the norm now: since Debian 12, rsyslog is no longer part of a default install, so a fresh Debian box has no auth.log at all. Fedora and Arch have worked this way for years. Go to Step 2b.

While you’re here, check whether the journal survives a reboot:

ls -d /var/log/journal

If that directory doesn’t exist, journald keeps logs in memory under /run/log/journal, and a reboot wipes them. On a machine you’re investigating, that’s worth knowing before anyone decides to “just restart it.”

One more point for incident work: if the box might be compromised, its local logs might be too. Wiping or editing auth.log is a classic cleanup step. If the server forwards logs to a SIEM, export from there as well and compare. Our [Splunk export guide] shows how.

Step 2a: Export from auth.log or secure

The current file only covers the last few days. Older entries sit in rotated files next to it. On Debian and Ubuntu they look like auth.log.1, auth.log.2.gz, and so on. On the Red Hat family they carry a date, like secure-20261012. If the incident started last week, you need those too.

This pulls sshd lines from the current and rotated files, oldest first, into one file:

# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo zgrep -h ‘sshd’ $(ls -tr /var/log/auth.log*) > web-03_sshd.log

# RHEL / Rocky / Alma
sudo zgrep -h ‘sshd’ $(ls -tr /var/log/secure*) > web-03_sshd.log

zgrep reads plain and gzipped files alike, so you don’t have to unpack anything. ls -tr sorts by modification time, so the oldest file goes first and the output stays roughly chronological. The sshd pattern also matches sshd-session, which matters on newer systems (see Step 2b).

Why filter at all? Besides cutting noise, auth.log also records sudo, and sudo lines include full command lines. People do occasionally type passwords into those. Filtering to sshd keeps that out of the file. The exception is when you’re investigating what an attacker did after logging in. Then you want the sudo lines too: take the whole file and let LogTotal’s sanitize step do its job.

Quick check before you upload:

wc -l web-03_sshd.log
head -3 web-03_sshd.log; tail -3 web-03_sshd.log

Look at the timestamps. Depending on the rsyslog config, they’re either classic syslog (Oct 19 10:15:01, no year, no time zone) or full ISO 8601. If they’re classic, write down the server’s time zone (timedatectl). You’ll need it the moment you try to line these events up with anything else.

Step 2b: Export from the systemd journal

On journal-only systems, this is the whole job:

sudo journalctl -u ssh -u sshd \
  –since “2026-10-19 00:00” –until “2026-10-20 00:00” \
  –no-pager -o short-iso > web-03_sshd.log

A few choices in there are deliberate.

Both unit names. The service is called ssh on Debian and Ubuntu and sshd almost everywhere else. journalctl combines repeated -u flags with OR, so the same command works on both families.

Filter by unit, not by tag. A lot of older guides use journalctl -t sshd. Since OpenSSH 9.8, the server is split into two binaries, and per-connection messages, including logins, are tagged sshd-session instead of sshd. Filter by tag, and you lose exactly the lines you came for. This broke plenty of fail2ban and sshguard setups when 9.8 landed in 2024. RHEL 10 and other current releases ship OpenSSH 9.8 or newer. Filtering by unit catches every process that belongs to the service, whatever it’s called.

-o short-iso. It gives you a syslog-style line with a full ISO 8601 timestamp, year and time zone included, so you don’t have to guess. [PROOF: confirm LogTotal parses short-iso; if not, use the default -o short]. If you’d rather keep every journal field (PID, boot ID, hostname, and so on), use -o json, which writes one JSON object per line. The file gets bigger, but nothing is lost.

The time filters take relative values too: –since “2 hours ago” or –since yesterday. With a persistent journal, -b -1 limits output to the previous boot, which helps if the server was restarted after the incident.

Don’t copy the binary .journal files from /var/log/journal and upload those. LogTotal reads text and JSON, and journal files are neither.

What to look for once you have the file

Most sshd lines fall into a handful of patterns:

Line starts withWhat it meansFailed password for from Wrong password for an account that existsInvalid user from The username doesn’t exist; typical of scanners cycling through admin, test, oracleAccepted password for / Accepted publickey forA successful login; the publickey line also carries the key’s SHA256 fingerprintDisconnecting authenticating user … Too many authentication failuresThe client hit MaxAuthTriesConnection closed by … [preauth]Dropped before authentication, usually scanners and banner grabberspam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for userThe session actually started

The sequence worth stopping for: a run of Failed or Invalid user lines from one IP, then an Accepted from the same IP. That’s a brute force that worked. Close behind: an Accepted for a service account, from an address nobody recognizes, at an hour nobody works.

On OpenSSH 9.8 and later you may also see messages about penalties: sshd now temporarily refuses addresses that keep failing authentication. Treat them as a symptom. They tell you someone was hammering the port, not that anyone got in.

Where are SSH logs on Ubuntu?

On a standard Ubuntu install, in /var/log/auth.log, plus the journal (journalctl -u ssh). Minimal cloud images sometimes leave out rsyslog. If the file isn’t there, use the journal.

How do I see only failed SSH logins?

LogTotal sanitizes uploads before analysis and doesn’t retain files; our [sanitization guide] shows what gets masked. Your organization’s data-handling rules still come first.

items.title: Log Analysis Tools: Key Features and 10 Top Picks
items.summary: Most investigations stall on a simple question: where are the logs, and how do I get them out? On Windows, event logs sit in %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs\ as binary .evtx files. Export them from Event Viewer (right-click a log, then Save All Events As… ) or from an elevated prompt with wevtutil epl Security C:\IR\Security.evtx. On systemd-based Linux, the journal lives in /var/log/journal/ when persistent storage is enabled, or /run/log/journal/ when it is volatile, and journalctl -o json writes it out as one JSON object per line. Classic text syslog remains in /var/log/auth.log on Debian and Ubuntu, or /var/log/secure on RHEL-family hosts. Cloud and SaaS platforms expose their audit trails as JSON through the console or API. Getting the file is the easy part. The hard part starts when a single host hands you 400,000 events, the clock is running, and legal wants to know who sees the raw data. This is where the top AI-driven log analytics tools separate from plain search consoles. Some apply machine-learning models on top of a SIEM. Others, like SOC Prime’s LogTotal , match every event against a precompiled detection library and return correlated attack chains, not a list of hits. This guide covers what log analysis tools do, which features matter during incident response, ten tools worth knowing in 2026, and a step-by-step workflow for exporting Windows and Linux logs and investigating them in LogTotal. It closes with troubleshooting steps and answers to common questions. Try LogTotal, free What Are Log Analysis Tools? Log analysis tools turn machine-generated records into answers: who acted, on which asset, when, from where, and through which mechanism. They parse raw formats, normalize fields, apply detection logic, and link related events so an analyst can reconstruct an intrusion instead of reading it line by line. The category is broader than the SIEM. In a typical SOC, four kinds of tooling share the work: SIEM and security analytics platforms (Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Google SecOps, Elastic) centralize ingestion, run scheduled and streaming detections, and handle triage and case management. Security data pipelines (Cribl Stream, Fluent Bit, Vector) route, filter, and enrich events before storage, which controls ingestion cost and normalizes schemas such as ECS or OCSF. DFIR utilities (Hayabusa, Chainsaw, EvtxECmd) process collected artifacts offline, usually EVTX, and produce timelines for a single host. Snapshot analyzers such as LogTotal take an exported log set and return a full investigation without onboarding or integration work. Log analysis is also distinct from log management. Management is plumbing: collection, retention, access control, integrity. Analysis is interpretation. A team can run a clean pipeline with 12 months of retention and still miss a Kerberoasting campaign if nothing evaluates the 4769 events with RC4 encryption type 0x17. So what separates the best log analytics tools from the rest? Three things: how many formats they read without conversion, how much maintained detection content they apply, and whether they correlate isolated hits into an attack narrative. Speed and data-handling controls decide the rest, especially when the logs come from a host that was never onboarded to the SIEM. Which Features Matter, and What Do They Buy You? Feature lists on vendor pages look alike. During an incident, seven capabilities do most of the work. Native parsers. EVTX is a chunked binary format with XML event payloads, so grep is useless against it. A tool should read EVTX, JSON/NDJSON, syslog (RFC 3164 and RFC 5424), and CEF without a conversion script. Field normalization. A source IP should be the same field whether it came from a firewall, an IdP, or Sysmon Event ID 3. Schemas such as ECS and OCSF make one detection work across vendors. Maintained detection content. Sigma rules, vendor analytics, and threat-intel matches. Volume matters, but so does update cadence: a library that lags emerging TTPs by months gives false comfort. Correlation. Atomic hits rarely prove compromise. Sequence and higher-order correlation link a 4625 burst, a 4624 Type 10 logon, and a 7045 service install into one chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. Time to result. A 15-minute scheduled search over an indexed backlog is fine for monitoring. For triage of an exported log set, minutes are the budget. Data-handling controls. Logs carry usernames, hostnames, bearer tokens, and session cookies. Keyed pseudonymization before upload keeps correlation intact and keeps the DPO on board. Export and API access. Findings should leave the tool as JSON or CSV for case management, ticketing, and reporting. The benefits follow directly. Faster scoping shortens time to containment. Correlated findings cut the alert queue an analyst has to read. Event-level evidence supports regulatory reporting, such as audit-log review under PCI DSS v4.0 Requirement 10. Real telemetry also feeds detection engineering, because rules get tested against what attackers actually leave behind. 10 Log Analysis Tools You Should Know No single product covers every stage. The list below mixes platforms for continuous monitoring with tools built for the first hours of an incident. LogTotal (SOC Prime). A free, browser-based analyzer for exported log sets. It sanitizes logs locally, auto-detects EVTX, JSON/NDJSON, and syslog, matches events against roughly 1,000,000 detection rules and 13,000 threat labels, and returns ranked attack chains mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. It handles up to 1.7 million events in under a minute. Splunk Enterprise Security. The reference SIEM for many large SOCs. SPL is expressive, risk-based alerting reduces noise, and the app ecosystem covers most sources. Microsoft Sentinel. Cloud-native SIEM on Log Analytics workspaces, queried with KQL. Native connectors for Entra ID, Microsoft 365, and Defender make it the default for Microsoft-heavy estates. Google Security Operations. Formerly Chronicle. It normalizes data into the Unified Data Model (UDM), detects with YARA-L, and searches large retention windows quickly. Elastic Security. Built on Elasticsearch with the Elastic Common Schema. EQL sequence queries suit multi-step behaviors, and the detection rules are public on GitHub. Sumo Logic. A SaaS log analytics platform with a Cloud SIEM tier. Graylog. Available as open source and commercial editions. GELF inputs, processing pipelines, and stream routing make it a practical choice for mid-size teams that want to run their own stack. Wazuh. An open-source XDR and SIEM with agents for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It ships decoders and rules for file integrity monitoring, vulnerability detection, and compliance mapping. Hayabusa. Yamato Security’s Rust-based EVTX timeline generator. It applies Sigma and its own rules to offline event logs and writes CSV or JSONL timelines for single-host triage. Chainsaw. WithSecure’s Rust tool for rapid hunting across EVTX files using Sigma and built-in detection logic. It is fast, scriptable, and leaves correlation to the analyst. The pattern is clear. SIEMs excel once data is onboarded. DFIR utilities are fast but run smaller rule sets and leave correlation to the analyst. LogTotal fills the gap between them: full detection depth applied to logs that never reached the SIEM. Most investigations stall on a simple question: where are the logs, and how do I get them out? On Windows, event logs sit in %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs\ as binary .evtx files. Export them from Event Viewer (right-click a log, then Save All Events As…) or from an elevated prompt with wevtutil epl Security C:\IR\Security.evtx. On systemd-based Linux, the journal lives in /var/log/journal/ when persistent storage is enabled, or /run/log/journal/ when it is volatile, and journalctl -o json writes it out as one JSON object per line. Classic text syslog remains in /var/log/auth.log on Debian and Ubuntu, or /var/log/secure on RHEL-family hosts. Cloud and SaaS platforms expose their audit trails as JSON through the console or API.

Getting the file is the easy part. The hard part starts when a single host hands you 400,000 events, the clock is running, and legal wants to know who sees the raw data. This is where the top AI-driven log analytics tools separate from plain search consoles. Some apply machine-learning models on top of a SIEM. Others, like SOC Prime’s LogTotal, match every event against a precompiled detection library and return correlated attack chains, not a list of hits.

This guide covers what log analysis tools do, which features matter during incident response, ten tools worth knowing in 2026, and a step-by-step workflow for exporting Windows and Linux logs and investigating them in LogTotal. It closes with troubleshooting steps and answers to common questions.

Try LogTotal, free

What Are Log Analysis Tools?

Log analysis tools turn machine-generated records into answers: who acted, on which asset, when, from where, and through which mechanism. They parse raw formats, normalize fields, apply detection logic, and link related events so an analyst can reconstruct an intrusion instead of reading it line by line.

The category is broader than the SIEM. In a typical SOC, four kinds of tooling share the work:

  • SIEM and security analytics platforms (Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Google SecOps, Elastic) centralize ingestion, run scheduled and streaming detections, and handle triage and case management.
  • Security data pipelines (Cribl Stream, Fluent Bit, Vector) route, filter, and enrich events before storage, which controls ingestion cost and normalizes schemas such as ECS or OCSF.
  • DFIR utilities (Hayabusa, Chainsaw, EvtxECmd) process collected artifacts offline, usually EVTX, and produce timelines for a single host.
  • Snapshot analyzers such as LogTotal take an exported log set and return a full investigation without onboarding or integration work.

Log analysis is also distinct from log management. Management is plumbing: collection, retention, access control, integrity. Analysis is interpretation. A team can run a clean pipeline with 12 months of retention and still miss a Kerberoasting campaign if nothing evaluates the 4769 events with RC4 encryption type 0x17.

So what separates the best log analytics tools from the rest? Three things: how many formats they read without conversion, how much maintained detection content they apply, and whether they correlate isolated hits into an attack narrative. Speed and data-handling controls decide the rest, especially when the logs come from a host that was never onboarded to the SIEM.

Which Features Matter, and What Do They Buy You?

Feature lists on vendor pages look alike. During an incident, seven capabilities do most of the work.

  • Native parsers. EVTX is a chunked binary format with XML event payloads, so grep is useless against it. A tool should read EVTX, JSON/NDJSON, syslog (RFC 3164 and RFC 5424), and CEF without a conversion script.
  • Field normalization. A source IP should be the same field whether it came from a firewall, an IdP, or Sysmon Event ID 3. Schemas such as ECS and OCSF make one detection work across vendors.
  • Maintained detection content. Sigma rules, vendor analytics, and threat-intel matches. Volume matters, but so does update cadence: a library that lags emerging TTPs by months gives false comfort.
  • Correlation. Atomic hits rarely prove compromise. Sequence and higher-order correlation link a 4625 burst, a 4624 Type 10 logon, and a 7045 service install into one chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.
  • Time to result. A 15-minute scheduled search over an indexed backlog is fine for monitoring. For triage of an exported log set, minutes are the budget.
  • Data-handling controls. Logs carry usernames, hostnames, bearer tokens, and session cookies. Keyed pseudonymization before upload keeps correlation intact and keeps the DPO on board.
  • Export and API access. Findings should leave the tool as JSON or CSV for case management, ticketing, and reporting.

The benefits follow directly. Faster scoping shortens time to containment. Correlated findings cut the alert queue an analyst has to read. Event-level evidence supports regulatory reporting, such as audit-log review under PCI DSS v4.0 Requirement 10. Real telemetry also feeds detection engineering, because rules get tested against what attackers actually leave behind.

10 Log Analysis Tools You Should Know

No single product covers every stage. The list below mixes platforms for continuous monitoring with tools built for the first hours of an incident.

  1. LogTotal (SOC Prime). A free, browser-based analyzer for exported log sets. It sanitizes logs locally, auto-detects EVTX, JSON/NDJSON, and syslog, matches events against roughly 1,000,000 detection rules and 13,000 threat labels, and returns ranked attack chains mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. It handles up to 1.7 million events in under a minute.
  2. Splunk Enterprise Security. The reference SIEM for many large SOCs. SPL is expressive, risk-based alerting reduces noise, and the app ecosystem covers most sources.
  3. Microsoft Sentinel. Cloud-native SIEM on Log Analytics workspaces, queried with KQL. Native connectors for Entra ID, Microsoft 365, and Defender make it the default for Microsoft-heavy estates.
  4. Google Security Operations. Formerly Chronicle. It normalizes data into the Unified Data Model (UDM), detects with YARA-L, and searches large retention windows quickly.
  5. Elastic Security. Built on Elasticsearch with the Elastic Common Schema. EQL sequence queries suit multi-step behaviors, and the detection rules are public on GitHub.
  6. Sumo Logic. A SaaS log analytics platform with a Cloud SIEM tier.
  7. Graylog. Available as open source and commercial editions. GELF inputs, processing pipelines, and stream routing make it a practical choice for mid-size teams that want to run their own stack.
  8. Wazuh. An open-source XDR and SIEM with agents for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It ships decoders and rules for file integrity monitoring, vulnerability detection, and compliance mapping.
  9. Hayabusa. Yamato Security’s Rust-based EVTX timeline generator. It applies Sigma and its own rules to offline event logs and writes CSV or JSONL timelines for single-host triage.
  10. Chainsaw. WithSecure’s Rust tool for rapid hunting across EVTX files using Sigma and built-in detection logic. It is fast, scriptable, and leaves correlation to the analyst.

The pattern is clear. SIEMs excel once data is onboarded. DFIR utilities are fast but run smaller rule sets and leave correlation to the analyst. LogTotal fills the gap between them: full detection depth applied to logs that never reached the SIEM.

items.title: CVE-2026-111943: Go Blocks Compromised eMudhra CA Keys After Certificate Authority Incident
items.summary: A major public key infrastructure incident has triggered emergency security measures across browsers, programming language ecosystems, certificate stores, and software packages. Private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority certificates were compromised, potentially allowing unauthorized parties to create certificates that could appear trustworthy to vulnerable clients. The incident affects six TLS intermediates used for domain-validated, organization-validated, and extended-validation certificates, along with two code-signing intermediates. Because an intermediate CA can issue certificates below a trusted root, possession of its private key creates a substantially different risk from the compromise of an ordinary website certificate. An attacker could potentially create fraudulent certificates that inherit trust from the affected chain. The Go Project responded by introducing CVE-2026-111943, which addresses cases where Go applications could continue trusting certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates. Go 1.26.10 and 1.27.3 add a denylist to crypto/x509, causing certificate verification to fail when one of the known untrusted intermediate keys appears in a chain. Security teams seeking CVE-2026-111943 detection opportunities should look beyond conventional vulnerability exploitation telemetry. This incident is fundamentally about certificate trust, so defenders should monitor TLS certificate chains, unexpected certificate issuers, certificate validation failures, suspicious encrypted sessions, and software that maintains its own certificate bundle rather than relying on rapidly updated browser revocation mechanisms. SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform enables security teams to strengthen visibility into emerging threats by leveraging continuously updated detection content across diverse SIEM, EDR, and Data Lake technologies. Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic for emerging attack behaviors. Security professionals can also use Prime Architect to turn fresh threat intelligence and indicators into hunting queries and detection logic, helping teams Detect CVE-2026-111943-related exposure and investigate suspicious certificate activity across their environments. Contact Sales CVE-2026-111943 analysis The incident began on October 17, 2026, when a security researcher identified a cryptographic weakness affecting eight intermediate certificates operated by eMudhra under its emSign certificate authority infrastructure. The researcher demonstrated possession of the corresponding private keys by submitting valid signed attestations for all eight certificates to browser root programs and eMudhra. Mozilla subsequently confirmed the compromise and, importantly, reported that its engineers were able to independently recover the affected private keys without receiving details about the researcher’s method. Mozilla concluded that the underlying key-generation process was flawed and straightforward to exploit. The affected certificate authorities included: EM DV TLS CA – G3B EM DV TLS CA – G3C EM OV TLS CA – G3B EM OV TLS CA – G3C EM EV TLS CA – G3B EM EV TLS CA – G3C EM OV CS CA – G3B EM OV CS CA – G3C The first six are TLS intermediates capable of participating in certificate chains used to authenticate websites. The remaining two are code-signing intermediates. The G3B certificates were associated with eMudhra BV in the Netherlands, while the G3C certificates were associated with eMudhra Inc. in the United States. The security implications are significant. Anyone able to derive or otherwise obtain an intermediate CA private key could potentially issue certificates below that intermediate without going through the legitimate certificate authority issuance process. In the TLS context, fraudulent certificates could be used to impersonate domains if an attacker were also able to intercept or redirect a victim’s connection. Mozilla noted that such an attacker could potentially impersonate websites and read or modify traffic when positioned to intercept the connection. This makes the issue particularly relevant to adversary-in-the-middle scenarios, compromised network infrastructure, malicious proxies, or DNS and routing manipulation. However, available evidence does not demonstrate widespread abuse of fraudulent TLS certificates before the defensive response. According to Chrome Root Program findings cited by The Hacker News, no TLS certificate chaining to the six affected website intermediates had appeared in Certificate Transparency logs before Chrome blocked the keys. Because Chrome and other browsers requiring CT logging would normally reject an unlogged publicly trusted certificate, this significantly limited opportunities for undetected public TLS abuse through those clients. Chrome received the report at 18:05 UTC on October 17 and deployed a CRLSet block for the six TLS intermediates by 19:45 UTC. Mozilla received the report later that evening and distributed a OneCRL block to standard Firefox configurations by 22:59 UTC. Firefox users receiving Remote Settings therefore gained protection without needing to manually update or restart the browser. The CVE-2026-111943 PoC situation is unusual because this is not a conventional memory-corruption or remote-code-execution vulnerability with exploit code. Instead, the researcher supplied cryptographic proof of control over all eight private keys, and Mozilla independently reproduced the key recovery, effectively demonstrating that the cryptographic failure could be exploited. The CVE itself has been assigned by the Go Project. It describes a narrower problem involving certificate validation in the Go standard library. On most platforms, Go relies on system root certificate stores. But systems where the relevant trust configuration is not updated promptly could continue accepting chains through intermediates that are no longer trustworthy. To close that gap, the Go Project added an explicit denylist to crypto/x509. The updated verification logic returns an error whenever a certificate chain contains one of the compromised intermediate public keys. CVE-2026-111943 affects Go standard library versions before 1.26.10 and the Go 1.27 branch before version 1.27.3. Applications built using affected versions may therefore require rebuilding with a patched Go release to receive the new protection. The details for CVE-2026-111943 are particularly important for application owners because browser remediation does not automatically protect every program that performs TLS validation. Many applications use language-specific or embedded certificate stores and may not consume browser revocation systems such as Chrome CRLSet or Mozilla OneCRL. The Hacker News reports that this distinction triggered updates across multiple ecosystems. Go added explicit blocking, Mozilla updated NSS, Python’s certifi certificate bundle removed the affected root, and the Rust webpki-roots ecosystem issued an update. RustSec separately identifies version 1.0.10 or newer as patched for the affected web PKI root package. The CVE-2026-111943 IOCs are therefore primarily certificate-oriented rather than traditional malware indicators such as IP addresses, domains, or file hashes. Organizations should focus on the eight affected intermediate certificate identities and the public-key hashes used by Go and other vendors to explicitly block those keys. Certificate-chain telemetry showing one of these intermediates should be treated as untrusted and investigated. CVE-2026-111943 mitigation The most important remediation for Go environments is to update to Go 1.26.10, Go 1.27.3, or a later supported release and rebuild applications that depend on Go’s TLS certificate verification. Simply upgrading the Go toolchain on a development server does not retroactively change already compiled binaries; affected applications need to be rebuilt and redeployed with the patched standard library. Organizations should also inventory applications that maintain independent CA stores or certificate bundles. Browsers such as Chrome and Firefox reacted rapidly through centralized revocation mechanisms, but command-line utilities, server applications, containers, agents, embedded devices, and language runtimes may depend on different certificate sources. Firefox users with normal configurations received the OneCRL block automatically on October 17. Mozilla additionally released Firefox 158.0.1, Firefox ESR 115.43.1, and Firefox ESR 153.5.1 to provide the updated block list to users whose policies or network environments prevented Remote Settings from functioning normally. Mozilla also released NSS 3.131.1 with changes to the trusted certificate set. Security teams should: Update Go applications and rebuild affected binaries. Update system CA bundles and language-specific trust stores. Ensure browser and operating-system certificate revocation mechanisms are functioning. Block or distrust the eight compromised intermediate certificate keys. Identify internal applications with embedded or statically packaged certificate stores. Inspect TLS telemetry for certificate chains containing the affected intermediates. Reissue legitimate certificates if existing services depend on certificate chains that have now been distrusted. Test critical services after root-store updates because removing a CA root can also break legitimate services that previously chained through it. Teams should also pay particular attention to long-lived software appliances, containers, internal developer tools, and unsupported software. These systems may continue trusting old certificate bundles long after mainstream browsers have blocked a compromised CA. Removing a root certificate may have operational consequences. Legitimate certificates chaining through that root can also stop validating even if those individual certificates were never compromised. For this reason, organizations should combine rapid distrust with dependency discovery and certificate replacement rather than assuming that trust-store removal has no availability impact. SOC teams can strengthen their defensive posture by correlating certificate validation failures, TLS interception telemetry, unusual DNS activity, unexpected proxy behavior, and certificate issuer changes. An attacker would generally require some mechanism to direct or intercept traffic before a fraudulent TLS certificate becomes useful, so certificate anomalies should be investigated alongside network-level evidence. FAQ What is CVE-2026-111943 and how does it work? CVE-2026-111943 is a security issue tracked by the Go Project in the crypto/x509 certificate verification package following the compromise of eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys. The compromised keys could potentially be used to create certificates chained through affected intermediates. Go applications relying on certificate stores that had not yet removed or revoked those intermediates could continue accepting such chains. Go addressed the risk by adding an explicit denylist that causes certificate verification to fail whenever one of the known compromised intermediate keys is encountered. When was CVE-2026-111943 first discovered? The underlying eMudhra key compromise was identified on October 17, 2026. According to Mozilla’s incident timeline, researcher Wayne discovered the cryptographic break that afternoon and reported the issue, along with proof of private-key control, to browser root programs and eMudhra. Chrome and Mozilla verified the findings within hours and began blocking the affected intermediates. CVE-2026-111943 was subsequently published by the Go Project as part of its response to residual certificate-trust risk. What is the impact of CVE-2026-111943 on systems? The principal risk is improper trust in certificate chains involving compromised intermediate CA keys. For TLS, possession of an intermediate CA private key could potentially allow fraudulent certificates to be issued for websites an attacker does not control. If the attacker can intercept or redirect network traffic and the victim’s software still trusts the affected certificate chain, this could facilitate website impersonation and potentially allow encrypted communications to be observed or altered. The compromise also included two code-signing intermediate keys, broadening concern beyond website authentication to software trust ecosystems that accept chains through those intermediates. Can CVE-2026-111943 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Exposure remains possible for software that has not received updated certificate distrust information. Standard Chrome and Firefox installations received rapid protection, but Go applications compiled with vulnerable standard-library versions, applications using outdated independent CA bundles, unsupported software, embedded systems, or environments where certificate revocation mechanisms are disabled may continue trusting the compromised certificate paths. Organizations should therefore not assume that updating their web browsers alone eliminates the risk. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-111943? Upgrade to Go 1.26.10, Go 1.27.3, or newer and rebuild affected Go applications. Update operating-system and application trust stores, browser versions, language-specific certificate bundles, and other software that performs TLS verification. Organizations should also verify that the eight compromised intermediates are no longer trusted, inspect certificate-chain telemetry for their presence, and identify applications that carry static or embedded CA bundles. If legitimate services currently depend on chains affected by the emergency distrust actions, replace those certificates with chains anchored in unaffected certificate authorities.

The CVE-2026-111943 PoC situation is unusual because this is not a conventional memory-corruption or remote-code-execution vulnerability with exploit code. Instead, the researcher supplied cryptographic proof of control over all eight private keys, and Mozilla independently reproduced the key recovery, effectively demonstrating that the cryptographic failure could be exploited.

The CVE itself has been assigned by the Go Project. It describes a narrower problem involving certificate validation in the Go standard library. On most platforms, Go relies on system root certificate stores. But systems where the relevant trust configuration is not updated promptly could continue accepting chains through intermediates that are no longer trustworthy.

To close that gap, the Go Project added an explicit denylist to crypto/x509. The updated verification logic returns an error whenever a certificate chain contains one of the compromised intermediate public keys.

CVE-2026-111943 affects Go standard library versions before 1.26.10 and the Go 1.27 branch before version 1.27.3. Applications built using affected versions may therefore require rebuilding with a patched Go release to receive the new protection.

The details for CVE-2026-111943 are particularly important for application owners because browser remediation does not automatically protect every program that performs TLS validation. Many applications use language-specific or embedded certificate stores and may not consume browser revocation systems such as Chrome CRLSet or Mozilla OneCRL.

The Hacker News reports that this distinction triggered updates across multiple ecosystems. Go added explicit blocking, Mozilla updated NSS, Python’s certifi certificate bundle removed the affected root, and the Rust webpki-roots ecosystem issued an update. RustSec separately identifies version 1.0.10 or newer as patched for the affected web PKI root package.

The CVE-2026-111943 IOCs are therefore primarily certificate-oriented rather than traditional malware indicators such as IP addresses, domains, or file hashes. Organizations should focus on the eight affected intermediate certificate identities and the public-key hashes used by Go and other vendors to explicitly block those keys. Certificate-chain telemetry showing one of these intermediates should be treated as untrusted and investigated.

CVE-2026-111943 mitigation

The most important remediation for Go environments is to update to Go 1.26.10, Go 1.27.3, or a later supported release and rebuild applications that depend on Go’s TLS certificate verification. Simply upgrading the Go toolchain on a development server does not retroactively change already compiled binaries; affected applications need to be rebuilt and redeployed with the patched standard library.

Organizations should also inventory applications that maintain independent CA stores or certificate bundles. Browsers such as Chrome and Firefox reacted rapidly through centralized revocation mechanisms, but command-line utilities, server applications, containers, agents, embedded devices, and language runtimes may depend on different certificate sources.

Firefox users with normal configurations received the OneCRL block automatically on October 17. Mozilla additionally released Firefox 158.0.1, Firefox ESR 115.43.1, and Firefox ESR 153.5.1 to provide the updated block list to users whose policies or network environments prevented Remote Settings from functioning normally. Mozilla also released NSS 3.131.1 with changes to the trusted certificate set.

Security teams should:

  • Update Go applications and rebuild affected binaries.
  • Update system CA bundles and language-specific trust stores.
  • Ensure browser and operating-system certificate revocation mechanisms are functioning.
  • Block or distrust the eight compromised intermediate certificate keys.
  • Identify internal applications with embedded or statically packaged certificate stores.
  • Inspect TLS telemetry for certificate chains containing the affected intermediates.
  • Reissue legitimate certificates if existing services depend on certificate chains that have now been distrusted.
  • Test critical services after root-store updates because removing a CA root can also break legitimate services that previously chained through it.

Teams should also pay particular attention to long-lived software appliances, containers, internal developer tools, and unsupported software. These systems may continue trusting old certificate bundles long after mainstream browsers have blocked a compromised CA.

Removing a root certificate may have operational consequences. Legitimate certificates chaining through that root can also stop validating even if those individual certificates were never compromised. For this reason, organizations should combine rapid distrust with dependency discovery and certificate replacement rather than assuming that trust-store removal has no availability impact.

SOC teams can strengthen their defensive posture by correlating certificate validation failures, TLS interception telemetry, unusual DNS activity, unexpected proxy behavior, and certificate issuer changes. An attacker would generally require some mechanism to direct or intercept traffic before a fraudulent TLS certificate becomes useful, so certificate anomalies should be investigated alongside network-level evidence.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-111943 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-111943 is a security issue tracked by the Go Project in the crypto/x509 certificate verification package following the compromise of eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys. The compromised keys could potentially be used to create certificates chained through affected intermediates. Go applications relying on certificate stores that had not yet removed or revoked those intermediates could continue accepting such chains. Go addressed the risk by adding an explicit denylist that causes certificate verification to fail whenever one of the known compromised intermediate keys is encountered.

When was CVE-2026-111943 first discovered?

The underlying eMudhra key compromise was identified on October 17, 2026. According to Mozilla’s incident timeline, researcher Wayne discovered the cryptographic break that afternoon and reported the issue, along with proof of private-key control, to browser root programs and eMudhra. Chrome and Mozilla verified the findings within hours and began blocking the affected intermediates. CVE-2026-111943 was subsequently published by the Go Project as part of its response to residual certificate-trust risk.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-111943 on systems?

The principal risk is improper trust in certificate chains involving compromised intermediate CA keys. For TLS, possession of an intermediate CA private key could potentially allow fraudulent certificates to be issued for websites an attacker does not control. If the attacker can intercept or redirect network traffic and the victim’s software still trusts the affected certificate chain, this could facilitate website impersonation and potentially allow encrypted communications to be observed or altered. The compromise also included two code-signing intermediate keys, broadening concern beyond website authentication to software trust ecosystems that accept chains through those intermediates.

Can CVE-2026-111943 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Exposure remains possible for software that has not received updated certificate distrust information. Standard Chrome and Firefox installations received rapid protection, but Go applications compiled with vulnerable standard-library versions, applications using outdated independent CA bundles, unsupported software, embedded systems, or environments where certificate revocation mechanisms are disabled may continue trusting the compromised certificate paths. Organizations should therefore not assume that updating their web browsers alone eliminates the risk.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-111943?

Upgrade to Go 1.26.10, Go 1.27.3, or newer and rebuild affected Go applications. Update operating-system and application trust stores, browser versions, language-specific certificate bundles, and other software that performs TLS verification. Organizations should also verify that the eight compromised intermediates are no longer trusted, inspect certificate-chain telemetry for their presence, and identify applications that carry static or embedded CA bundles. If legitimate services currently depend on chains affected by the emergency distrust actions, replace those certificates with chains anchored in unaffected certificate authorities.

items.title: PHP2Shell Vulnerability Gets a Public PoC Exploit for Security Testing
items.summary: A public proof-of-concept repository shares verification tools and a lab setup to test two critical PHP vulnerabilities known as php2shell. The flaws, tracked by researchers as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are reported to affect PHP’s session.upload_progress feature and could lead to remote code execution under certain conditions. The release adds technical detail to a fast-moving security issue. PHP’s security team announced that an emergency release would address two critical vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, and urged users to prepare to upgrade. Its notice scheduled the release for October 21 at 14:00 UTC. At the time of writing, that release time has not yet passed, so PHP’s official notice has not confirmed the technical details, affected versions or fixed builds described in the research repository. The repository says the vulnerabilities affect PHP versions 5.4.0 through 8.5.11. It lists PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12 as planned fixed versions, but administrators should verify these against the PHP team’s release advisory before updating. The PHP project’s advance notice confirms the severity and planned release, but not those version details. PHP branch Current support status PHP 8.2 Security fixes only PHP 8.3 Security fixes only PHP 8.4 Active support PHP 8.5 Active support These are the branches eligible for official security updates. PHP 8.1 and older—including PHP 8.0, 7.x, and 5.x—are end-of-life and will not receive official PHP project fixes. PHP2Shell Vulnerability PoC Exploit The researcher’s write-up describes several paths to code execution, rather than one universal exploit that works against every PHP website. One chain combines session-file injection with a local file inclusion flaw in an application. According to the repository, this path depends on upload progress being enabled and an application flaw that allows a local file to be included. A local file inclusion bug occurs when an application can be made to load a file from its server in an unintended way. The repository says PHP’s upload-progress handler stores a supplied filename in session data without validating it. It also reports that a session identifier sent in a POST body can bypass the session.use_only_cookies setting, which is meant to restrict how session IDs are accepted. These claims describe how a weakness in PHP’s session handling could combine with a separate application bug. They should not be taken to mean that every PHP site is immediately exploitable through this route. A second reported issue involves a use-after-free, a memory error that can occur when software continues to use data after it has been released. The researcher says that re-entry into a var_destroy destructor can trigger this condition and reports confirming it with AddressSanitizer, a tool used to find memory errors. The repository also describes a PHP-FPM serializer state that may persist across requests, and a handler mismatch that may cause a destructor to run after deserialization fails. The researchers say some of these paths need additional conditions, such as an application gadget or access to a local file. These technical claims remain those of the independent research project until they can be compared with PHP’s full advisory and patches. Security teams should avoid treating every listed path as independently confirmed for all versions or configurations. The project’s verification repository provides the research overview and lab files. Its stated purpose is controlled testing, not use against systems without permission. PHP runs a wide range of websites and applications, so a flaw in its core session handling could affect many types of deployments. The risk can be greater when an application already has a file inclusion weakness or unsafe deserialization behavior. Mallory report highlights the scale of outdated PHP deployments as administrators prepare for the php2shell security updates. Using Shodan data collected on October 20, the company identified 883,717 internet-facing hosts running PHP 8.1 or earlier. These represent about 59% of the roughly 1.5 million hosts that disclosed a PHP version. Those branches no longer receive official PHP project security fixes, making migration to a supported release a key concern. PHP hosts Counts (Source: Mallory) As previous PHP security coverage has shown, memory errors in PHP components can have a serious impact, though the technical causes differ. This report also covers another example of application-level risk on ScriptCase vulnerabilities . The reported score of 9.2 signals a critical issue, but it does not tell administrators whether a particular server is exposed. That depends on the PHP version, configuration, application behavior, and whether the necessary conditions for a specific chain exist. The public repository includes a PHP-FPM and Nginx lab for testing. Organizations should use such environments only for authorized validation and should not run proof-of-concept code against production systems. Administrators should inventory PHP installations across web servers, containers and managed hosting environments, then check the official PHP security release for confirmed affected and fixed versions. Once a suitable update is available, apply it promptly and restart PHP-FPM or the relevant web service so the new binaries take effect. Systems running end-of-life PHP branches require special attention because they may not receive official fixes. The repository identifies PHP 5.x, 7.x, 8.0 and 8.1 as unsupported, but teams should confirm support status with the PHP project. The researcher lists disabling session.upload_progress and setting session.use_only_cookies to On as temporary safeguards. These settings may reduce exposure to some reported paths, but the repository warns that they do not address every attack chain. They are not a substitute for a security update. Review applications for local file inclusion and unsafe deserialization issues, and check server logs for unusual requests involving PHP session handling while the official advisory is being reviewed. For now, the public proof-of-concept is best treated as a signal to prepare and validate safely. The key next step is to compare the research claims with PHP’s official release details, then patch affected systems as soon as the project publishes confirmed fixed versions.
